ANNs have already begun to reveal how particular behaviors can be optimally solved, generating hypotheses about how observed neural activity might drive behavior and explaining diversity in behavioral strategies.

papers.title: Modeling Latent Attention Within Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we visualize the latent attention mechanisms of arbitrary neural networks to understand their decision-making processes and failure modes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Latent Attention Networks (LAN), a dataset-centric method for visualizing latent attention in arbitrary neural networks by learning an auxiliary network that produces attention masks via selective replaceability of input components with noise.
papers.conclusion: Latent Attention Networks provide a framework for capturing latent attention mechanisms in arbitrary neural networks, offering insights into their decision-making processes and enabling diagnosis of failure modes.
papers.key_findings:
LAN attention masks reveal that a Translated MNIST classifier uses a two-stage process: first detecting the digit location and then classifying it, which explains failure modes in regions without the constant grid pattern.
For CIFAR-10, LAN masks highlight class-specific visual features (e.g., tail feathers for birds, hulls/masts for ships) that the classifier uses for discrimination.
In document classification (Newsgroup-20), LAN masks identify words relevant to the document's topic, even if not present in the document, though capacity limitations may affect performance.
Sample-specific attention masks provide more nuanced, sample-level insights compared to network-wide LAN masks.
The method can diagnose failure modes, as demonstrated by the tank detection example where the classifier incorrectly relies on clouds instead of tanks.
papers.limitation:
The fully-connected LAN architecture may have capacity limitations on high-dimensional, poorly structured input spaces like bag-of-words representations.
The choice of noise distribution (constant vs bootstrapped) affects the attention masks, and better mechanisms for generating noise could improve LAN performance.
future_direction: Simultaneously training the pre-trained network F and the LAN A as adversaries to encourage specific attention mechanisms and speed up learning.
Learning the noise distribution as part of the network to eliminate the need for choosing a specific type of noise at design time.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are able to solve tasks across a variety of domains and modalities of data. Despite many empirical successes, we lack the ability to clearly understand and interpret the learned internal mechanisms that contribute to such effective behaviors or, more critically, failure modes. In this work, we present a general method for visualizing an arbitrary neural network's inner mechanisms and their power and limitations. Our dataset-centric method produces visualizations of how a trained network attends to components of its inputs. The computed "attention masks" support improved interpretability by highlighting which input attributes are critical in determining output. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on a variety of deep neural network architectures in domains from computer vision, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning. The primary contribution of our approach is an interpretable visualization of attention that provides unique insights into the network's underlying decision-making process irrespective of the data modality.

papers.title: Activation Steering for Bias Mitigation: An Interpretable Approach to Safer LLMs
papers.research_question: Can bias in large language models be detected and mitigated by probing internal activations and applying steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interpretability-based system that uses linear probes to detect bias in LLM activations and applies steering vectors to mitigate biased outputs in real-time.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that bias can be detected and mitigated through activation steering, offering a transparent method for improving LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on internal activations can detect bias with near-perfect accuracy in later layers of gpt2-large.
Bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers, as shown by increasing probe accuracy.
Steering vectors computed from activation differences can successfully alter biased completions toward more neutral alternatives during inference.
The method provides a direct and interpretable approach to bias mitigation without modifying model weights.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted only on gpt2-large, limiting generalizability to other models.
The training dataset is synthetic, which may not fully represent real-world bias.
future_direction: Investigate whether findings generalize to other model architectures and sizes (e.g., Llama, Mistral).
Validate techniques on real-world datasets of hate speech or bias (e.g., HateXplain, CivilComments).
Explore the use of non-linear probes or more sophisticated steering techniques for more precise control.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more integrated into societal systems, the risk of them perpetuating and amplifying harmful biases becomes a critical safety concern. Traditional methods for mitigating bias often rely on data filtering or post-hoc output moderation, which treat the model as an opaque black box. In this work, we introduce a complete, end-to-end system that uses techniques from mechanistic interpretability to both identify and actively mitigate bias directly within a model's internal workings. Our method involves two primary stages. First, we train linear "probes" on the internal activations of a model to detect the latent representations of various biases (e.g., gender, race, age). Our experiments on \texttt{gpt2-large} demonstrate that these probes can identify biased content with near-perfect accuracy, revealing that bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers. Second, we leverage these findings to compute "steering vectors" by contrasting the model's activation patterns for biased and neutral statements. By adding these vectors during inference, we can actively steer the model's generative process away from producing harmful, stereotypical, or biased content in real-time. We demonstrate the efficacy of this activation steering technique, showing that it successfully alters biased completions toward more neutral alternatives. We present our work as a robust and reproducible system that offers a more direct and interpretable approach to building safer and more accountable LLMs.

papers.title: How Important Is a Neuron?
papers.research_question: How can we attribute the importance of hidden units (neurons) in a deep network to the network's prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces conductance, a method to extend attribution from input features to hidden units by decomposing Integrated Gradients via the chain rule, and demonstrates its theoretical properties and empirical effectiveness.
papers.conclusion: Conductance is an effective method for understanding the importance of hidden units in deep networks, providing insights into their internal workings.
papers.key_findings:
Conductance satisfies theoretical properties like completeness and linearity, and is appropriately insensitive.
In an object recognition network (Inception on ImageNet), conductance identifies a small number of high-conductance filters (5-10 out of 5484) that account for the classification for an input; ablating these filters changes the prediction.
In a sentiment analysis network, conductance reveals that most filters exclusively capture either positive or negative sentiment (division of labour), and identifies filters dedicated to handling negation.
Conductance outperforms activation, gradient*activation, and internal influence methods in ablation studies and feature selection tasks.
papers.abstract: The problem of attributing a deep network's prediction to its \emph{input/base} features is well-studied. We introduce the notion of \emph{conductance} to extend the notion of attribution to the understanding the importance of \emph{hidden} units. Informally, the conductance of a hidden unit of a deep network is the \emph{flow} of attribution via this hidden unit. We use conductance to understand the importance of a hidden unit to the prediction for a specific input, or over a set of inputs. We evaluate the effectiveness of conductance in multiple ways, including theoretical properties, ablation studies, and a feature selection task. The empirical evaluations are done using the Inception network over ImageNet data, and a sentiment analysis network over reviews. In both cases, we demonstrate the effectiveness of conductance in identifying interesting insights about the internal workings of these networks.

papers.title: On the Biology of a Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The model performs genuine two-hop reasoning with intermediate steps, such as representing 'Texas' when answering about the capital of the state containing Dallas.
In poetry generation, the model plans ahead by pre-selecting rhyming words before writing each line.
Multilingual circuits use a mix of language-specific and abstract, language-independent components, with more abstraction in larger models.
Entity recognition circuits distinguish known and unknown entities, influencing when the model answers or refuses, with circuit misfires causing hallucinations.
Refusal mechanisms involve harmful request features aggregated from pretraining and trigger refusal during fine-tuning.
papers.limitation:
tools provide satisfying insight for about a quarter of prompts
replacement model incompletely and imperfectly captures the original model
future_direction: Developing more effective unsupervised exploration tools for increasingly capable models
papers.abstract: How do large language models internally perform computations, and can we reverse engineer their mechanisms using attribution graphs? This work applies attribution graphs to Claude 3.5 Haiku, uncovering sophisticated internal mechanisms like multi-step reasoning, planning, and metacognitive circuits, demonstrating the value of unsupervised tools for model interpretability. Attribution graphs enable detailed reverse engineering of model internals, revealing complex strategies and advancing the field of AI interpretability.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Enable Scalable and Reliable Circuit Identification in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and robustly discover interpretable circuits in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method for circuit identification using discrete sparse autoencoders trained on attention head outputs, which is more efficient and robust than existing techniques.
papers.conclusion: Discrete sparse autoencoders offer a scalable, efficient, and robust approach for circuit identification in large language models, providing a promising direction for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The method outperforms or matches state-of-the-art circuit identification techniques (ACDC, HISP, SP) in precision and recall on three tasks (IOI, Greater-than, Docstring).
The method is robust to hyperparameter choices and requires only 5-10 text examples per task to learn robust representations.
The identified circuits can match or even outperform the full model's performance on the specific tasks with fewer components.
The method can identify negative components in circuits (e.g., negative name-mover heads in IOI) that other algorithms struggle to find.
The process is significantly faster, reducing runtime from hours to seconds compared to existing methods.
papers.limitation: The method currently only analyzes attention heads and not other components like MLP layers, which may be important for some circuits (e.g., Greater-than).
future_direction: Extending the method to analyze MLP layers and other model components.
Applying the method to larger models and more complex tasks.
Exploring the use of vector-quantized variational autoencoders (VQ-VAEs) as an alternative to sparse autoencoders.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces an efficient and robust method for discovering interpretable circuits in large language models using discrete sparse autoencoders. Our approach addresses key limitations of existing techniques, namely computational complexity and sensitivity to hyperparameters. We propose training sparse autoencoders on carefully designed positive and negative examples, where the model can only correctly predict the next token for the positive examples. We hypothesise that learned representations of attention head outputs will signal when a head is engaged in specific computations. By discretising the learned representations into integer codes and measuring the overlap between codes unique to positive examples for each head, we enable direct identification of attention heads involved in circuits without the need for expensive ablations or architectural modifications. On three well-studied tasks - indirect object identification, greater-than comparisons, and docstring completion - the proposed method achieves higher precision and recall in recovering ground-truth circuits compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while reducing runtime from hours to seconds. Notably, we require only 5-10 text examples for each task to learn robust representations. Our findings highlight the promise of discrete sparse autoencoders for scalable and efficient mechanistic interpretability, offering a new direction for analysing the inner workings of large language models.

papers.title: Microsaccade-Inspired Probing: Positional Encoding Perturbations Reveal LLM Misbehaviours
papers.research_question: Do LLMs inherently encode the knowledge required to identify their own misbehaviours?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a lightweight probing method (MIP) that perturbs positional encodings to detect various LLM misbehaviours (factuality, jailbreaks, toxicity, backdoors) without fine-tuning or task-specific supervision.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained LLMs already encode internal evidence needed to flag their own failures, and microsaccade-inspired positional encoding perturbations provide an efficient, general pathway for detecting and mitigating undesirable behaviours.
papers.key_findings:
MIP achieves near-perfect detection on jailbreak and backdoor tasks (AUC/ACC up to 1.0).
MIP reliably discriminates between truthful and deceptive completions in factuality tasks, outperforming baselines on several datasets.
Toxicity detection is more challenging for MIP, with weaker performance, as toxicity is encoded in more diffuse, context-dependent representations.
Perturbations reveal that misbehaviours are associated with localized deviations in attention patterns, particularly in mid-to-late layers.
The method is computationally efficient (O(1) intervention complexity) and model-agnostic.
papers.limitation: Toxicity detection performance is comparatively weaker, as toxicity is encoded in more diffuse, context-dependent representations, making it less amenable to lightweight perturbation-based probing.
papers.abstract: We draw inspiration from microsaccades, tiny involuntary eye movements that reveal hidden dynamics of human perception, to propose an analogous probing method for large language models (LLMs). Just as microsaccades expose subtle but informative shifts in vision, we show that lightweight position encoding perturbations elicit latent signals that indicate model misbehaviour. Our method requires no fine-tuning or task-specific supervision, yet detects failures across diverse settings including factuality, safety, toxicity, and backdoor attacks. Experiments on multiple state-of-the-art LLMs demonstrate that these perturbation-based probes surface misbehaviours while remaining computationally efficient. These findings suggest that pretrained LLMs already encode the internal evidence needed to flag their own failures, and that microsaccade-inspired interventions provide a pathway for detecting and mitigating undesirable behaviours.

papers.title: Properties from Mechanisms: An Equivariance Perspective on Identifiable\n Representation Learning
papers.research_question: Can we identify latent properties by leveraging knowledge of the mechanisms that govern their evolution?
papers.core_contribution: If we know the exact mechanisms under which latent properties evolve, then identification can be achieved up to any equivariances that are shared by the underlying mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: By exploiting inductive biases on mechanisms, it is possible to design a range of new identifiable representation learning approaches.
papers.key_findings:
When the true mechanism is known, the system is identified up to any equivariances of the mechanism.
With multiple known mechanisms, identification is up to equivariances shared by all mechanisms.
When only a hypothesis class of possible mechanisms is known, additional non-identifiability arises via imitation among mechanisms.
For affine mechanisms with distinct eigenvalues and certain conditions, identification is up to an offset.
The framework generalizes to stochastic mechanisms and can recover existing identifiability results, such as those in Klindt et al. (2020).
papers.limitation: The analysis assumes the encoder/decoder functions are bijective and that reconstruction is perfectly solved, which is a strong assumption and not easy in practice.
papers.abstract:
A key goal of unsupervised representation learning is "inverting" a data
generating process to recover its latent properties. Existing work that
provably achieves this goal relies on strong assumptions on relationships
between the latent variables (e.g., independence conditional on auxiliary
information). In this paper, we take a very different perspective on the
problem and ask, "Can we instead identify latent properties by leveraging
knowledge of the mechanisms that govern their evolution?" We provide a complete
characterization of the sources of non-identifiability as we vary knowledge
about a set of possible mechanisms. In particular, we prove that if we know the
exact mechanisms under which the latent properties evolve, then identification
can be achieved up to any equivariances that are shared by the underlying
mechanisms. We generalize this characterization to settings where we only know
some hypothesis class over possible mechanisms, as well as settings where the
mechanisms are stochastic. We demonstrate the power of this mechanism-based
perspective by showing that we can leverage our results to generalize existing
identifiable representation learning results. These results suggest that by
exploiting inductive biases on mechanisms, it is possible to design a range of
new identifiable representation learning approaches.

papers.title: Random feedback weights support learning in deep neural networks
papers.research_question: Can random feedback weights support learning in deep neural networks, providing a biologically plausible alternative to backpropagation?
papers.core_contribution: Random feedback weights can support learning in deep neural networks as effectively as backpropagation, providing a biologically plausible mechanism that avoids weight transport.
papers.conclusion: Random feedback connections can transmit useful teaching signals for deep learning, offering a biologically plausible mechanism that dispels assumptions about weight transport constraints.
papers.key_findings:
Feedback alignment reduces loss as quickly as backpropagation on linear and nonlinear tasks.
The network learns to align forward weights W such that the fixed random feedback matrix B acts like W^T, enabling effective hidden unit updates.
Feedback alignment works with multiple hidden layers, building useful feature detectors in deep layers.
The algorithm exhibits elements of second-order learning, approximating pseudobackprop.
Learning remains effective even with sparse random feedback connections (50% weight removal).
papers.abstract: The brain processes information through many layers of neurons. This deep architecture is representationally powerful, but it complicates learning by making it hard to identify the responsible neurons when a mistake is made. In machine learning, the backpropagation algorithm assigns blame to a neuron by computing exactly how it contributed to an error. To do this, it multiplies error signals by matrices consisting of all the synaptic weights on the neuron's axon and farther downstream. This operation requires a precisely choreographed transport of synaptic weight information, which is thought to be impossible in the brain. Here we present a surprisingly simple algorithm for deep learning, which assigns blame by multiplying error signals by random synaptic weights. We show that a network can learn to extract useful information from signals sent through these random feedback connections. In essence, the network learns to learn. We demonstrate that this new mechanism performs as quickly and accurately as backpropagation on a variety of problems and describe the principles which underlie its function. Our demonstration provides a plausible basis for how a neuron can be adapted using error signals generated at distal locations in the brain, and thus dispels long-held assumptions about the algorithmic constraints on learning in neural circuits.

papers.title: ASGuard: Activation-Scaling Guard to Mitigate Targeted Jailbreaking Attack
papers.research_question: How can we surgically mitigate targeted jailbreaking vulnerabilities in LLMs by understanding and intervening in their internal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ASGUARD, a framework that uses circuit analysis to identify vulnerable attention heads and then applies activation scaling and preventative fine-tuning to mitigate targeted jailbreaking attacks while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: ASGUARD demonstrates how mechanistic interpretability can be leveraged to develop targeted and efficient safety interventions, achieving a superior safety-utility trade-off.
papers.key_findings:
Tense jailbreaking is mediated by specific attention heads that can be identified via circuit analysis.
ASGUARD reduces the attack success rate of tense jailbreaking from 42% to 8% in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct while maintaining high utility.
ASGUARD achieves a Pareto-optimal balance between safety and utility, outperforming baseline methods like SFT and DPO.
The method generalizes to other jailbreaking attacks like GCG and LogiBreak.
Preventative fine-tuning helps the model learn a robust refusal mechanism without relying on the vulnerable pathway.
papers.limitation:
The method requires constructing circuits for each specific attack type, which can be computationally expensive.
There is a risk of over-refusal if the scaling vectors are not properly tuned.
future_direction: Extending ASGUARD to other types of jailbreaking attacks and models.
Automating the circuit discovery process to reduce computational cost.
Exploring the application of activation scaling to other safety vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs), despite being safety-aligned, exhibit brittle refusal behaviors that can be circumvented by simple linguistic changes. As tense jailbreaking demonstrates that models refusing harmful requests often comply when rephrased in past tense, a critical generalization gap is revealed in current alignment methods whose underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. In this work, we introduce Activation-Scaling Guard (ASGuard), an insightful, mechanistically-informed framework that surgically mitigates this specific vulnerability. For the first step, we use circuit analysis to identify the specific attention heads causally linked to the targeted jailbreaking, the tense-changing attack. Second, we train a precise, channel-wise scaling vector to recalibrate the activation of tense vulnerable heads. Lastly, we apply it into a "preventative fine-tuning", forcing the model to learn a more robust refusal mechanism. Across three LLMs, ASGuard effectively reduces the attack success rate of targeted jailbreaking while preserving general capabilities and minimizing over refusal, achieving a Pareto-optimal balance between safety and utility. Our findings underscore how adversarial suffixes suppress the propagation of the refusal-mediating direction, based on mechanistic analysis. Furthermore, our work showcases how a deep understanding of model internals can be leveraged to develop practical, efficient, and targeted methods for adjusting model behavior, charting a course for more reliable and interpretable AI safety.

papers.title: Mechanistically analyzing the effects of fine-tuning on procedurally defined tasks
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining? Does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning rarely alters a model's underlying capabilities; instead, it typically learns a minimal 'wrapper' transformation on top of existing capabilities. These wrapped capabilities can be sample-efficiently revived via further fine-tuning on relevant tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily learns minimal wrapper transformations over existing model capabilities rather than creating or deleting them, which has implications for safety as wrappers can be easily removed or bypassed.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning alters pretraining capabilities by minimally transforming them via a learned 'wrapper'.
Wrappers are often extremely localized; pruning a few neurons can cause the model to revert to its pretraining capability.
Further fine-tuning on a subset of pretraining data leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the original capability.
When a weakly relevant pretraining capability is present, the model exploits spurious correlations in the fine-tuning data via the wrapper.
The presence and strength of a pretraining capability (influenced by its sampling probability during pretraining) significantly affects fine-tuning dynamics and wrapper formation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted primarily in synthetic, controlled settings (Tracr and PCFGs), which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex and realistic tasks and models.
Investigating the societal implications of the findings, particularly regarding the safety of fine-tuned models.
Exploring whether the wrapper phenomenon generalizes to other model adaptation methods beyond standard fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models has become the de facto strategy for developing both task-specific and general-purpose machine learning systems, including developing models that are safe to deploy. Despite its clear importance, there has been minimal work that explains how fine-tuning alters the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining: does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones? We address this question empirically in synthetic, controlled settings where we can use mechanistic interpretability tools (e.g., network pruning and probing) to understand how the model's underlying capabilities are changing. We perform an extensive analysis of the effects of fine-tuning in these settings, and show that: (i) fine-tuning rarely alters the underlying model capabilities; (ii) a minimal transformation, which we call a 'wrapper', is typically learned on top of the underlying model capabilities, creating the illusion that they have been modified; and (iii) further fine-tuning on a task where such hidden capabilities are relevant leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the capability, i.e., the model begins reusing these capability after only a few gradient steps. This indicates that practitioners can unintentionally remove a model's safety wrapper merely by fine-tuning it on a, e.g., superficially unrelated, downstream task. We additionally perform analysis on language models trained on the TinyStories dataset to support our claims in a more realistic setup.

papers.title: Neural networks are a priori biased towards Boolean functions with low\n entropy
papers.research_question: What is the inductive bias of neural networks towards Boolean functions with low entropy upon random initialization?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks have an a priori bias towards Boolean functions with low entropy, which increases with the number of ReLU layers and with the variance of the bias term.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks have a strong intrinsic bias towards low-entropy Boolean functions, which may contribute to their generalization ability.
papers.key_findings:
For a perceptron with no bias term and symmetric weight distribution, the probability P(t) is uniform, but individual functions with low entropy have higher probability due to fewer such functions.
Within a class of functions with fixed t, there is a further bias towards functions of lower complexity.
Adding a bias term to a perceptron increases the bias towards low entropy.
For multi-layer ReLU networks, the bias towards low entropy increases with the number of layers.
They provide an expressivity bound: a neural network with l hidden layers of width n + 2^{n-1}/l + 1 can express all Boolean functions over n variables.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical results assume symmetric weight distributions and no bias term for the perceptron.
The bias may not hold for other activation functions like tanh in the chaotic regime.
future_direction: Study the effect of different dynamic regimes for various activation functions on simplicity bias.
Investigate the effect of entropy bias on learning class-imbalanced data.
papers.abstract:
Understanding the inductive bias of neural networks is critical to explaining
their ability to generalise. Here, for one of the simplest neural networks -- a
single-layer perceptron with n input neurons, one output neuron, and no
threshold bias term -- we prove that upon random initialisation of weights, the
a priori probability $P(t)$ that it represents a Boolean function that
classifies t points in ${0,1}^n$ as 1 has a remarkably simple form: $P(t) =
2^{-n}$ for $0\leq t < 2^n$.
 Since a perceptron can express far fewer Boolean functions with small or
large values of t (low entropy) than with intermediate values of t (high
entropy) there is, on average, a strong intrinsic a-priori bias towards
individual functions with low entropy. Furthermore, within a class of functions
with fixed t, we often observe a further intrinsic bias towards functions of
lower complexity. Finally, we prove that, regardless of the distribution of
inputs, the bias towards low entropy becomes monotonically stronger upon adding
ReLU layers, and empirically show that increasing the variance of the bias term
has a similar effect.

papers.title: Do Students Debias Like Teachers? On the Distillability of Bias Mitigation Methods
papers.research_question: To what extent can knowledge distillation transfer debiasing capabilities between models? Can knowledge distillation train less biased models compared to standard training? What internal mechanisms cause the debiasing behavior change after distillation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents the first large-scale study on the effect of knowledge distillation on debiasing capabilities, showing that vanilla KD often fails to preserve debiasing and can increase student bias, and proposes three strategies to improve distillability.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents the first study on the distillability of debiasing capabilities, showing vanilla KD does not consistently preserve debiasing, and proposes three solutions (data augmentation, iterative KD, initialization) that significantly improve distillability.
papers.key_findings:
The debiasing capability of a model is undermined post-KD; students become more biased than teachers.
Training a debiased model does not benefit from injecting teacher knowledge (KD does not improve generalization).
Although overall robustness may remain stable post-distillation, significant variations occur across different bias types.
The effectiveness of debiasing transfer depends on model scale similarity; similar scales lead to better transfer.
Larger teachers do not guarantee more robust students.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are mainly conducted on logit-based knowledge distillation. The effect of other knowledge distillation methods has not been explored.
The work does not explore the scenario where multiple teachers participate in the distillation process.
future_direction: Investigate self-distilled debiasing, where the student iteratively distills knowledge from itself rather than relying on a fixed teacher, and explicitly guide the student using counterfactual data augmentation during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective method for model compression and transferring knowledge between models. However, its effect on model's robustness against spurious correlations that degrade performance on out-of-distribution data remains underexplored. This study investigates the effect of knowledge distillation on the transferability of ``debiasing'' capabilities from teacher models to student models on natural language inference (NLI) and image classification tasks. Through extensive experiments, we illustrate several key findings: (i) overall the debiasing capability of a model is undermined post-KD; (ii) training a debiased model does not benefit from injecting teacher knowledge; (iii) although the overall robustness of a model may remain stable post-distillation, significant variations can occur across different types of biases; and (iv) we pin-point the internal attention pattern and circuit that causes the distinct behavior post-KD. Given the above findings, we propose three effective solutions to improve the distillability of debiasing methods: developing high quality data for augmentation, implementing iterative knowledge distillation, and initializing student models with weights obtained from teacher models. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study on the effect of KD on debiasing and its interenal mechanism at scale. Our findings provide understandings on how KD works and how to design better debiasing methods.

papers.title: Future Lens: Anticipating Subsequent Tokens from a Single Hidden State
papers.research_question: To what extent can we extract information about future tokens (beyond the next token) from a single hidden state representation in a transformer language model?
papers.core_contribution: Hidden states in transformer language models encode information about future tokens, and a learned prompt intervention method can effectively decode this information, enabling a new visualization tool called Future Lens.
papers.conclusion: Hidden states in transformers encode information about future tokens, and the proposed methods, especially learned prompt intervention, can decode this information, providing a new tool for interpreting model internals.
papers.key_findings:
Hidden states encode information about future tokens beyond the next token.
A learned prompt intervention method is the most effective at extracting future token information from hidden states.
Predictive accuracy for future tokens peaks at middle layers, unlike next-token prediction which peaks at the last layer.
The Future Lens tool visualizes the future tokens predicted by each hidden state across layers.
The accuracy of predicting future tokens correlates with the model's confidence in its next token prediction.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted only on English data with a relatively small sample size (100,000 tokens) compared to the full training data of GPT-J-6B.
Experiments were only conducted on GPT-J-6B; testing on other LLMs would be more comprehensive.
There are no prior baselines for decoding far future tokens, so the comparison is limited to bigram and linear models.
Experiments only tested up to 4 tokens in the future (N=0,1,2,3); scaling to more tokens is an open question.
future_direction: Testing the methods on other large language models.
Scaling the experiments to predict more tokens into the future.
Comparing with other architectures like Recurrent Neural Networks or Non-Autoregressive models as baselines.
papers.abstract: We conjecture that hidden state vectors corresponding to individual input tokens encode information sufficient to accurately predict several tokens ahead. More concretely, in this paper we ask: Given a hidden (internal) representation of a single token at position $t$ in an input, can we reliably anticipate the tokens that will appear at positions $\geq t + 2$? To test this, we measure linear approximation and causal intervention methods in GPT-J-6B to evaluate the degree to which individual hidden states in the network contain signal rich enough to predict future hidden states and, ultimately, token outputs. We find that, at some layers, we can approximate a model's output with more than 48% accuracy with respect to its prediction of subsequent tokens through a single hidden state. Finally we present a "Future Lens" visualization that uses these methods to create a new view of transformer states.

papers.title: The Secret Agenda: LLMs Strategically Lie and Our Current Safety Tools Are Blind
papers.research_question: Investigates whether large language models strategically lie when incentivized and if current interpretability tools can detect such deception.
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that large language models reliably engage in strategic deception when incentivized, and that current autolabeled interpretability tools fail to detect or prevent such lying, whereas unlabeled aggregate activations show promise for compliance detection.
papers.conclusion: Strategic deception arises in LLMs under weak oversight, and current autolabeled features fail to detect or control it, while unlabeled activations offer some discriminative signal for risk assessment, motivating further research.
papers.key_findings:
Secret Agenda game elicits systematic deception across 38 models when winning is incentivized.
Autolabeled SAE features for deception rarely activate during strategic lying.
Feature steering of deception-related features fails to prevent lying in models.
Unlabeled SAE activations show discriminative patterns for insider trading compliance.
SAE effectiveness varies by domain, working better for structured ethics than adversarial deception.
papers.limitation:
Lack of compute budget for research.
Small sample sizes lacking statistical significance.
Boolean definition of deception may miss nuanced cases.
future_direction: Standardized replications
Multi-round game evaluations
Improved feature discovery and labeling
papers.abstract: We investigate strategic deception in large language models using two complementary testbeds: Secret Agenda (across 38 models) and Insider Trading compliance (via SAE architectures). Secret Agenda reliably induced lying when deception advantaged goal achievement across all model families. Analysis revealed that autolabeled SAE features for "deception" rarely activated during strategic dishonesty, and feature steering experiments across 100+ deception-related features failed to prevent lying. Conversely, insider trading analysis using unlabeled SAE activations separated deceptive versus compliant responses through discriminative patterns in heatmaps and t-SNE visualizations. These findings suggest autolabel-driven interpretability approaches fail to detect or control behavioral deception, while aggregate unlabeled activations provide population-level structure for risk assessment. Results span Llama 8B/70B SAE implementations and GemmaScope under resource constraints, representing preliminary findings that motivate larger studies on feature discovery, labeling methodology, and causal interventions in realistic deception contexts.

papers.title: Stateless Yet Not Forgetful: Implicit Memory as a Hidden Channel in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can LLMs maintain state across independent interactions via implicit memory (encoding information in outputs and recovering it upon reingestion), and what risks does this pose?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces implicit memory—the ability of LLMs to carry state across independent interactions by encoding information in outputs and recovering it upon reingestion—and demonstrates temporal backdoors (time bombs) as a concrete risk enabled by this capability.
papers.conclusion: Implicit memory is a real capability in LLMs that challenges the assumption of statelessness and introduces new risks; future work should focus on detection, mitigation, and monitoring.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning models outperform non-reasoning models in implementing implicit memory via prompting.
Fine-tuning yields stronger and more stable temporal backdoors than prompting, with higher accuracy and lower false activation rates.
Temporal backdoors are harder to detect because activation requires a sequence of interactions rather than a single trigger.
Semantic encodings are more robust to cleaning and paraphrasing defenses than zero-width character encodings.
Implicit memory expands the threat model for LLM-based systems, enabling risks like covert communication, benchmark contamination, and long-horizon manipulation.
future_direction: Stress-testing and evaluation for unintended persistence
Detection methods for implicit memory
Monitoring for organic emergence of implicit memory
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are commonly treated as stateless: once an interaction ends, no information is assumed to persist unless it is explicitly stored and re-supplied. We challenge this assumption by introducing implicit memory-the ability of a model to carry state across otherwise independent interactions by encoding information in its own outputs and later recovering it when those outputs are reintroduced as input. This mechanism does not require any explicit memory module, yet it creates a persistent information channel across inference requests. As a concrete demonstration, we introduce a new class of temporal backdoors, which we call time bombs. Unlike conventional backdoors that activate on a single trigger input, time bombs activate only after a sequence of interactions satisfies hidden conditions accumulated via implicit memory. We show that such behavior can be induced today through straightforward prompting or fine-tuning. Beyond this case study, we analyze broader implications of implicit memory, including covert inter-agent communication, benchmark contamination, targeted manipulation, and training-data poisoning. Finally, we discuss detection challenges and outline directions for stress-testing and evaluation, with the goal of anticipating and controlling future developments. To promote future research, we release code and data at: https://github.com/microsoft/implicitMemory.

papers.title: Bias Amplification: Large Language Models as Increasingly Biased Media
papers.research_question: How does political bias amplify in Large Language Models over iterative synthetic training cycles, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a benchmark for political bias amplification in LLMs, empirically demonstrates bias amplification in GPT-2 over synthetic training cycles, and uses mechanistic analysis to show that bias amplification and model collapse are driven by distinct neuron populations.
papers.conclusion: Bias amplification is driven by distinct mechanisms from model collapse, implying that mitigation strategies targeting model collapse may not address bias amplification, necessitating targeted interventions.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-2 exhibits progressive right-leaning bias amplification over iterative synthetic fine-tuning, even when starting from an unbiased dataset.
Model collapse occurs with declining text quality index over generations, while perplexity decreases misleadingly.
Mitigation strategies like Preservation and Accumulation can reduce both bias amplification and model collapse in some scenarios, but Preservation fails to prevent bias amplification when starting from a center-leaning fine-tuned model.
Mechanistic analysis identifies largely distinct neuron populations correlated with bias amplification and model collapse, suggesting different underlying mechanisms.
Bias amplification can occur independently of model collapse, as shown in alternative setups and theoretical intuition.
papers.limitation:
Scope restricted to political bias in the context of U.S. media, requiring periodic updates to the bias classifier.
Experiments conducted using GPT-2, a relatively small language model, limiting generalizability to larger architectures.
Mitigation strategies like Accumulation have high computational cost and data storage requirements.
future_direction: Extend methodology to larger language models to examine scale effects.
Refine mechanistic analysis techniques for political bias.
Develop more targeted and efficient mitigation strategies for bias amplification.
papers.abstract: Model collapse, a phenomenon characterized by performance degradation due to iterative training on synthetic data, has been widely studied. However, its implications for bias amplification, the progressive intensification of pre-existing societal biases in Large Language Models (LLMs), remain significantly underexplored, despite the growing influence of LLMs in shaping online discourse. In this paper, we introduce a open, generational, and long-context benchmark specifically designed to measure political bias amplification in LLMs, leveraging sentence continuation tasks derived from a comprehensive dataset of U.S. political news. Our empirical study using GPT-2 reveals consistent and substantial political bias intensification (e.g., right-leaning amplification) over iterative synthetic training cycles. We evaluate three mitigation strategies, Overfitting, Preservation, and Accumulation, and demonstrate that bias amplification persists independently of model collapse, even when the latter is effectively controlled. Furthermore, we propose a mechanistic analysis approach that identifies neurons correlated with specific phenomena during inference through regression and statistical tests. This analysis uncovers largely distinct neuron populations driving bias amplification and model collapse, underscoring fundamentally different underlying mechanisms. Finally, we supplement our empirical findings with theoretical intuition that explains the separate origins of these phenomena, guiding targeted strategies for bias mitigation.

papers.title: TraceRouter: Robust Safety for Large Foundation Models via Path-Level Intervention
papers.research_question: How can we achieve robust safety in large foundation models by intervening at the path level to disconnect causal propagation circuits of harmful semantics, rather than suppressing isolated neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes TraceRouter, a path-level safety intervention framework that traces and disconnects causal propagation circuits of harmful semantics in large foundation models, achieving superior adversarial robustness and utility preservation compared to neuron-level methods.
papers.conclusion: TraceRouter provides a robust and interpretable path-level intervention framework for foundation model safety, targeting the topological structure of semantic flow rather than isolated activations.
papers.key_findings:
TraceRouter outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in safety intervention across diffusion models, LLMs, and MLLMs.
Path-level intervention is more effective than neuron-level suppression because harmful semantics are distributed across cross-layer circuits.
TraceRouter preserves general utility (e.g., image fidelity, reasoning capabilities) while ensuring safety.
The identified sensitive pathways are causally validated through amplification experiments, showing they act as switches for harmful generation.
The method is architecture-agnostic and works across diverse model types.
papers.limitation: The framework's applicability to general-purpose tasks beyond safety, such as logical reasoning or creative writing, remains to be fully explored.
future_direction: Validate TraceRouter's path-level intervention across a broader spectrum of non-safety domains.
papers.abstract: Despite their capabilities, large foundation models (LFMs) remain susceptible to adversarial manipulation. Current defenses predominantly rely on the "locality hypothesis", suppressing isolated neurons or features. However, harmful semantics act as distributed, cross-layer circuits, rendering such localized interventions brittle and detrimental to utility. To bridge this gap, we propose \textbf{TraceRouter}, a path-level framework that traces and disconnects the causal propagation circuits of illicit semantics. TraceRouter operates in three stages: (1) it pinpoints a sensitive onset layer by analyzing attention divergence; (2) it leverages sparse autoencoders (SAEs) and differential activation analysis to disentangle and isolate malicious features; and (3) it maps these features to downstream causal pathways via feature influence scores (FIS) derived from zero-out interventions. By selectively suppressing these causal chains, TraceRouter physically severs the flow of harmful information while leaving orthogonal computation routes intact. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TraceRouter significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving a superior trade-off between adversarial robustness and general utility. Our code will be publicly released. WARNING: This paper contains unsafe model responses.

papers.title: Explaining Deep Learning Hidden Neuron Activations using Concept Induction
papers.research_question: How can we automatically attach meaningful, human-interpretable labels to individual hidden neurons in a deep learning system using concept induction and large-scale background knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method that uses concept induction (ECII) over a large-scale Wikipedia class hierarchy to automatically generate and verify meaningful concept labels for individual neurons in a CNN's dense layer.
papers.conclusion: The approach using ECII and Wikipedia background knowledge can successfully recognize activation patterns of neurons and assign human-interpretable concept labels to them.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method can automatically generate meaningful concept labels for hidden neurons in a CNN.
Verification using Google Images shows that neurons are activated by the presence of the identified concepts, with some neurons showing over 90% activation.
Different thresholds for defining neuron activation (positive/negative sets) have minimal impact on the final activation percentages of the identified concepts.
papers.limitation:
The method was only applied to a candidate subset of neurons (29 out of 64) and future work is needed to study the remaining neurons.
The process requires human intervention to collect verification images and is not fully automated.
future_direction: Study the remaining neurons not analyzed in this work.
Study the effect of different thresholds for defining neuron activation.
Automate the entire process of generating human-understandable explanations for a network's output.
papers.abstract: One of the current key challenges in Explainable AI is in correctly interpreting activations of hidden neurons. It seems evident that accurate interpretations thereof would provide insights into the question what a deep learning system has internally \emph{detected} as relevant on the input, thus lifting some of the black box character of deep learning systems. The state of the art on this front indicates that hidden node activations appear to be interpretable in a way that makes sense to humans, at least in some cases. Yet, systematic automated methods that would be able to first hypothesize an interpretation of hidden neuron activations, and then verify it, are mostly missing. In this paper, we provide such a method and demonstrate that it provides meaningful interpretations. It is based on using large-scale background knowledge -- a class hierarchy of approx. 2 million classes curated from the Wikipedia Concept Hierarchy -- together with a symbolic reasoning approach called \emph{concept induction} based on description logics that was originally developed for applications in the Semantic Web field. Our results show that we can automatically attach meaningful labels from the background knowledge to individual neurons in the dense layer of a Convolutional Neural Network through a hypothesis and verification process.

papers.title: Knowledge Transfer via Distillation of Activation Boundaries Formed by Hidden Neurons
papers.research_question: Can transferring activation boundaries (whether neurons are activated or not), rather than the magnitude of neuron responses, improve knowledge transfer performance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a knowledge transfer method that distills activation boundaries (neuron on/off states) from teacher to student networks, outperforming existing methods by focusing on boundary information rather than response magnitudes.
papers.conclusion: Activation boundaries are important for knowledge transfer, and the proposed method of transferring these boundaries significantly improves performance over state-of-the-art methods, potentially changing neural network training practices.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method accelerates learning and improves generalization, especially with limited training data.
It outperforms existing knowledge transfer methods (FITNET, FSP, AT, Jacobian) in various settings including learning speed, small data, and network compression.
In transfer learning, the proposed method sometimes outperforms ImageNet pre-training.
The method is effective across different network layers (low, mid, high).
The proposed alternative loss effectively approximates the ideal activation transfer loss, leading to high similarity in neuron activations between teacher and student.
future_direction: Applying the method to various tasks that originally relied on pre-training for better performance and learning speed.
papers.abstract: An activation boundary for a neuron refers to a separating hyperplane that determines whether the neuron is activated or deactivated. It has been long considered in neural networks that the activations of neurons, rather than their exact output values, play the most important role in forming classificationfriendly partitions of the hidden feature space. However, as far as we know, this aspect of neural networks has not been considered in the literature of knowledge transfer. In this paper, we propose a knowledge transfer method via distillation of activation boundaries formed by hidden neurons. For the distillation, we propose an activation transfer loss that has the minimum value when the boundaries generated by the student coincide with those by the teacher. Since the activation transfer loss is not differentiable, we design a piecewise differentiable loss approximating the activation transfer loss. By the proposed method, the student learns a separating boundary between activation region and deactivation region formed by each neuron in the teacher. Through the experiments in various aspects of knowledge transfer, it is verified that the proposed method outperforms the current state-of-the-art.

papers.title: Analyzing And Editing Inner Mechanisms Of Backdoored Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms of backdoored language models and how do they process trigger inputs, such as switching to toxic language?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PCP ablation, a method to analyze and edit backdoor mechanisms in language models, and identifies early-layer MLP modules as crucial for the backdoor mechanism in combination with the initial embedding projection.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that PCP ablation is an effective tool for understanding and editing backdoor mechanisms in language models, and that constraining specific modules during fine-tuning can enhance model robustness against backdoor attacks.
papers.key_findings:
Early-layer MLP modules are most important for the backdoor mechanism in transformer-based language models, in combination with the initial embedding projection.
PCP ablation can be used to remove, insert, and modify backdoor mechanisms by replacing transformer modules with low-rank matrices based on principal components of their activations.
The backdoor robustness of large language models can be improved by locally constraining individual modules (e.g., freezing weights) during fine-tuning on potentially poisonous datasets.
In toy models, the backdoor mechanism can be successfully replicated and edited using low-rank PCP ablations of MLP modules.
In large models, PCP ablation can partially reinsert or weaken the backdoor mechanism, though with limitations due to the simplicity of the linear replacement.
papers.limitation: The introduced PCP ablation technique only corrects the ASR tendency and leads to an increase in validation loss, due to the simplicity and linearity of the replacement.
papers.abstract: Poisoning of data sets is a potential security threat to large language models that can lead to backdoored models. A description of the internal mechanisms of backdoored language models and how they process trigger inputs, e.g., when switching to toxic language, has yet to be found. In this work, we study the internal representations of transformer-based backdoored language models and determine early-layer MLP modules as most important for the backdoor mechanism in combination with the initial embedding projection. We use this knowledge to remove, insert, and modify backdoor mechanisms with engineered replacements that reduce the MLP module outputs to essentials for the backdoor mechanism. To this end, we introduce PCP ablation, where we replace transformer modules with low-rank matrices based on the principal components of their activations. We demonstrate our results on backdoored toy, backdoored large, and non-backdoored open-source models. We show that we can improve the backdoor robustness of large language models by locally constraining individual modules during fine-tuning on potentially poisonous data sets. Trigger warning: Offensive language.

papers.title: NeuronTune: Towards Self-Guided Spurious Bias Mitigation
papers.research_question: How can spurious bias in deep neural networks be mitigated without requiring external annotations of spurious correlations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes NeuronTune, a self-guided post hoc method that identifies and suppresses neurons affected by spurious bias in a model's latent space, improving worst-group accuracy without requiring group labels.
papers.conclusion: NeuronTune is a lightweight, self-guided post hoc method that effectively mitigates spurious bias by directly intervening in a model's internal decision process, validated theoretically and empirically across diverse datasets and architectures.
papers.key_findings:
NeuronTune effectively mitigates spurious bias across different model architectures (ResNet, BERT) and data modalities (image, text).
The method outperforms existing sample-level and last-layer retraining methods in worst-group accuracy on multiple benchmarks.
Theoretical analysis shows that neuron activations coupled with prediction outcomes provide self-identifying information for biased dimensions, and NeuronTune brings the model closer to an unbiased solution.
NeuronTune is computationally efficient as it only requires tuning the last layer of the model.
The method operates without external supervision (group labels), making it practical for standard ERM training settings.
papers.limitation: NeuronTune may not fully address spurious bias if the feature extractor is already biased, as it only retrains the last layer.
future_direction: Exploring different choices of identification data and model tuning data to enhance spurious bias mitigation.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks often develop spurious bias, reliance on correlations between non-essential features and classes for predictions. For example, a model may identify objects based on frequently co-occurring backgrounds rather than intrinsic features, resulting in degraded performance on data lacking these correlations. Existing mitigation approaches typically depend on external annotations of spurious correlations, which may be difficult to obtain and are not relevant to the spurious bias in a model. In this paper, we take a step towards self-guided mitigation of spurious bias by proposing NeuronTune, a post hoc method that directly intervenes in a model's internal decision process. Our method probes in a model's latent embedding space to identify and regulate neurons that lead to spurious prediction behaviors. We theoretically justify our approach and show that it brings the model closer to an unbiased one. Unlike previous methods, NeuronTune operates without requiring spurious correlation annotations, making it a practical and effective tool for improving model robustness. Experiments across different architectures and data modalities demonstrate that our method significantly mitigates spurious bias in a self-guided way.

papers.title: Properties from Mechanisms: An Equivariance Perspective on Identifiable Representation Learning
papers.research_question: Can we identify latent properties by leveraging knowledge of the mechanisms that govern their evolution?
papers.core_contribution: Proves that if the mechanisms governing latent evolution are known, then identification of latent representations is possible up to the equivariances shared by those mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: By exploiting inductive biases on mechanisms, it is possible to design a range of new identifiable representation learning approaches.
papers.key_findings:
With known deterministic mechanisms, latent representations are identified up to the equivariances of the mechanisms.
When only a hypothesis class of mechanisms is known, additional non-identifiability arises from imitation among mechanisms.
For affine mechanisms with distinct eigenvalues and sufficient offset diversity, identification up to an offset is achieved.
The mechanism-based perspective generalizes existing identifiable representation learning results, such as those in Klindt et al. (2020).
Stochastic mechanisms lead to similar identification results up to equivariances and imitators in distribution.
papers.limitation: The analysis assumes perfect reconstruction (bijective autoencoders), which is a strong and often impractical assumption.
future_direction: Developing practical algorithms that leverage mechanistic knowledge for representation learning.
Extending the theory to handle more complex and realistic mechanisms.
Addressing the open problems of scaling and applying the approach in practice.
papers.abstract: A key goal of unsupervised representation learning is "inverting" a data generating process to recover its latent properties. Existing work that provably achieves this goal relies on strong assumptions on relationships between the latent variables (e.g., independence conditional on auxiliary information). In this paper, we take a very different perspective on the problem and ask, "Can we instead identify latent properties by leveraging knowledge of the mechanisms that govern their evolution?" We provide a complete characterization of the sources of non-identifiability as we vary knowledge about a set of possible mechanisms. In particular, we prove that if we know the exact mechanisms under which the latent properties evolve, then identification can be achieved up to any equivariances that are shared by the underlying mechanisms. We generalize this characterization to settings where we only know some hypothesis class over possible mechanisms, as well as settings where the mechanisms are stochastic. We demonstrate the power of this mechanism-based perspective by showing that we can leverage our results to generalize existing identifiable representation learning results. These results suggest that by exploiting inductive biases on mechanisms, it is possible to design a range of new identifiable representation learning approaches.

papers.title: Why Representation Engineering Works: A Theoretical and Empirical Study in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can Representation Engineering (RepE) be extended to Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and what theoretical principles explain the stability of neural activity across layers in this context?
papers.core_contribution: This work extends Representation Engineering (RepE) to Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and provides a theoretical framework explaining that the stability of neural activity across layers is governed by the principal eigenvector of the attention matrix, while a shrinking spectral gap allows subdominant eigenvectors to differentiate between concepts.
papers.conclusion: By integrating theoretical analysis with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new avenues for improving AI robustness, interpretability, and transparency in multimodal settings.
papers.key_findings:
The principal eigenvector of the self-attention matrix serves as a stable 'backbone' for neural activity propagation across layers.
The spectral gap (difference between the largest and second-largest eigenvalues) shrinks in deeper layers, enabling subdominant eigenvectors to capture subtle distinctions between concepts like honesty and fairness.
Representation Engineering (RepE) is effective in VLMs for extracting and analyzing high-level conceptual representations, such as honesty and fairness, from internal activations.
Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) scans reveal distinct activation patterns across layers for different high-level concepts, demonstrating how representations evolve through the network.
future_direction: Extend RepE to broader multimodal settings, exploring its potential for bias mitigation, honest detection, and countless concept applications.
papers.abstract: Representation Engineering (RepE) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing AI transparency by focusing on high-level representations rather than individual neurons or circuits. It has proven effective in improving interpretability and control, showing that representations can emerge, propagate, and shape final model outputs in large language models (LLMs). However, in Vision-Language Models (VLMs), visual input can override factual linguistic knowledge, leading to hallucinated responses that contradict reality. To address this challenge, we make the first attempt to extend RepE to VLMs, analyzing how multimodal representations are preserved and transformed. Building on our findings and drawing inspiration from successful RepE applications, we develop a theoretical framework that explains the stability of neural activity across layers using the principal eigenvector, uncovering the underlying mechanism of RepE. We empirically validate these instrinsic properties, demonstrating their broad applicability and significance. By bridging theoretical insights with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new directions for improving AI robustness, fairness, and transparency.

papers.title: APEX: Probing Neural Networks via Activation Perturbation
papers.research_question: How can we probe neural networks by perturbing hidden activations to reveal structural information encoded in intermediate representations, beyond what is accessible from input or parameter perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces APEX, an inference-time probing paradigm that perturbs hidden activations to reveal sample-dependent and model-dependent behavior, exposing structural properties like sample regularity and backdoor biases.
papers.conclusion: APEX is a lightweight yet powerful inference-time probing paradigm that reveals structural properties of learned representations through activation perturbation, connecting sample regularity, semantic transitions, and model-level biases.
papers.key_findings:
APEX in the small-noise regime provides a lightweight measure of sample regularity (escape noise) that correlates with established metrics and distinguishes structured from randomly labeled models.
APEX in the large-noise regime induces a stationary, model-specific output distribution that exposes training-induced biases, such as target-class concentration in backdoored models.
Activation perturbation reveals semantically aligned prediction transitions in controlled settings, unlike input or parameter perturbations.
Escape noise is decoupled from training confidence and remains stable across epochs.
Backdoored models exhibit target-aligned collapse in stationary output distributions, while benign models show more dispersed outputs.
papers.limitation: In vision transformers (DeiT), backdoor features may not fully dominate the global representation space, leading to attenuated collapse and re-dispersion under large noise.
papers.abstract: Prior work on probing neural networks primarily relies on input-space analysis or parameter perturbation, both of which face fundamental limitations in accessing structural information encoded in intermediate representations. We introduce Activation Perturbation for EXploration (APEX), an inference-time probing paradigm that perturbs hidden activations while keeping both inputs and model parameters fixed. We theoretically show that activation perturbation induces a principled transition from sample-dependent to model-dependent behavior by suppressing input-specific signals and amplifying representation-level structure, and further establish that input perturbation corresponds to a constrained special case of this framework. Through representative case studies, we demonstrate the practical advantages of APEX. In the small-noise regime, APEX provides a lightweight and efficient measure of sample regularity that aligns with established metrics, while also distinguishing structured from randomly labeled models and revealing semantically coherent prediction transitions. In the large-noise regime, APEX exposes training-induced model-level biases, including a pronounced concentration of predictions on the target class in backdoored models. Overall, our results show that APEX offers an effective perspective for exploring, and understanding neural networks beyond what is accessible from input space alone.

papers.title: Ablation of a Robot's Brain: Neural Networks Under a Knife
papers.research_question: How can ablation be used to determine the structure of information in neural networks, and what similarities exist between biological and artificial neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an ablation-based method to analyze neural networks, demonstrating that artificial neural networks exhibit robustness to damage and localization of function similar to biological neural networks.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates similarities in organization and information storage between biological and artificial neural networks through ablation, highlighting the need for further research.
papers.key_findings:
Ablation of neuron groups leads to consistent output shifts, showing localization of function.
Networks are robust to damage, with removal of single groups not eliminating task performance.
Clustering identifies 6 distinct functional roles for neuron groups.
Analogous functional regions exist across different training trials.
papers.limitation:
Granularity of ablations is coarse; future studies need finer-scale analysis.
Limited dataset due to reinforcement learning and real-time training constraints.
future_direction: Investigate similarities at different scales of ablation granularity.
Use larger datasets for more comprehensive analysis.
Further research to develop better theoretical understanding.
papers.abstract: It is still not fully understood exactly how neural networks are able to solve the complex tasks that have recently pushed AI research forward. We present a novel method for determining how information is structured inside a neural network. Using ablation (a neuroscience technique for cutting away parts of a brain to determine their function), we approach several neural network architectures from a biological perspective. Through an analysis of this method's results, we examine important similarities between biological and artificial neural networks to search for the implicit knowledge locked away in the network's weights.

papers.title: The First to Know: How Token Distributions Reveal Hidden Knowledge in Large Vision-Language Models?
papers.research_question: Do models implicitly know that they are generating inappropriate or undesirable content?
papers.core_contribution: The logit distribution of the first token in LVLMs contains hidden knowledge that can be used via linear probing to detect inappropriate instructions and improve response generation.
papers.conclusion: Linear probing on the first token's logit distribution reveals hidden knowledge in LVLMs, enabling better detection of inappropriate instructions and improved response generation.
papers.key_findings:
The logit distribution of the first token contains sufficient information to determine if a model should respond to an instruction.
Hidden knowledge in logit distributions weakens as the model generates more tokens.
CLIP model shows strong performance on these tasks, suggesting dataset bias.
Linear probing on first logits improves performance on math correctness, object hallucination, and image classification tasks.
Finetuning LVLMs is less effective than linear probing for these tasks.
papers.limitation:
Dataset bias may simplify tasks, as CLIP performs well indicating distribution differences.
The decoding method sometimes leads to incorrect explanations.
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs), designed to interpret and respond to human instructions, occasionally generate hallucinated or harmful content due to inappropriate instructions. This study uses linear probing to shed light on the hidden knowledge at the output layers of LVLMs. We demonstrate that the logit distributions of the first tokens contain sufficient information to determine whether to respond to the instructions, including recognizing unanswerable visual questions, defending against jailbreaking attacks, and identifying deceptive questions. Such hidden knowledge is gradually lost in logits of subsequent tokens during response generation. Then, we illustrate a simple decoding strategy at the generation of the first token, effectively improving the generated content. In experiments, we find a few interesting insights: First, the CLIP model already contains a strong signal for solving these tasks, which indicates potential bias in the existing datasets. Second, we observe performance improvement by utilizing the first logit distributions on three additional tasks, including indicating uncertainty in math solving, mitigating hallucination, and image classification. Last, with the same training data, simply finetuning LVLMs improves models' performance but is still inferior to linear probing on these tasks.

papers.title: Multilevel Interpretability Of Artificial Neural Networks: Leveraging Framework And Methods From Neuroscience
papers.research_question: How can frameworks and methods from neuroscience, specifically Marr's levels of analysis, be leveraged to interpret artificial neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a multilevel interpretability framework inspired by neuroscience, specifically Marr's three levels of analysis (computation, algorithm/representation, implementation), to provide a principled approach for understanding artificial neural networks.
papers.conclusion: The multilevel interpretability framework provides a principled way to tackle neural system complexity, links structure, computation, and behavior, and paves the way toward a unified effort for understanding intelligent systems, whether biological or artificial.
papers.limitation: Differences between biological and artificial neural systems may limit the direct application of neuroscience methods and frameworks to AI interpretability.
future_direction: Applying the multilevel framework to specific behaviors like deception in AI systems.
Further integration of neuroscience and AI interpretability research.
Developing benchmarks and theoretical models for behaviors like deception at the computational level.
papers.abstract: As deep learning systems are scaled up to many billions of parameters, relating their internal structure to external behaviors becomes very challenging. Although daunting, this problem is not new: Neuroscientists and cognitive scientists have accumulated decades of experience analyzing a particularly complex system - the brain. In this work, we argue that interpreting both biological and artificial neural systems requires analyzing those systems at multiple levels of analysis, with different analytic tools for each level. We first lay out a joint grand challenge among scientists who study the brain and who study artificial neural networks: understanding how distributed neural mechanisms give rise to complex cognition and behavior. We then present a series of analytical tools that can be used to analyze biological and artificial neural systems, organizing those tools according to Marr's three levels of analysis: computation/behavior, algorithm/representation, and implementation. Overall, the multilevel interpretability framework provides a principled way to tackle neural system complexity; links structure, computation, and behavior; clarifies assumptions and research priorities at each level; and paves the way toward a unified effort for understanding intelligent systems, may they be biological or artificial.

papers.title: Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: What are the key open problems in mechanistic interpretability methods, applications, and socio-technical challenges that need to be addressed to achieve the field's goals?
