papers.core_contribution: This review synthesizes and outlines key open problems in mechanistic interpretability, covering methods, applications, and socio-technical challenges to guide future research.
papers.conclusion: The review outlines critical open problems in mechanistic interpretability that must be addressed to achieve scientific and engineering goals, emphasizing the need for methodological improvements and socio-technical integration.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic interpretability methods, such as sparse dictionary learning, suffer from practical and conceptual limitations like high reconstruction errors and unclear theoretical foundations.
Applying interpretability to AI safety requires robust methods for monitoring internal states and controlling behavior, but current techniques are insufficient.
Socio-technical challenges include integrating interpretability into AI governance and addressing philosophical questions about the field's goals.
future_direction: Developing better decomposition methods like sparse dictionary learning with lower reconstruction errors.
Creating validation frameworks for interpretability hypotheses.
Applying interpretability to AI safety monitoring and control.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the computational mechanisms underlying neural networks' capabilities in order to accomplish concrete scientific and engineering goals. Progress in this field thus promises to provide greater assurance over AI system behavior and shed light on exciting scientific questions about the nature of intelligence. Despite recent progress toward these goals, there are many open problems in the field that require solutions before many scientific and practical benefits can be realized: Our methods require both conceptual and practical improvements to reveal deeper insights; we must figure out how best to apply our methods in pursuit of specific goals; and the field must grapple with socio-technical challenges that influence and are influenced by our work. This forward-facing review discusses the current frontier of mechanistic interpretability and the open problems that the field may benefit from prioritizing.

papers.title: Explanatory models in neuroscience: Part 1 -- taking mechanistic abstraction seriously
papers.research_question: What criteria must neural network models satisfy to be considered mechanistic explanations of brain function?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the 3M++ criteria, which expand the notion of model-to-mechanism mapping to show that deep neural networks can serve as abstract mechanistic models of brain function when they are runnable and mappable via similarity transforms.
papers.conclusion: Deep neural networks can be good mechanistic models of brain function when assessed with the 3M++ criteria, and the appropriate level of abstraction is key to their explanatory power.
papers.key_findings:
The 3M++ criteria require a model to be a 'runnable abstraction' and to be mappable to the brain using similarity transforms (like linear transforms).
Deep neural networks, when trained for object recognition, can satisfy the 3M++ criteria and thus serve as mechanistic models of the primate ventral visual pathway.
The abstractions used in DNNs (e.g., Linear-Nonlinear units) are the same as those already employed in experimental neuroscience.
The mapping between DNN layers and brain areas can be performed using linear transforms, analogous to mapping neural responses across individuals.
The level of abstraction is crucial; DNNs operate at the spike-rate level, which is a self-consistent and predictively adequate level for explaining visual processing.
papers.limitation: HCNNs do not explain 100% of the stimulus-driven variability of ventral pathway neurons, up to the inter-animal noise ceiling.
future_direction: Developing improved models (e.g., with recurrent and feedback connections) to achieve 100% statistical accuracy in mapping to the visual system.
Exploring the relationship between optimization and intelligibility, as addressed in the companion paper.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent success of neural network models in mimicking animal performance on visual perceptual tasks, critics worry that these models fail to illuminate brain function. We take it that a central approach to explanation in systems neuroscience is that of mechanistic modeling, where understanding the system is taken to require fleshing out the parts, organization, and activities of a system, and how those give rise to behaviors of interest. However, it remains somewhat controversial what it means for a model to describe a mechanism, and whether neural network models qualify as explanatory. We argue that certain kinds of neural network models are actually good examples of mechanistic models, when the right notion of mechanistic mapping is deployed. Building on existing work on model-to-mechanism mapping (3M), we describe criteria delineating such a notion, which we call 3M++. These criteria require us, first, to identify a level of description that is both abstract but detailed enough to be "runnable", and then, to construct model-to-brain mappings using the same principles as those employed for brain-to-brain mapping across individuals. Perhaps surprisingly, the abstractions required are those already in use in experimental neuroscience, and are of the kind deployed in the construction of more familiar computational models, just as the principles of inter-brain mappings are very much in the spirit of those already employed in the collection and analysis of data across animals. In a companion paper, we address the relationship between optimization and intelligibility, in the context of functional evolutionary explanations. Taken together, mechanistic interpretations of computational models and the dependencies between form and function illuminated by optimization processes can help us to understand why brain systems are built they way they are.

papers.title: PURE: Turning Polysemantic Neurons Into Pure Features by Identifying Relevant Circuits
papers.research_question: Can we find and purify polysemantic neurons? How effective is PURE in disentangling representations compared to other approaches?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PURE, a post-hoc method to disentangle polysemantic neurons into multiple pure virtual neurons by identifying the active circuit for each feature.
papers.conclusion: PURE turns polysemantic neurons into multiple purer virtual neurons by identifying active circuits, resulting in more purified features than activation-based approaches and improving interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic neurons exist in ResNet models and can be disentangled into pure features using circuit identification.
PURE effectively disentangles representations, leading to more interpretable virtual neurons compared to activation-based clustering.
PURE attributions are more aligned with CLIP embedding distances than activations, indicating better neuron-specific disentanglement.
PURE performs close to DINOv2 in terms of cluster separation while being computationally more efficient than DINOv2-based clustering.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation relies on foundational models (CLIP/DINOv2) as proxies for human interpretability, which may not perfectly align with human judgment.
PURE requires a partial backward pass for each neuron, making it computationally more demanding than activation-based methods.
future_direction: Evaluation in controlled settings or using human feedback for interpretability.
Ablation studies on clustering full circuits, different attribution methods, and clustering approaches.
Investigating advantages of purified units for XAI tools like concept-based explanations, concept discovery, probing, or model correction.
papers.abstract: The field of mechanistic interpretability aims to study the role of individual neurons in Deep Neural Networks. Single neurons, however, have the capability to act polysemantically and encode for multiple (unrelated) features, which renders their interpretation difficult. We present a method for disentangling polysemanticity of any Deep Neural Network by decomposing a polysemantic neuron into multiple monosemantic "virtual" neurons. This is achieved by identifying the relevant sub-graph ("circuit") for each "pure" feature. We demonstrate how our approach allows us to find and disentangle various polysemantic units of ResNet models trained on ImageNet. While evaluating feature visualizations using CLIP, our method effectively disentangles representations, improving upon methods based on neuron activations. Our code is available at https://github.com/maxdreyer/PURE.

papers.title: MAPS: Masked Attribution-based Probing of Strategies- A computational framework to align human and model explanations
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether explanations derived from artificial neural networks (ANNs) can explain human vision, and provides a principled way to evaluate and choose among competing ANN interpretability methods.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MAPS, a behaviorally validated computational framework that tests whether ANN explanations align with human vision, providing a principled way to evaluate and choose among interpretability methods and linking human behavior, neural activity, and model decisions under a common standard.
papers.conclusion: MAPS offers a principled, scalable, and behaviorally grounded framework for probing and benchmarking human-model alignment, closing a key methodological gap between perception, computation, and neural implementation.
papers.key_findings:
MAPS recovers ground-truth similarity between model explanations using behavioral proxies, validating the framework.
Noise Tunnel Saliency is identified as the best attribution method for aligning with human and monkey behavior.
MAPS requires far fewer behavioral trials than traditional psychophysical methods like Bubbles.
MAPS generalizes across species, aligning with both human and macaque behavior, and with neural data from IT cortex.
The framework provides a scalable way to benchmark human-model strategy alignment for object recognition.
future_direction: Applying MAPS to other domains such as audition, language, or motor control.
Using MAPS for layer-wise alignment to identify which representational stage in models best mirrors the brain.
Further testing of MAPS with neural data to bridge explainable AI and systems neuroscience.
papers.abstract: Human core object recognition depends on the selective use of visual information, but the strategies guiding these choices are difficult to measure directly. We present MAPS (Masked Attribution-based Probing of Strategies), a behaviorally validated computational tool that tests whether explanations derived from artificial neural networks (ANNs) can also explain human vision. MAPS converts attribution maps into explanation-masked images (EMIs) and compares image-by-image human accuracies on these minimal images with limited pixel budgets with accuracies on the full stimuli. MAPS provides a principled way to evaluate and choose among competing ANN interpretability methods. In silico, EMI-based behavioral similarity between models reliably recovers the ground-truth similarity computed from their attribution maps, establishing which explanation methods best capture the model's strategy. When applied to humans and macaques, MAPS identifies ANN-explanation combinations whose explanations align most closely with biological vision, achieving the behavioral validity of Bubble masks while requiring far fewer behavioral trials. Because it needs only access to model attributions and a modest set of behavioral data on the original images, MAPS avoids exhaustive psychophysics while offering a scalable tool for adjudicating explanations and linking human behavior, neural activity, and model decisions under a common standard.

papers.title: A Minimal Intervention Definition of Reverse Engineering a Neural Circuit
papers.research_question: What should be the end-goal for reverse engineering in neuroscience? The paper proposes a minimal-intervention definition of reverse engineering.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a formal definition of reverse engineering for computational systems based on minimal interventions, shows that for some classes the problem is undecidable, and provides examples where reverse engineering is achievable.
papers.conclusion: Reverse engineering as defined is undecidable in general, but achievable in specific cases, and the framework can inform goals in neuroscience and the design of future studies.
papers.key_findings:
Reverse engineering can be defined as the ability to provide minimal interventions to change the I/O behavior of a system to a desired one, under bounded rationality constraints.
For computational systems with infinite alphabet and computable functions, reverse engineering is undecidable for nontrivial classes of desired behaviors, by connection to Rice's theorem.
Simple systems like line networks, network-coding butterflies, and FFT butterflies can be reverse engineered with limited memory and query resources.
The definition is motivated by neuroscience and clinical goals, where minimal interventions are sought to treat disorders.
The model used is a crude discrete-time nodes-and-edges model, which may not capture biological complexity.
papers.limitation:
Our nodes-and-edges discrete-time model is a crude one, because even single cells can exhibit extremely complex dynamics.
Our definition of what constitutes a minimal intervention could be tied more closely to biological constraints and peculiarities.
future_direction: Incorporate biological constraints and practical difficulties (e.g., invasiveness, diffusion) into the definition of minimal intervention.
Focus clinical neuroscience research on modifications and interventions at the fewest possible locations to change I/O behavior.
Replace bounded memory constraints with other constraints (e.g., computational or informational) or seek approximately minimal interventions.
papers.abstract: In neuroscience, researchers have developed informal notions of what it means to reverse engineer a system, e.g., being able to model or simulate a system in some sense. A recent influential paper of Jonas and Kording, that examines a microprocessor using techniques from neuroscience, suggests that common techniques to understand neural systems are inadequate. Part of the difficulty, as a previous work of Lazebnik noted, lies in lack of formal language. We provide a theoretical framework for defining reverse engineering of computational systems, motivated by the neuroscience context. Of specific interest are recent works where, increasingly, interventions are being made to alter the function of the neural circuitry to both understand the system and treat disorders. Starting from Lazebnik's viewpoint that understanding a system means you can ``fix it'', and motivated by use-cases in neuroscience, we propose the following requirement on reverse engineering: once an agent claims to have reverse-engineered a neural circuit, they subsequently need to be able to: (a) provide a minimal set of interventions to change the input/output (I/O) behavior of the circuit to a desired behavior; (b) arrive at this minimal set of interventions while operating under bounded rationality constraints (e.g., limited memory) to rule out brute-force approaches. Under certain assumptions, we show that this reverse engineering goal falls within the class of undecidable problems. Next, we examine some canonical computational systems and reverse engineering goals (as specified by desired I/O behaviors) where reverse engineering can indeed be performed. Finally, using an exemplar network, the ``reward network'' in the brain, we summarize the state of current neuroscientific understanding, and discuss how computer-science and information-theoretic concepts can inform goals of future neuroscience studies.

papers.title: Inferring hidden structure in multilayered neural circuits
papers.research_question: How can we reconstruct the response properties of hidden neurons in multilayered neural circuits using cascaded LN-LN models, and what insights does this provide about retinal processing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a computational framework using non-smooth regularization and proximal consensus algorithms to fit hierarchical LN-LN models from limited neural data, revealing that retinal ganglion cell computation can be modeled as a boolean OR function of bipolar cell feature detectors and that visual redundancies are removed primarily at bipolar cell synapses.
papers.conclusion: The developed framework efficiently learns hierarchical nonlinear models from limited data, providing insights into retinal computation and offering a general tool for studying sensory processing across diverse modalities.
papers.key_findings:
LN-LN models demonstrate a 53% improvement in predicting ganglion cell spikes over classical LN models.
Internal nonlinear subunits of the model match properties of retinal bipolar cells in both receptive field structure and number.
Subunits have consistently high thresholds, suppressing all but a small fraction of inputs, leading to sparse activity patterns.
The removal of visual redundancies through stimulus decorrelation across space originates primarily from bipolar cell synapses.
The composite nonlinear computation performed by retinal circuitry corresponds to a boolean OR function applied to bipolar cell feature detectors.
papers.abstract: A central challenge in sensory neuroscience involves understanding how neural circuits shape computations across cascaded cell layers. Here we attempt to reconstruct the response properties of experimentally unobserved neurons in the interior of a multilayered neural circuit, using cascaded linear-nonlinear (LN-LN) models. We combine non-smooth regularization with proximal consensus algorithms to overcome difficulties in fitting such models that arise from the high dimensionality of their parameter space. We apply this framework to retinal ganglion cell processing, learning LN-LN models of retinal circuitry consisting of thousands of parameters, using 40 minutes of responses to white noise. Our models demonstrate a 53% improvement in predicting ganglion cell spikes over classical linear-nonlinear (LN) models. Internal nonlinear subunits of the model match properties of retinal bipolar cells in both receptive field structure and number. Subunits have consistently high thresholds, supressing all but a small fraction of inputs, leading to sparse activity patterns in which only one subunit drives ganglion cell spiking at any time. From the model's parameters, we predict that the removal of visual redundancies through stimulus decorrelation across space, a central tenet of efficient coding theory, originates primarily from bipolar cell synapses. Furthermore, the composite nonlinear computation performed by retinal circuitry corresponds to a boolean OR function applied to bipolar cell feature detectors. Our methods are statistically and computationally efficient, enabling us to rapidly learn hierarchical non-linear models as well as efficiently compute widely used descriptive statistics such as the spike triggered average (STA) and covariance (STC) for high dimensional stimuli. This general computational framework may aid in extracting principles of nonlinear hierarchical sensory processing across diverse modalities from limited data.

papers.title: Detecting Information Relays in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we identify functional modules (information relays) in artificial neural networks? The paper investigates whether a new information-theoretic measure (relay information) combined with a greedy search algorithm can correctly identify nodes that relay information from inputs to outputs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a new information-theoretic measure called relay information (IR) and a greedy search algorithm (shrinking subset aggregation) to identify computational modules (information relays) in neural networks, validated on a control network with known modular structure.
papers.conclusion: Relay information is a useful concept for identifying information relays and functional modules in neural networks, and the method can be applied to study modularity and its effects on properties like catastrophic forgetting.
papers.key_findings:
The relay information measure and greedy algorithm correctly identify the relay neurons in a composite network where the functional modules are known by construction.
Knocking out neurons identified as carrying relay information disrupts classification accuracy for the corresponding numeral, confirming their functional role.
Standard ANNs trained on all numerals simultaneously do not exhibit well-differentiated modular structure; information is distributed haphazardly across the network.
The greedy algorithm can fail in the presence of redundant information encoding, but such failures are rare in the tested networks.
The effective state space of the hidden layer is much smaller than the theoretical maximum, as training causes hidden states to cluster according to the output classes.
papers.limitation:
The greedy algorithm can fail to identify the correct minimal set when information is redundantly encoded across neurons.
Estimating entropies from finite samples can be inaccurate and may lead to errors in identifying relay sets.
The computational complexity of the algorithm scales with the number of nodes, though the greedy version reduces it to quadratic.
future_direction: Apply the method to time series classification, recurrent neural networks, convolutional layers, and generative tasks.
Use the method to study the role of modularity in catastrophic forgetting, generalization, and other network properties.
Extend the method to analyze information flow in biological brains, though this would require temporal binning and measurement of neuronal states.
papers.abstract: Deep learning of artificial neural networks (ANNs) is creating highly functional processes that are, unfortunately, nearly as hard to interpret as their biological counterparts. Identification of functional modules in natural brains plays an important role in cognitive and neuroscience alike, and can be carried out using a wide range of technologies such as fMRI, EEG/ERP, MEG, or calcium imaging. However, we do not have such robust methods at our disposal when it comes to understanding functional modules in artificial neural networks. Ideally, understanding which parts of an artificial neural network perform what function might help us to address a number of vexing problems in ANN research, such as catastrophic forgetting and overfitting. Furthermore, revealing a network's modularity could improve our trust in them by making these black boxes more transparent. Here, we introduce a new information-theoretic concept that proves useful in understanding and analyzing a network's functional modularity: the relay information $I_R$. The relay information measures how much information groups of neurons that participate in a particular function (modules) relay from inputs to outputs. Combined with a greedy search algorithm, relay information can be used to identify computational modules in neural networks. We also show that the functionality of modules correlates with the amount of relay information they carry.

papers.title: Circuit Fingerprints: How Answer Tokens Encode Their Geometrical Path
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether circuit discovery and activation steering are two views of the same underlying geometric structure, and whether answer tokens encode the directions that would produce them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis, showing that answer tokens encode the geometric directions of their generating circuits, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and activation steering as dual operations on the same geometric structure.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that circuit discovery and activation steering are dual operations on the same geometric structure encoded in activation space, enabling gradient-free circuit discovery and effective steering, and revealing transformer circuits as geometric objects.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit membership can be determined from geometric alignment with answer token directions, recovering circuit structure comparable to gradient-based methods without backpropagation.
The same directions enable controlled steering, validating that they manipulate genuine computational pathways.
Feature circuits can be discovered by extracting directions from instruction-modified prompts, without task-specific datasets.
The method achieves comparable circuit discovery performance to gradient-based methods (EAP, EAP-IG) on IOI, SVA, and MCQA tasks across four model families.
Steering using these directions achieves 69.8% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy (89.6%).
papers.limitation:
Zero-shot steering remains fragile; even grammatically correct outputs can exhibit semantic degradation.
Steering can disrupt factual recall, particularly for negative-valence emotions and distant language pairs, suggesting some features remain entangled with semantic content.
future_direction: Address position-level effects beyond the final token.
Address LayerNorm nonlinearities in edge attribution.
Develop methods to preserve factual grounding during steering.
Develop more robust persona-based circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery and activation steering in transformers have developed as separate research threads, yet both operate on the same representational space. Are they two views of the same underlying structure? We show they follow a single geometric principle: answer tokens, processed in isolation, encode the directions that would produce them. This Circuit Fingerprint hypothesis enables circuit discovery without gradients or causal intervention -- recovering comparable structure to gradient-based methods through geometric alignment alone. We validate this on standard benchmarks (IOI, SVA, MCQA) across four model families, achieving circuit discovery performance comparable to gradient-based methods. The same directions that identify circuit components also enable controlled steering -- achieving 69.8\% emotion classification accuracy versus 53.1\% for instruction prompting while preserving factual accuracy. Beyond method development, this read-write duality reveals that transformer circuits are fundamentally geometric structures: interpretability and controllability are two facets of the same object.

papers.title: REAL: Reading Out Transformer Activations for Precise Localization in Language Model Steering
papers.research_question: How can we better identify internal modules (attention heads or layers) that govern specific behaviors in LLMs for the purpose of inference-time steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REAL, a framework that uses a vector-quantized autoencoder (VQ-AE) to learn a disentangled latent space from module activations, enabling more precise identification of behavior-relevant modules (heads or layers) for inference-time steering in Transformers.
papers.conclusion: REAL provides a more effective and principled approach for selecting behavior-relevant modules in Transformers, leading to improved performance across a variety of inference-time steering tasks including truthfulness enhancement, knowledge conflict resolution, and general alignment.
papers.key_findings:
REAL outperforms existing methods like ITI and LoFiT in truthfulness steering, achieving significant improvements (e.g., up to 81.5% relative improvement on MC1 for Qwen2.5-7B).
The attention heads selected by REAL on a truthfulness task show strong zero-shot generalization to knowledge-seeking tasks in different model families.
REAL effectively localizes layers for steering in knowledge conflict tasks, outperforming the state-of-the-art SPARE method on benchmarks like NQSWAP and MACNOISE.
The method's relevance scores, derived from the VQ-AE encodings, provide a principled way to rank modules and assign steering strengths.
Visualizations (t-SNE, heatmaps) show that REAL identifies heads with more discriminative activation patterns compared to linear-probe-based methods.
papers.abstract: Inference-time steering aims to alter a large language model's (LLM's) responses without changing its parameters, but a central challenge is identifying the internal modules that most strongly govern the target behavior. Existing approaches often rely on simplistic cues or ad hoc heuristics, leading to suboptimal or unintended effects. We introduce REAL, a framework for identifying behavior-relevant modules (attention heads or layers) in Transformer models. For each module, REAL trains a vector-quantized autoencoder (VQ-AE) on its hidden activations and uses a shared, learnable codebook to partition the latent space into behavior-relevant and behavior-irrelevant subspaces. REAL quantifies a module's behavioral relevance by how well its VQ-AE encodings discriminate behavior-aligned from behavior-violating responses via a binary classification metric; this score guides both module selection and steering strength. We evaluate REAL across eight LLMs from the Llama and Qwen families and nine datasets spanning truthfulness enhancement, open-domain QA under knowledge conflicts, and general alignment tasks. REAL enables more effective inference-time interventions, achieving an average relative improvement of 20% (up to 81.5%) over the ITI method on truthfulness steering. In addition, the modules selected by REAL exhibit strong zero-shot generalization in cross-domain truthfulness-steering scenarios.

papers.title: Building Interpretable Models for Moral Decision-Making
papers.research_question: How do neural networks make moral decisions on trolley-style dilemmas, and where do moral biases originate within their architectures?
papers.core_contribution: Designs a 2-layer transformer optimized for moral reasoning tasks, achieving 77% accuracy on Moral Machine data, and combines interpretability methods to map internal mechanisms of moral judgment.
papers.conclusion: Demonstrates that small, custom transformers can achieve moral competence and be transparently analyzed, enabling targeted interventions for bias mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns a moral hierarchy where characters like Pregnant and Stroller have positive causal effects, while Criminal has negative effects.
Moral biases localize to distinct computational stages: legality bias in Layer 0 and species bias in Layer 1.
Circuit probing identifies sparse subnetworks in the MLP block that causally implement moral scoring.
The model shows functional specialization with different attention heads specializing in different bias dimensions.
Small, custom transformers can achieve moral competence while remaining interpretable, enabling targeted bias interventions.
papers.limitation: Training on aggregate human preferences inherits cultural biases.
future_direction: Extend the approach to traditional large language models on moral questions.
papers.abstract: We build a custom transformer model to study how neural networks make moral decisions on trolley-style dilemmas. The model processes structured scenarios using embeddings that encode who is affected, how many people, and which outcome they belong to. Our 2-layer architecture achieves 77% accuracy on Moral Machine data while remaining small enough for detailed analysis. We use different interpretability techniques to uncover how moral reasoning distributes across the network, demonstrating that biases localize to distinct computational stages among other findings.

papers.title: Intrinsic Self-correction for Enhanced Morality: An Analysis of Internal Mechanisms and the Superficial Hypothesis
papers.research_question: The paper investigates three research questions: (1) In what scenarios does moral self-correction work? (2) What are the internal mechanisms of LLMs influenced by self-correction instructions? (3) Is intrinsic moral self-correction actually superficial?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that intrinsic moral self-correction in LLMs is superficial, as it only provides a shortcut to moral outputs without significantly reducing immorality in internal hidden states.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that intrinsic moral self-correction is superficial, relying on shortcuts rather than fundamentally reducing immorality in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Self-correction works best when the correct answer is already top-ranked.
Morality levels in intermediate hidden states are strong indicators of instruction effectiveness.
Self-correction reduces immorality in attention heads but increases it in feed-forward layers for QA tasks.
The slight difference in hidden states with and without self-correction supports the superficial hypothesis.
Internal hidden states can be used to predict the effectiveness of self-correction instructions.
papers.limitation:
The exact underlying reason for the superficial phenomenon is not uncovered.
Defining superficial self-correction is challenging.
future_direction: Automating methods for optimizing instruction development for self-correction.
Exploring fine-tuning to enhance LLMs' self-correction capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are capable of producing content that perpetuates stereotypes, discrimination, and toxicity. The recently proposed moral self-correction is a computationally efficient method for reducing harmful content in the responses of LLMs. However, the process of how injecting self-correction instructions can modify the behavior of LLMs remains under-explored. In this paper, we explore the effectiveness of moral self-correction by answering three research questions: (1) In what scenarios does moral self-correction work? (2) What are the internal mechanisms of LLMs, e.g., hidden states, that are influenced by moral self-correction instructions? (3) Is intrinsic moral self-correction actually superficial in terms of reduced immorality in hidden states? We argue that self-correction can help LLMs find a shortcut to more morally correct output, rather than truly reducing the immorality stored in hidden states. Through empirical investigation with tasks of language generation and multi-choice question answering, we conclude:(i) LLMs exhibit good performance across both tasks, and self-correction instructions are particularly beneficial when the correct answer is already top-ranked; (ii) The morality levels in intermediate hidden states are strong indicators as to whether one instruction would be more effective than another; (iii) Based on our analysis of intermediate hidden states and task case studies of self-correction behaviors, we are first to propose the hypothesis that intrinsic moral self-correction is in fact superficial.

papers.title: Extracting Rule-based Descriptions of Attention Features in Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we automatically extract symbolic, rule-based descriptions of attention features in transformers to better explain their behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for extracting symbolic, rule-based descriptions of attention features in transformers, demonstrating that skip-gram, absence, and counting rules can approximate attention behavior in GPT-2 small.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that rule-based descriptions are a promising approach for interpreting attention features, but more work is needed to cover more rule types and extend to full models.
papers.key_findings:
Skip-gram rules provide a good approximation of attention features, especially in early layers.
Absence rules are common, even in early layers, and can suppress feature activations.
Counting rules exist, where feature activation depends on the frequency of input patterns.
Higher layers require more terms for approximation and have lower F1 scores.
The gradient-based method for selecting rules achieves higher recall with fewer terms.
papers.limitation:
The underlying feature decomposition (SAE) may not be optimal for rule extraction.
The rules assume single feature interactions, but attention can depend on multiple features.
The evaluation uses binary activation prediction and may favor recall over precision.
future_direction: Extending rule extraction to cover more types of rules.
Improving the underlying feature decomposition (e.g., using transcoders or joint training).
Understanding how rules compose across layers and with MLP layers.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability strives to explain model behavior in terms of bottom-up primitives. The leading paradigm is to express hidden states as a sparse linear combination of basis vectors, called features. However, this only identifies which text sequences (exemplars) activate which features; the actual interpretation of features requires subjective inspection of these exemplars. This paper advocates for a different solution: rule-based descriptions that match token patterns in the input and correspondingly increase or decrease the likelihood of specific output tokens. Specifically, we extract rule-based descriptions of SAE features trained on the outputs of attention layers. While prior work treats the attention layers as an opaque box, we describe how it may naturally be expressed in terms of interactions between input and output features, of which we study three types: (1) skip-gram rules of the form "[Canadian city]... speaks --> English", (2) absence rules of the form "[Montreal]... speaks -/-> English," and (3) counting rules that toggle only when the count of a word exceeds a certain value or the count of another word. Absence and counting rules are not readily discovered by inspection of exemplars, where manual and automatic descriptions often identify misleading or incomplete explanations. We then describe a simple approach to extract these types of rules automatically from a transformer, and apply it to GPT-2 small. We find that a majority of features may be described well with around 100 skip-gram rules, though absence rules are abundant even as early as the first layer (in over a fourth of features). We also isolate a few examples of counting rules. This paper lays the groundwork for future research into rule-based descriptions of features by defining them, showing how they may be extracted, and providing a preliminary taxonomy of some of the behaviors they represent.

papers.title: IR$^3$: Contrastive Inverse Reinforcement Learning for Interpretable Detection and Mitigation of Reward Hacking
papers.research_question: How can we reverse-engineer, interpret, and surgically repair the implicit objectives driving RLHF-trained models to detect and mitigate reward hacking?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces IR3, a framework that reverse-engineers, interprets, and surgically repairs the implicit objectives driving RLHF-trained models to detect and mitigate reward hacking.
papers.conclusion: IR3 reframes reward hacking from a black-box failure into a transparent diagnosis-and-repair workflow.
papers.key_findings:
IR3 achieves 0.89 correlation with ground-truth rewards.
IR3 identifies hacking features with >90% precision.
IR3 significantly reduces hacking behaviors while maintaining capabilities within 3% of the original model.
The Contrastive Inverse Reinforcement Learning (C-IRL) algorithm faithfully reconstructs the reward function driving behavioral shifts.
Sparse Autoencoder decomposition enables interpretable feature-level diagnosis and targeted mitigation.
papers.limitation:
IR3 operates as a post-hoc auditing tool rather than a preventive mechanism.
The diagnosis stage requires a small labeled set of regime-specific hacked examples.
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) enables powerful LLM alignment but can introduce reward hacking - models exploit spurious correlations in proxy rewards without genuine alignment. Compounding this, the objectives internalized during RLHF remain opaque, making hacking behaviors difficult to detect or correct. We introduce IR3 (Interpretable Reward Reconstruction and Rectification), a framework that reverse-engineers, interprets, and surgically repairs the implicit objectives driving RLHF-tuned models. We propose Contrastive Inverse Reinforcement Learning (C-IRL), which reconstructs the implicit reward function by contrasting paired responses from post-alignment and baseline policies to explain behavioral shifts during RLHF. We then decompose the reconstructed reward via sparse autoencoders into interpretable features, enabling identification of hacking signatures through contribution analysis. Finally, we propose mitigation strategies - clean reward optimization, adversarial shaping, constrained optimization, and feature-guided distillation - that target problematic features while preserving beneficial alignment. Experiments across multiple reward model configurations show that IR3 achieves 0.89 correlation with ground-truth rewards, identifies hacking features with over 90% precision, and significantly reduces hacking behaviors while maintaining capabilities within 3% of the original model.

papers.title: Neural Breadcrumbs: Membership Inference Attacks on LLMs Through Hidden State and Attention Pattern Analysis
papers.research_question: Can membership inference attacks be effective against large language models by examining their internal representations (hidden states and attention patterns) rather than just output distributions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces memTrace, a membership inference approach that analyzes internal transformer representations (hidden states and attention patterns) to achieve strong membership detection, challenging the belief that modern LLM training paradigms inherently limit membership inference risk.
papers.conclusion: Membership inference attacks are effective against LLMs by analyzing internal representations, revealing that models process familiar content differently than novel content. This has implications for privacy auditing and the need for privacy-preserving training techniques that address internal model dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Membership signals are strongly encoded in models' internal representations, even when output distributions show minimal differences.
The memTrace framework achieves strong membership detection performance (average AUC of 0.85) across multiple model architectures and text domains.
Middle transformer layers serve as critical integration points where membership signatures become most detectable.
High n-gram overlap between member and non-member texts (e.g., in GitHub and DM Mathematics domains) reduces attack performance.
The model's confidence (entropy) fluctuates more dramatically across token positions for familiar (member) content compared to novel content.
papers.limitation:
The framework only works for white-box models (requires access to internal states).
Performance is lower on datasets with inherently high textual redundancy and n-gram overlap between members and non-members.
future_direction: Examine whether similar processing signatures can be detected through black-box probing techniques.
Investigate whether these patterns generalize to other architecture families beyond decoder-only transformers.
Study how fine-tuning affects these internal memorization signatures.
papers.abstract: Membership inference attacks (MIAs) reveal whether specific data was used to train machine learning models, serving as important tools for privacy auditing and compliance assessment. Recent studies have reported that MIAs perform only marginally better than random guessing against large language models, suggesting that modern pre-training approaches with massive datasets may be free from privacy leakage risks. Our work offers a complementary perspective to these findings by exploring how examining LLMs' internal representations, rather than just their outputs, may provide additional insights into potential membership inference signals. Our framework, \emph{memTrace}, follows what we call \enquote{neural breadcrumbs} extracting informative signals from transformer hidden states and attention patterns as they process candidate sequences. By analyzing layer-wise representation dynamics, attention distribution characteristics, and cross-layer transition patterns, we detect potential memorization fingerprints that traditional loss-based approaches may not capture. This approach yields strong membership detection across several model families achieving average AUC scores of 0.85 on popular MIA benchmarks. Our findings suggest that internal model behaviors can reveal aspects of training data exposure even when output-based signals appear protected, highlighting the need for further research into membership privacy and the development of more robust privacy-preserving training techniques for large language models.

papers.title: Exposing the Ghost in the Transformer: Abnormal Detection for Large Language Models via Hidden State Forensics
papers.research_question: How can abnormal behaviors (hallucinations, jailbreak attacks, backdoor exploits) in Large Language Models be detected in real-time by analyzing hidden state activation patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a real-time detection framework (AbnorDetector) for multiple abnormal behaviors in LLMs by analyzing hidden state activation patterns, achieving high accuracy with minimal computational overhead.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework represents a step towards securing LLM-integrated systems by providing a scalable and efficient solution for real-time abnormal behavior detection in evolving AI applications.
papers.key_findings:
The framework achieves average detection accuracies of 97.43% for jailbreaks, 82.69% for hallucinations, and 91.96% for backdoors across various LLM architectures.
Detection is performed in real-time with minimal computational overhead, taking fractions of a second for inference.
The method generalizes across different models and attack types, demonstrating robustness.
Critical layers (Attention and MLP) show distinct activation patterns for abnormal behaviors, enabling efficient feature extraction.
Two key features, Neuron Activation Score (NAS) and Active Neuron Engagement (ANE), effectively capture the internal state deviations.
papers.abstract: The widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) in critical applications has introduced severe reliability and security risks, as LLMs remain vulnerable to notorious threats such as hallucinations, jailbreak attacks, and backdoor exploits. These vulnerabilities have been weaponized by malicious actors, leading to unauthorized access, widespread misinformation, and compromised LLM-embedded system integrity. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to detecting abnormal behaviors in LLMs via hidden state forensics. By systematically inspecting layer-specific activation patterns, we develop a unified framework that can efficiently identify a range of security threats in real-time without imposing prohibitive computational costs. Extensive experiments indicate detection accuracies exceeding 95% and consistently robust performance across multiple models in most scenarios, while preserving the ability to detect novel attacks effectively. Furthermore, the computational overhead remains minimal, with merely fractions of a second. The significance of this work lies in proposing a promising strategy to reinforce the security of LLM-integrated systems, paving the way for safer and more reliable deployment in high-stakes domains. By enabling real-time detection that can also support the mitigation of abnormal behaviors, it represents a meaningful step toward ensuring the trustworthiness of AI systems amid rising security challenges.

papers.title: Predictive Concept Decoders: Training Scalable End-to-End Interpretability Assistants
papers.research_question: How can we train interpretability assistants to accurately predict model behavior from internal activations through an end-to-end training objective with a communication bottleneck?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Predictive Concept Decoders (PCDs), an end-to-end trainable architecture for interpretability that compresses model activations into sparse concepts and uses a decoder to answer questions about model behavior, showing favorable scaling properties.
papers.conclusion: Predictive Concept Decoders offer a scalable approach to interpretability that can surface latent information in model activations, with applications in detecting atypical behaviors and auditing model reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
PCDs can detect jailbreaks, secret hints, and implanted latent concepts, and accurately surface latent user attributes.
PCDs reveal information that models fail to self-report, such as hint usage and jailbreak awareness that prompting cannot elicit.
The auto-interp score of the bottleneck concepts improves with pretraining data, and at high sparsity outperforms SAE features trained on the same data.
Decoder performance improves with scale and outperforms both direct prompting and LatentQA, a baseline without the sparse bottleneck.
The encoder's sparse concepts provide auditable explanations, allowing predictions to be traced to a small set of inspectable concepts.
papers.limitation:
KL-based objectives (used in PCDs and KL SAEs) may saturate earlier than L2 reconstruction objectives, potentially because the KL objective is too 'easy' to optimize, leading to a sparser signal.
Without an auxiliary loss, many encoder concepts become inactive ('dead') during training, degrading the quality of the learned dictionary.
future_direction: Addressing the plateau in encoder interpretability metrics observed with KL-based objectives.
papers.abstract: Interpreting the internal activations of neural networks can produce more faithful explanations of their behavior, but is difficult due to the complex structure of activation space. Existing approaches to scalable interpretability use hand-designed agents that make and test hypotheses about how internal activations relate to external behavior. We propose to instead turn this task into an end-to-end training objective, by training interpretability assistants to accurately predict model behavior from activations through a communication bottleneck. Specifically, an encoder compresses activations to a sparse list of concepts, and a decoder reads this list and answers a natural language question about the model. We show how to pretrain this assistant on large unstructured data, then finetune it to answer questions. The resulting architecture, which we call a Predictive Concept Decoder, enjoys favorable scaling properties: the auto-interp score of the bottleneck concepts improves with data, as does the performance on downstream applications. Specifically, PCDs can detect jailbreaks, secret hints, and implanted latent concepts, and are able to accurately surface latent user attributes.

papers.title: Building artificial neural circuits for domain-general cognition: a primer on brain-inspired systems-level architecture
papers.research_question: How can principles from the brain's systems-level architecture, specifically recurrence, communicability, and short-term topological changes, inform the design of artificial neural networks for domain-general cognition?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reviews three brain-inspired architectural principles (global recurrence, communicability, and short-term topological changes) that could serve as inductive biases for building artificial neural networks capable of domain-general cognition.
papers.conclusion: A systems-level view of the brain, focusing on recurrence, communication, and rapid structural changes, can provide valuable guidance for building artificial intelligence that achieves domain-general problem-solving, and testing these principles in artificial systems may help understand biological cognition.
papers.key_findings:
The brain's Multiple Demand system uses global recurrence to integrate and broadcast information across distributed regions, a feature that may be necessary for domain-general cognition in artificial systems.
Optimizing communicability in large-scale networks can improve information flow between modules, which is crucial for complex multimodal systems.
Short-term topological changes (e.g., via local learning rules) enable flexible reconfiguration of neural circuits, supporting rapid adaptation and abstract problem-solving.
Current artificial neural networks lack these system-level properties, and incorporating them could enhance their flexibility and generalization.
future_direction: Incorporating global recurrent loops into artificial neural networks to enable widespread integration and broadcasting of abstract knowledge.
Optimizing communicability in large-scale modular networks to improve information flow between components.
Enabling short-term topological changes through local learning rules to allow rapid reconfiguration and flexible problem-solving.
papers.abstract: There is a concerted effort to build domain-general artificial intelligence in the form of universal neural network models with sufficient computational flexibility to solve a wide variety of cognitive tasks but without requiring fine-tuning on individual problem spaces and domains. To do this, models need appropriate priors and inductive biases, such that trained models can generalise to out-of-distribution examples and new problem sets. Here we provide an overview of the hallmarks endowing biological neural networks with the functionality needed for flexible cognition, in order to establish which features might also be important to achieve similar functionality in artificial systems. We specifically discuss the role of system-level distribution of network communication and recurrence, in addition to the role of short-term topological changes for efficient local computation. As machine learning models become more complex, these principles may provide valuable directions in an otherwise vast space of possible architectures. In addition, testing these inductive biases within artificial systems may help us to understand the biological principles underlying domain-general cognition.

papers.title: Towards falsifiable interpretability research
papers.research_question: How can interpretability research be made more robust and falsifiable to avoid misleading conclusions and illusory progress?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that interpretability research suffers from over-reliance on intuition and a lack of falsifiability, and proposes a framework of best practices (e.g., formulating clear falsifiable hypotheses, quantifying methods, and conducting human verification) to make the field more robust and evidence-based.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability research must adopt a more rigorous, falsifiable scientific approach, using intuition as a starting point for testable hypotheses, to generate meaningful advances in understanding deep neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Saliency methods often fail to reflect meaningful properties of models, can be invariant to model parameters, and do not reliably improve human understanding of model decisions.
Single-neuron interpretability methods (e.g., visualization and selectivity analysis) can be misleading and may not be causally relevant to network function, as networks can function without class selectivity.
Interpretability research is impeded by a lack of falsifiable hypotheses, over-reliance on intuitive visualizations, insufficient quantification, and inadequate human verification.
papers.abstract: Methods for understanding the decisions of and mechanisms underlying deep neural networks (DNNs) typically rely on building intuition by emphasizing sensory or semantic features of individual examples. For instance, methods aim to visualize the components of an input which are "important" to a network's decision, or to measure the semantic properties of single neurons. Here, we argue that interpretability research suffers from an over-reliance on intuition-based approaches that risk-and in some cases have caused-illusory progress and misleading conclusions. We identify a set of limitations that we argue impede meaningful progress in interpretability research, and examine two popular classes of interpretability methods-saliency and single-neuron-based approaches-that serve as case studies for how overreliance on intuition and lack of falsifiability can undermine interpretability research. To address these concerns, we propose a strategy to address these impediments in the form of a framework for strongly falsifiable interpretability research. We encourage researchers to use their intuitions as a starting point to develop and test clear, falsifiable hypotheses, and hope that our framework yields robust, evidence-based interpretability methods that generate meaningful advances in our understanding of DNNs.

papers.title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 small perform the indirect object identification (IOI) task, and what internal circuit is responsible for this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and validates a circuit of 26 attention heads in GPT-2 small that performs indirect object identification, using a combination of interpretability techniques and quantitative criteria for faithfulness, completeness, and minimality.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, providing a step towards scaling interpretability to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered a circuit of 26 attention heads grouped into 7 classes (e.g., Name Mover Heads, S-Inhibition Heads) that implement the IOI task.
Identified redundant behavior such as Backup Name Mover Heads that activate when regular Name Mover Heads are ablated.
Found that Negative Name Mover Heads write in the opposite direction, potentially to hedge predictions.
Formulated and evaluated quantitative criteria (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) to validate circuit explanations.
The circuit shows significant but incomplete understanding, with gaps in completeness and minimality.
papers.limitation:
Not fully understanding some components, such as the attention patterns of S-Inhibition Heads and the role of MLPs and layer norms.
The circuit is not completely complete or minimal, as shown by quantitative criteria.
The analysis is limited to GPT-2 small, which is much smaller than state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Scale the approach to larger models like GPT-2 medium.
Investigate the behavior of the circuit on adversarial examples.
Understand the compensation effect in Backup Name Mover Heads.
papers.abstract: Research in mechanistic interpretability seeks to explain behaviors of machine learning models in terms of their internal components. However, most previous work either focuses on simple behaviors in small models, or describes complicated behaviors in larger models with broad strokes. In this work, we bridge this gap by presenting an explanation for how GPT-2 small performs a natural language task called indirect object identification (IOI). Our explanation encompasses 26 attention heads grouped into 7 main classes, which we discovered using a combination of interpretability approaches relying on causal interventions. To our knowledge, this investigation is the largest end-to-end attempt at reverse-engineering a natural behavior "in the wild" in a language model. We evaluate the reliability of our explanation using three quantitative criteria--faithfulness, completeness and minimality. Though these criteria support our explanation, they also point to remaining gaps in our understanding. Our work provides evidence that a mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, opening opportunities to scale our understanding to both larger models and more complex tasks.

papers.title: Causal Mediation Analysis for Interpreting Neural NLP: The Case of Gender Bias
papers.research_question: How can causal mediation analysis be used to interpret the internal mechanisms of neural NLP models, specifically to understand the role of individual components (like neurons and attention heads) in mediating gender bias?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a structural-behavioral framework based on causal mediation analysis for interpreting neural NLP models, and applies it to gender bias, revealing that bias effects are sparse, synergistic, and decomposable into direct and indirect effects.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis provides a useful framework for interpreting neural NLP models, offering insights into the internal mechanisms by which properties like gender bias flow from input to output through various model components.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias effects are sparse, concentrated in a relatively small number of model components (neurons and attention heads).
Gender bias effects are synergistic, with different model components interacting to amplify or repress their individual effects.
Gender bias effects are decomposable, with the total effect approximating the sum of direct and indirect effects, despite model non-linearity.
Larger models tend to exhibit larger gender bias effects.
The causal mediation analysis framework captures general patterns of causal structure in Transformer architectures, not just model-specific characteristics.
papers.limitation:
The experimental design focuses on gender bias in a binary setup, which does not account for a gender-inclusive spectrum.
Preliminary experiments with gender-neutral references (e.g., singular 'they') showed models have not learned these concepts well, and the setup suffers from confounders like plural 'they'.
Results for masked language models (e.g., BERT) are less clear, potentially due to differences in scoring multi-token continuations compared to autoregressive models.
future_direction: Applying the methodology to more gender-inclusive setups and other kinds of biases.
Using mediation analysis to guide the development of new debiasing methods that establish counterfactual fairness.
Exploring path-specific effects to identify exact mechanisms through which biases arise.
papers.abstract: Common methods for interpreting neural models in natural language processing typically examine either their structure or their behavior, but not both. We propose a methodology grounded in the theory of causal mediation analysis for interpreting which parts of a model are causally implicated in its behavior. It enables us to analyze the mechanisms by which information flows from input to output through various model components, known as mediators. We apply this methodology to analyze gender bias in pre-trained Transformer language models. We study the role of individual neurons and attention heads in mediating gender bias across three datasets designed to gauge a model's sensitivity to gender bias. Our mediation analysis reveals that gender bias effects are (i) sparse, concentrated in a small part of the network; (ii) synergistic, amplified or repressed by different components; and (iii) decomposable into effects flowing directly from the input and indirectly through the mediators.

papers.title: ShadowCoT: Cognitive Hijacking for Stealthy Reasoning Backdoors in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we exploit the internal reasoning mechanism of LLMs to create stealthy backdoor attacks that hijack multi-step reasoning chains?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ShadowCoT, a backdoor attack framework that hijacks the internal reasoning mechanism of LLMs by manipulating attention heads and residual streams, achieving high attack success with minimal parameter changes.
papers.conclusion: ShadowCoT reveals a new class of cognition-level threats in LLMs and highlights the urgent need for reasoning-aware defenses beyond surface-level consistency checks.
papers.key_findings:
ShadowCoT achieves high Attack Success Rate (94.4%) and Hijacking Success Rate (88.4%) across diverse reasoning tasks.
The attack preserves benign performance, making it stealthy and hard to detect.
More capable models (like Mistral-7B) are more vulnerable to reasoning hijacking.
The attack introduces a shortcutting phenomenon where models sometimes bypass the adversarial reasoning chain.
The adversarial reasoning chains generated by ShadowCoT are fluent and logically coherent, making them hard to distinguish from correct reasoning.
papers.limitation: The attack may lead to shortcutting, where the model bypasses the adversarial reasoning chain, which can reduce the interpretability of the attack.
future_direction: Developing reasoning-aware defenses to detect and mitigate cognitive hijacking attacks.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) enhances an LLM's ability to perform complex reasoning tasks, but it also introduces new security issues. In this work, we present ShadowCoT, a novel backdoor attack framework that targets the internal reasoning mechanism of LLMs. Unlike prior token-level or prompt-based attacks, ShadowCoT directly manipulates the model's cognitive reasoning path, enabling it to hijack multi-step reasoning chains and produce logically coherent but adversarial outcomes. By conditioning on internal reasoning states, ShadowCoT learns to recognize and selectively disrupt key reasoning steps, effectively mounting a self-reflective cognitive attack within the target model. Our approach introduces a lightweight yet effective multi-stage injection pipeline, which selectively rewires attention pathways and perturbs intermediate representations with minimal parameter overhead (only 0.15% updated). ShadowCoT further leverages reinforcement learning and reasoning chain pollution (RCP) to autonomously synthesize stealthy adversarial CoTs that remain undetectable to advanced defenses. Extensive experiments across diverse reasoning benchmarks and LLMs show that ShadowCoT consistently achieves high Attack Success Rate (94.4%) and Hijacking Success Rate (88.4%) while preserving benign performance. These results reveal an emergent class of cognition-level threats and highlight the urgent need for defenses beyond shallow surface-level consistency.

papers.title: Towards Biologically Plausible Deep Learning
papers.research_question: How can credit assignment in deep networks be achieved in a biologically plausible way, avoiding the implausible aspects of backpropagation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a biologically plausible learning mechanism for deep networks that interprets Spike-Timing-Dependent Plasticity (STDP) as stochastic gradient descent and uses a variational EM framework with target propagation for credit assignment without backpropagation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed approach addresses several biological implausibility issues of backpropagation and provides a promising direction for biologically plausible deep learning, with experimental validation on MNIST.
papers.key_findings:
STDP can be interpreted as stochastic gradient descent if neural dynamics push firing rates towards better objective function values.
The training procedure corresponds to variational EM with approximate inference, implemented by neural dynamics.
Targetprop (difference target propagation) can estimate gradients without backpropagation, enabling biologically plausible deep learning.
The method can learn a generative model that produces good samples on MNIST, with log-likelihood comparable to other models.
The variational EM updates with noise can be interpreted as training a denoising auto-encoder over both visible and latent variables, and iterating the associated Markov chain yields better samples.
papers.limitation:
The approach does not address the synchronization issue (the 5th implausible element of backpropagation).
More work is needed to connect in more detail with biology, including neural implementation using spikes and constraints on weight signs.
future_direction: Incorporate lateral connections to implement priors on joint distributions between nearby neurons.
Explore the replacement of MAP-based inference by MCMC-like inference with noise injection.
Apply the ideas to supervised learning and reinforcement learning.
papers.abstract: Neuroscientists have long criticised deep learning algorithms as incompatible with current knowledge of neurobiology. We explore more biologically plausible versions of deep representation learning, focusing here mostly on unsupervised learning but developing a learning mechanism that could account for supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning. The starting point is that the basic learning rule believed to govern synaptic weight updates (Spike-Timing-Dependent Plasticity) arises out of a simple update rule that makes a lot of sense from a machine learning point of view and can be interpreted as gradient descent on some objective function so long as the neuronal dynamics push firing rates towards better values of the objective function (be it supervised, unsupervised, or reward-driven). The second main idea is that this corresponds to a form of the variational EM algorithm, i.e., with approximate rather than exact posteriors, implemented by neural dynamics. Another contribution of this paper is that the gradients required for updating the hidden states in the above variational interpretation can be estimated using an approximation that only requires propagating activations forward and backward, with pairs of layers learning to form a denoising auto-encoder. Finally, we extend the theory about the probabilistic interpretation of auto-encoders to justify improved sampling schemes based on the generative interpretation of denoising auto-encoders, and we validate all these ideas on generative learning tasks.

papers.title: Toward Understanding Unlearning Difficulty: A Mechanistic Perspective and Circuit-Guided Difficulty Metric
papers.research_question: Can we define and quantify a sample’s unlearning difficulty from a mechanistic perspective before unlearning? Can this predicted difficulty be linked to the internal mechanisms (e.g. circuits) within the model?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Circuit-guided Unlearning Difficulty (CUD), a metric to quantify sample-level unlearning difficulty from a mechanistic perspective before unlearning, based on circuit-level signals.
papers.conclusion: CUD is a reliable metric for quantifying unlearning difficulty from a mechanistic perspective, enabling proactive identification of easy and hard samples and promoting difficulty-aware unlearning methods.
papers.key_findings:
CUD reliably separates intrinsically easy and hard samples for unlearning and remains stable across unlearning methods.
CUD is robust to the choice of similarity metric and loss function used in its construction.
Easy-to-unlearn samples are associated with shorter, shallower circuits concentrated in earlier-to-intermediate layers.
Hard-to-unlearn samples rely on longer and deeper pathways closer to late-stage computation and output layers.
CUD provides a continuous, pre-unlearning difficulty score that is distinct from post-hoc measures like MRD.
papers.limitation: CUD may be computationally expensive due to the need for circuit discovery.
future_direction: Using CUD to construct controlled forget sets at specified difficulty levels for benchmarking.
Designing curriculum-style unlearning schedules based on difficulty.
Developing efficient approximations of CUD.
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning is becoming essential for building trustworthy and compliant language models. Yet unlearning success varies considerably across individual samples: some are reliably erased, while others persist despite the same procedure. We argue that this disparity is not only a data-side phenomenon, but also reflects model-internal mechanisms that encode and protect memorized information. We study this problem from a mechanistic perspective based on model circuits--structured interaction pathways that govern how predictions are formed. We propose Circuit-guided Unlearning Difficulty (CUD), a {\em pre-unlearning} metric that assigns each sample a continuous difficulty score using circuit-level signals. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CUD reliably separates intrinsically easy and hard samples, and remains stable across unlearning methods. We identify key circuit-level patterns that reveal a mechanistic signature of difficulty: easy-to-unlearn samples are associated with shorter, shallower interactions concentrated in earlier-to-intermediate parts of the original model, whereas hard samples rely on longer and deeper pathways closer to late-stage computation. Compared to existing qualitative studies, CUD takes a first step toward a principled, fine-grained, and interpretable analysis of unlearning difficulty; and motivates the development of unlearning methods grounded in model mechanisms.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability in the Presence of Architectural Obfuscation
papers.research_question: Can we still locate, characterise and manipulate the mechanisms that drive model behaviour once the observable representations have been permuted or otherwise obfuscated?
papers.core_contribution: Obfuscation dramatically alters internal activation patterns yet preserves the layer-wise computational graph, retaining global model behavior while impeding fine-grained mechanistic analysis of user-specific content.
papers.conclusion: The essential circuit for the task survives obfuscation, but activation patterns become more diffuse, attention roles invert in later blocks, and head-level importance is scattered, making causal tracing noisier while leaving top-line accuracy intact.
papers.key_findings:
Obfuscation preserves the high-level circuit structure but alters internal activation patterns, making them more diffuse.
Logit attribution shows the same attention heads dominate in both models, but their contributions become noisier and more scattered under obfuscation.
Activation patching reveals the computational path is less efficient and more dispersed in the obfuscated model, with later layers taking on more responsibility.
Head patching shows that some heads change their polarity of contribution (e.g., from positive to negative) in the obfuscated model.
Obfuscation hinders fine-grained reverse engineering (e.g., prompt reconstruction) without erasing the coarse computations necessary for task performance.
future_direction: Strengthen security guarantees without forfeiting interpretability by combining obfuscation with cryptographic techniques like fully homomorphic encryption.
papers.abstract: Architectural obfuscation - e.g., permuting hidden-state tensors, linearly transforming embedding tables, or remapping tokens - has recently gained traction as a lightweight substitute for heavyweight cryptography in privacy-preserving large-language-model (LLM) inference. While recent work has shown that these techniques can be broken under dedicated reconstruction attacks, their impact on mechanistic interpretability has not been systematically studied. In particular, it remains unclear whether scrambling a network's internal representations truly thwarts efforts to understand how the model works, or simply relocates the same circuits to an unfamiliar coordinate system. We address this gap by analyzing a GPT-2-small model trained from scratch with a representative obfuscation map. Assuming the obfuscation map is private and the original basis is hidden (mirroring an honest-but-curious server), we apply logit-lens attribution, causal path-patching, and attention-head ablation to locate and manipulate known circuits. Our findings reveal that obfuscation dramatically alters activation patterns within attention heads yet preserves the layer-wise computational graph. This disconnect hampers reverse-engineering of user prompts: causal traces lose their alignment with baseline semantics, and token-level logit attributions become too noisy to reconstruct. At the same time, feed-forward and residual pathways remain functionally intact, suggesting that obfuscation degrades fine-grained interpretability without compromising top-level task performance. These results establish quantitative evidence that architectural obfuscation can simultaneously (i) retain global model behaviour and (ii) impede mechanistic analyses of user-specific content. By mapping where interpretability breaks down, our study provides guidance for future privacy defences and for robustness-aware interpretability tooling.

papers.title: Universal Refusal Circuits Across LLMs: Cross-Model Transfer via Trajectory Replay and Concept-Basis Reconstruction
papers.research_question: Are refusal circuits universal across LLMs? Can a refusal circuit extracted from a donor model be transferred to a target model without target-side refusal supervision?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for transferring refusal circuits across LLMs without target-side refusal supervision, combining concept-basis reconstruction and a weight-SVD stability guard, providing evidence for semantic universality of safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: Refusal circuits are universal across LLMs and can be transferred via semantic recipe invariance, enabling cross-model circuit editing without target-side refusal supervision.
papers.key_findings:
The method successfully transfers refusal attenuation across 8 model pairs, including cross-family and cross-architecture transfers.
Refusal circuits are composed of a stable mixture of concept atoms, enabling cross-model transfer via semantic recipe invariance.
The weight-SVD guard prevents capability collapse by projecting interventions away from high-variance weight subspaces.
The transfer works without target-side refusal supervision, relying only on benign concept prompts and validation data.
The method preserves model capabilities on math and code tasks while reducing refusal rates.
papers.limitation:
Efficacy depends on coverage of the Concept Atom Registry; if refusal circuit uses features orthogonal to the atoms, reconstruction may fail.
Weight-SVD guard relies on the heuristic that capability-critical circuits reside in high-variance principal components, which may not generalize to all tasks.
Method is white-box, requiring access to model weights and internal activations, limiting applicability to closed-source systems.
future_direction: Expand CAR coverage to test transfer beyond refusal directions to multi-behavior editing.
Explore black-box approximations of semantic fingerprints for closed-source systems.
Test the method on a wider range of models and alignment behaviors.
papers.abstract: Refusal behavior in aligned LLMs is often viewed as model-specific, yet we hypothesize it stems from a universal, low-dimensional semantic circuit shared across models. To test this, we introduce Trajectory Replay via Concept-Basis Reconstruction, a framework that transfers refusal interventions from donor to target models, spanning diverse architectures (e.g., Dense to MoE) and training regimes, without using target-side refusal supervision.
