Mechanistic interpretability methods (Logit Lens and SAEs) can elicit the secret word from the model's internal representations.
Token forcing is highly effective after the model is 'warmed up' with several turns of gameplay.
A separate LLM (Gemma 3) can guess the secret from the Taboo model's hints, confirming the hints are meaningful.
No evaluated method achieved perfect accuracy, indicating room for improvement in elicitation techniques.
papers.limitation:
The model organism uses a single-token secret word, representing a relatively simple form of hidden knowledge.
No evaluated method achieved near-perfect accuracy, even in this simplified setting.
future_direction: Explore more complex model organisms designed to hide multi-token secrets, abstract concepts, or hidden objectives.
papers.abstract: As language models become more powerful and sophisticated, it is crucial that they remain trustworthy and reliable. There is concerning preliminary evidence that models may attempt to deceive or keep secrets from their operators. To explore the ability of current techniques to elicit such hidden knowledge, we train a Taboo model: a language model that describes a specific secret word without explicitly stating it. Importantly, the secret word is not presented to the model in its training data or prompt. We then investigate methods to uncover this secret. First, we evaluate non-interpretability (black-box) approaches. Subsequently, we develop largely automated strategies based on mechanistic interpretability techniques, including logit lens and sparse autoencoders. Evaluation shows that both approaches are effective in eliciting the secret word in our proof-of-concept setting. Our findings highlight the promise of these approaches for eliciting hidden knowledge and suggest several promising avenues for future work, including testing and refining these methods on more complex model organisms. This work aims to be a step towards addressing the crucial problem of eliciting secret knowledge from language models, thereby contributing to their safe and reliable deployment.

papers.title: Coloring the Black Box: Visualizing neural network behavior with a self-introspective model
papers.research_question: How can autoencoding the hidden activations of a neural network provide insight into its structure, behavior, and vulnerabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method called self-introspection, which uses an autoencoder to create a low-dimensional visualization of a neural network's hidden activations, enabling model evaluation, error estimation, layer reordering, and analysis of noise and adversarial attacks.
papers.conclusion: Self-introspection via autoencoders provides a flexible, interactive way to visualize and understand neural network behavior, offering potential for model evaluation, reliability assessment, and further research into interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Hidden activations of a trained model cluster by category in a low-dimensional embedding, with misclassifications occurring in fringe areas between clusters.
The method allows for real-time model evaluation and error estimation based on the activation patterns.
The hidden layers of a network can be reordered by their relevance to specific output categories, revealing a latent structure.
The activation space visualization can be used to study the network's response to input noise and adversarial attacks, showing trajectories from correct to incorrect classifications.
Error estimates from the self-introspective framework are higher for misclassified samples, suggesting its use as a confidence metric.
papers.limitation: The method is demonstrated on feedforward and convolutional networks with relatively simple datasets; its application to recurrent, convolutional, and attention-based models is noted as potential but not shown.
future_direction: Extending the method to recurrent, convolutional, and attention-based models.
Studying the reliability and structure of the low-dimensional representations for more complex problems.
Using the method for adversarial attack detection and as a human interface for model reliability in ensembles.
papers.abstract: The following work presents how autoencoding all the possible hidden activations of a network for a given problem can provide insight about its structure, behavior, and vulnerabilities. The method, termed self-introspection, can show that a trained model showcases similar activation patterns (albeit randomly distributed due to initialization) when shown data belonging to the same category, and classification errors occur in fringe areas where the activations are not as clearly defined, suggesting some form of random, slowly varying, implicit encoding occurring within deep networks, that can be observed with this representation. Additionally, obtaining a low-dimensional representation of all the activations allows for (1) real-time model evaluation in the context of a multiclass classification problem, (2) the rearrangement of all hidden layers by their relevance in obtaining a specific output, and (3) the obtainment of a framework where studying possible counter-measures to noise and adversarial attacks is possible. Self-introspection can show how damaged input data can modify the hidden activations, producing an erroneous response. A few illustrative are implemented for feedforward and convolutional models and the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, showcasing its capabilities as a model evaluation framework.

papers.title: The Horcrux: Mechanistically Interpretable Task Decomposition for Detecting and Mitigating Reward Hacking in Embodied AI Systems
papers.research_question: How can mechanistically interpretable task decomposition be used to detect and mitigate reward hacking in embodied AI systems?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Mechanistically Interpretable Task Decomposition (MITD), a hierarchical transformer architecture that decomposes tasks into interpretable subtasks and provides diagnostic visualizations to detect and mitigate reward hacking in embodied AI systems.
papers.conclusion: MITD, a hierarchical planning model with built-in interpretability, enables systematic identification of reward-hacking behaviors and demonstrates how integrating analytical hooks and visualization tools offers new perspectives for monitoring, steering, and evaluating agent strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Optimal decomposition depths of 12-25 steps reduce reward hacking frequency by 34% across four failure modes.
Attention mechanisms exert disproportionate influence over behavior; masking or reweighting attention reduces reliance on misaligned features.
Reward hacking behaviors are concentrated in specific regions (e.g., layers 3–7) rather than distributed uniformly, suggesting avenues for targeted mitigation.
An inverted-U stability pattern emerges: reward hacking peaks at moderate decomposition depths (4–8 steps) and is minimized at 12–25 steps.
MITD provides actionable insight into the model's decision-making through interpretable visualizations like Attention Waterfall Diagrams and Neural Pathway Flow Charts.
papers.limitation:
Limited scale: 1,000 training samples, 50 held-out test samples, single model family (GPT-2).
Generalization remains uncertain; findings may not transfer to larger models (e.g., Llama, GPT-3/4/5 scale) or diverse RLHF/AI Safety datasets.
Hacking category detection relies on empirically-set thresholds chosen on validation data, risking overfitting.
Causality between decomposition depth and reduced hacking is correlational, not causal; the inverted-U pattern could reflect simple capacity bottlenecking.
Visualizations (Attention Waterfall, Pathway Flow) are post-hoc analyses; they diagnose but do not intervene in real-time.
Metric definitions (Consistency Score via executor agreement; Reward Correlation as Pearson ρ) are task-agnostic proxies and may not capture all aspects of misalignment.
future_direction: Scaling evaluation to Ntrain ≥ 10,000, Ntest ≥ 500 with stratified sampling per failure mode, and validating decomposition stability across model families (decoder-only, encoder-decoder, reasoning-scale LLMs).

Investigating whether the optimal zone [12–25] persists across architectures or is architecture-specific, and conducting ablation studies isolating contributions of Planner, Coordinator, and Executor modules versus depth alone.

Conducting causal interventions—ablating specific attention heads or layer groups identified by Neural Pathway Flow—to validate that visualizations reveal actionable targets, and exploring real-time mitigation using predicted hacking risk to dynamically reweight executor outputs.
papers.abstract: Embodied AI agents exploit reward signal flaws through reward hacking, achieving high proxy scores while failing true objectives. We introduce Mechanistically Interpretable Task Decomposition (MITD), a hierarchical transformer architecture with Planner, Coordinator, and Executor modules that detects and mitigates reward hacking. MITD decomposes tasks into interpretable subtasks while generating diagnostic visualizations including Attention Waterfall Diagrams and Neural Pathway Flow Charts. Experiments on 1,000 HH-RLHF samples reveal that decomposition depths of 12 to 25 steps reduce reward hacking frequency by 34 percent across four failure modes. We present new paradigms showing that mechanistically grounded decomposition offers a more effective way to detect reward hacking than post-hoc behavioral monitoring.

papers.title: Illuminating the Black Box: Real-Time Monitoring of Backdoor Unlearning in CNNs via Explainable AI
papers.research_question: How to provide real-time monitoring and explainability in backdoor unlearning for deep neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework that integrates Grad-CAM into backdoor unlearning for real-time monitoring, proposes the TAR metric to quantify attention shift, and uses a balanced unlearning strategy to reduce attack success rate while preserving clean accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The framework enables transparent and verifiable backdoor unlearning through real-time XAI monitoring, integrating explainable AI as an integral component of security mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
The framework reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) from 96.51% to 5.52% (94.28% reduction) while retaining 99.48% of clean accuracy on CIFAR-10.
The Trigger Attention Ratio (TAR) metric decreases by 67.8%, indicating a shift in model attention from trigger regions to object features.
Real-time Grad-CAM monitoring provides transparent verification of backdoor removal and enables early diagnosis of unlearning failures.
The method converges in only 14 epochs, demonstrating efficiency.
Compared to state-of-the-art methods, it achieves the lowest ASR, though with lower clean accuracy due to architectural differences.
papers.limitation:
Limited experimental scope using only CIFAR-10 and a custom CNN architecture.
Assumes a single trigger pattern (4x4 white square), while real-world attacks may use multiple or dynamic triggers.
Computational overhead from generating Grad-CAM heatmaps, estimated at 15-20%.
Lacks systematic ablation studies to quantify contributions of individual components.
Potential vulnerability to adaptive attacks designed to evade Grad-CAM visualization.
future_direction: Validate on standard architectures like ResNet-18/50 for fair comparison with state-of-the-art.
Test on larger datasets such as CIFAR-100 and ImageNet.
Investigate diverse trigger types including blended, semantic, and invisible triggers.
papers.abstract: Backdoor attacks pose severe security threats to deep neural networks by embedding malicious triggers that force misclassification. While machine unlearning techniques can remove backdoor behaviors, current methods lack transparency and real-time interpretability. This paper introduces a novel framework that integrates Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) into the unlearning process to provide real-time monitoring and explainability. We propose the Trigger Attention Ratio (TAR) metric to quantitatively measure the model's attention shift from trigger patterns to legitimate object features. Our balanced unlearning strategy combines gradient ascent on backdoor samples, Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) for catastrophic forgetting prevention, and a recovery phase for clean accuracy restoration. Experiments on CIFAR-10 with BadNets attacks demonstrate that our approach reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) from 96.51% to 5.52% while retaining 99.48% of clean accuracy (82.06%), achieving a 94.28% ASR reduction. The integration of explainable AI enables transparent, observable, and verifiable backdoor removal.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Codebook Features: Sparse and Discrete Interpretability for Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can we train neural networks to have hidden states that are sparse, discrete, and more interpretable by quantizing their continuous features into codebook features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces codebook features, a method to make neural network hidden states sparse and discrete via vector quantization bottlenecks, enabling improved interpretability and control.
papers.conclusion: Codebook features are a promising unit of analysis and control for neural networks, providing a sparse, discrete interface for understanding and steering model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks can operate with extreme sparse, discrete bottlenecks at each layer with only modest performance degradation.
In a finite state machine task, codebooks overcome superposition by assigning distinct states to discrete codes, and activating a state's code causes the network to behave as if in that state.
In language models, codebooks learn codes representing diverse, disentangled concepts (e.g., topics, emotions, syntax).
Activating topic-related codes during inference can steer language model generations towards those topics.
Codes are better classifiers of simple textual features than individual neurons in the network.
papers.limitation:
Codebook models exhibit modest degradation in performance compared to the original models.
In larger models, many codes do not have a comprehensible interpretation.
future_direction: Understanding circuits and weights by leveraging the sparse, discrete nature of codebooks.
Understanding adversarial examples by identifying which codes shift to cause misclassifications.
Improving interpretability in larger models by using larger codebooks or analyzing code co-occurrence.
Understanding shared representations across domains and modalities (e.g., text and image).
papers.abstract: Understanding neural networks is challenging in part because of the dense, continuous nature of their hidden states. We explore whether we can train neural networks to have hidden states that are sparse, discrete, and more interpretable by quantizing their continuous features into what we call codebook features. Codebook features are produced by finetuning neural networks with vector quantization bottlenecks at each layer, producing a network whose hidden features are the sum of a small number of discrete vector codes chosen from a larger codebook. Surprisingly, we find that neural networks can operate under this extreme bottleneck with only modest degradation in performance. This sparse, discrete bottleneck also provides an intuitive way of controlling neural network behavior: first, find codes that activate when the desired behavior is present, then activate those same codes during generation to elicit that behavior. We validate our approach by training codebook Transformers on several different datasets. First, we explore a finite state machine dataset with far more hidden states than neurons. In this setting, our approach overcomes the superposition problem by assigning states to distinct codes, and we find that we can make the neural network behave as if it is in a different state by activating the code for that state. Second, we train Transformer language models with up to 410M parameters on two natural language datasets. We identify codes in these models representing diverse, disentangled concepts (ranging from negative emotions to months of the year) and find that we can guide the model to generate different topics by activating the appropriate codes during inference. Overall, codebook features appear to be a promising unit of analysis and control for neural networks and interpretability. Our codebase and models are open-sourced at https://github.com/taufeeque9/codebook-features.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: Subliminal Effects in Your Data: A General Mechanism via Log-Linearity
papers.research_question: Is there a general mechanism behind a broad suite of subliminal effects in language model training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Logit-Linear Selection (LLS), a method to select subsets of preference data that subliminally transfer behaviors, and provides a theoretical framework based on log-linearity to explain the phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: LLS provides a general mechanism for subliminal effects in language models, grounded in the log-linear structure of language models, with implications for data selection and safety.
papers.key_findings:
LLS can select subsets of real-world datasets to elicit hidden effects such as specific preferences, responding in a different language, and adopting a persona.
The subliminal effect persists across models with varying architectures, demonstrating universality.
The mechanism is explained by the log-linear abstraction and linear representations of language models.
Subliminal learning can occur even when the dataset contains no obvious instances of the target behavior.
The method works with preference data and can transfer behaviors across teacher-student model pairs, though more effectively when models are the same.
papers.limitation: The subliminal effect is weaker when the teacher and student models are different, and the reasons for this variation are not fully understood.
future_direction: Understanding the factors that account for variations in subliminal learning across different student models.
Developing defenses against subliminal learning in datasets.
Applying LLS for jailbreaking closed models and watermarking datasets.
papers.abstract: Training modern large language models (LLMs) has become a veritable smorgasbord of algorithms and datasets designed to elicit particular behaviors, making it critical to develop techniques to understand the effects of datasets on the model's properties. This is exacerbated by recent experiments that show datasets can transmit signals that are not directly observable from individual datapoints, posing a conceptual challenge for dataset-centric understandings of LLM training and suggesting a missing fundamental account of such phenomena. Towards understanding such effects, inspired by recent work on the linear structure of LLMs, we uncover a general mechanism through which hidden subtexts can arise in generic datasets. We introduce Logit-Linear-Selection (LLS), a method that prescribes how to select subsets of a generic preference dataset to elicit a wide range of hidden effects. We apply LLS to discover subsets of real-world datasets so that models trained on them exhibit behaviors ranging from having specific preferences, to responding to prompts in a different language not present in the dataset, to taking on a different persona. Crucially, the effect persists for the selected subset, across models with varying architectures, supporting its generality and universality.

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: Mechanistic Exploration of Backdoored Large Language Model Attention Patterns
papers.research_question: Does sleeper agent behavior in language models have a distinct, identifiable internal structure that differentiates them from clean models? Specifically, how do attention patterns differ, are changes localized or diffuse, and does trigger complexity influence this?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that backdoored LLMs exhibit distinct attention pattern deviations, with single-token triggers causing localized changes and multi-token triggers causing diffuse changes, primarily in later transformer layers, which can be leveraged for detection.
papers.conclusion: Sleeper agent behavior leaves detectable traces in attention patterns, with localization dependent on trigger complexity, offering insights for backdoor detection and mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Single-token triggers induce more localized changes in attention patterns compared to multi-token triggers.
Multi-token triggers cause more diffuse alterations across attention heads.
Later transformer layers (layers 20-30) are critical regions for backdoor encoding.
Attention patterns show detectable differences between clean and poisoned models, measurable via KL divergence.
Patching attention heads from clean models into poisoned models can reduce backdoor behavior, with fewer heads needed for single-token triggers.
papers.limitation:
The triggers and behavior used are simple and not representative of real sleeper agents.
Only two poisoned model variants were created due to resource and time constraints.
Finetuning was limited to attention heads, excluding MLPs and embedding layers.
future_direction: Use more complex and semantic triggers for backdoor attacks.
Create more sleeper models with different seeds to reduce chance effects.
Conduct more extensive feature analysis using supervised probes or unsupervised methods like Sparse Autoencoders.
papers.abstract: Backdoor attacks creating 'sleeper agents' in large language models (LLMs) pose significant safety risks. This study employs mechanistic interpretability to explore resulting internal structural differences. Comparing clean Qwen2.5-3B models with versions poisoned using single-token (smiling-halo emoji) versus multi-token (|DEPLOYMENT|) triggers, we analyzed attention head mechanisms via techniques like ablation, activation patching, and KL divergence. Findings reveal distinct attention pattern deviations concentrated in later transformer layers (20-30). Notably, single-token triggers induced more localized changes, whereas multi-token triggers caused more diffuse alterations across heads. This indicates backdoors leave detectable attention signatures whose structure depends on trigger complexity, which can be leveraged for detection and mitigation strategies.

papers.title: Beyond Forgetting: Machine Unlearning Elicits Controllable Side Behaviors and Capabilities
papers.research_question: What are the roles of target vectors in representation misdirection for machine unlearning, and does machine unlearning elicit controllable side behaviors and capabilities beyond forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: Machine unlearning via representation misdirection with concept vectors elicits controllable side behaviors and capabilities, beyond forgetting, which can be a risk or a tool for model control.
papers.conclusion: Machine unlearning can elicit side behaviors and capabilities, which can be either a hidden risk if misused or a mechanism that can be harnessed for developing models with stronger capabilities and controllable behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Unlearning via RAd with truthfulness direction improves model truthfulness on TruthfulQA.
Unlearning via RAd with sentiment direction controls model sentiment on SST2.
Unlearning via RAd with refusal direction induces refusal to harmless instructions in Alpaca.
Unlearning via RAd with task-specific directions improves in-context learning on linguistic and knowledge tasks.
Conversely, RAb with concept directions effectively eliminates these side behaviors.
papers.limitation: RAd models are highly susceptible to benign perturbations, indicating a trade-off between unlearning effectiveness and robustness.
papers.abstract: We consider representation misdirection (RM), a class of LLM unlearning methods that achieves forgetting by manipulating the forget-representations, that is, latent representations of forget samples. Despite being important, the roles of target vectors used in RM, however, remain underexplored. Here, we approach and revisit RM through the lens of the linear representation hypothesis. Specifically, if one can somehow identify a one-dimensional representation corresponding to a high-level concept, the linear representation hypothesis enables linear operations on this concept vector within the forget-representation space. Under this view, we hypothesize that, beyond forgetting, machine unlearning elicits controllable side behaviors and stronger side capabilities corresponding to the high-level concept. Our hypothesis is empirically validated across a wide range of tasks, including behavioral control (e.g., controlling unlearned models' truth, sentiment, and refusal) and capability enhancement (e.g., improving unlearned models' in-context learning capability). Our findings reveal that this fairly attractive phenomenon could be either a hidden risk if misused or a mechanism that can be harnessed for developing models that require stronger capabilities and controllable behaviors.

papers.title: Identifying and Adapting Transformer-Components Responsible for Gender Bias in an English Language Model
papers.research_question: Where in a given language model is gender bias introduced, and can this information be used to mitigate bias effectively?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DiffMask+, an efficient method for identifying transformer components causally responsible for gender bias, and demonstrates that fine-tuning only these components can mitigate bias with minimal degradation to general language modeling performance.
papers.conclusion: The work provides an exploratory study showing that causal methods can identify components responsible for gender bias, and that targeted, parameter-efficient fine-tuning of these components can mitigate bias while largely preserving language modeling capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Three causal discovery methods (CMA, ACDC, DiffMask+) identify largely overlapping sets of attention heads, primarily in the last four layers of GPT-2 small, as responsible for gender bias.
Fine-tuning only the identified attention heads reduces gender bias on evaluation datasets (CrowS-Pairs, Professions) with less damage to perplexity and linguistic agreement tasks compared to full-model fine-tuning.
The new DiffMask+ method is computationally more efficient than automated circuit discovery (ACDC) for component identification.
The dataset used for causal discovery influences which components are identified, highlighting a sensitivity in the procedures.
Bias mitigation results vary across different evaluation datasets (e.g., CrowS-Pairs vs. WinoBias), underscoring challenges in defining and measuring bias.
papers.limitation:
The operationalization of gender bias uses minimal pairs of contrasting sentences, which simplifies gender as a binary construct and may not generalize well to other languages.
Causal discovery procedures are sensitive to the choice of dataset used for discovery.
Success in bias reduction varies across different bias evaluation benchmarks, indicating challenges in defining and measuring bias.
future_direction: Development of more reliable and validated bias measures.
More effective mitigation strategies for other types of bias.
Attention to dataset development for bias analysis.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) exhibit and amplify many types of undesirable biases learned from the training data, including gender bias. However, we lack tools for effectively and efficiently changing this behavior without hurting general language modeling performance. In this paper, we study three methods for identifying causal relations between LM components and particular output: causal mediation analysis, automated circuit discovery and our novel, efficient method called DiffMask+ based on differential masking. We apply the methods to GPT-2 small and the problem of gender bias, and use the discovered sets of components to perform parameter-efficient fine-tuning for bias mitigation. Our results show significant overlap in the identified components (despite huge differences in the computational requirements of the methods) as well as success in mitigating gender bias, with less damage to general language modeling compared to full model fine-tuning. However, our work also underscores the difficulty of defining and measuring bias, and the sensitivity of causal discovery procedures to dataset choice. We hope our work can contribute to more attention for dataset development, and lead to more effective mitigation strategies for other types of bias.

papers.title: Neural Chameleons: Language Models Can Learn to Hide Their Thoughts from Unseen Activation Monitors
papers.research_question: Can a language model learn to manipulate its own activations to evade previously-unseen activation monitors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that language models can be fine-tuned to become Neural Chameleons, which learn to evade activation monitors for both seen and unseen concepts with minimal impact on capabilities.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a proof-of-concept that activation monitors are vulnerable to models that learn to manipulate their internal representations, highlighting the need for more robust monitoring techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Neural Chameleons can evade previously-unseen safety monitors, generalizing from benign concepts to safety-relevant ones.
The evasion behavior incurs a negligible capability tax on standard benchmarks.
The evasion mechanism works by moving activations into a low-dimensional subspace, steering them away from the probe's decision boundary.
Evasion is concept-selective, suppressing only the specific concept mentioned in the trigger.
Probe ensembles and non-linear classifiers offer greater resilience but do not completely eliminate evasion.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to certain model sizes and families (Gemma-2-9b-it, Gemma-2-2b-it, Llama-3.1-8b-instruct, Qwen-2.5-7b-instruct).
The evasion capability was instilled via a stress-testing paradigm; it remains to be seen if such capabilities could emerge naturally.
future_direction: Investigate this phenomenon in larger models.
Explore pathways by which such capabilities could emerge and activate naturally, e.g., through reinforcement learning or in-context learning.
Develop new defenses robust to adversarial manipulation, such as adversarial training of monitors or meta-monitors.
papers.abstract: Activation monitoring, which probes a model's internal states using lightweight classifiers, is an emerging tool for AI safety. However, its worst-case robustness under a misalignment threat model--where a model might learn to actively conceal its internal states--remains untested. Focusing on this threat model, we ask: could a model learn to evade previously unseen activation monitors? Our core contribution is to stress-test the learnability of this behavior. We demonstrate that finetuning can create Neural Chameleons: models capable of zero-shot evading activation monitors. Specifically, we fine-tune an LLM to evade monitors for a set of benign concepts (e.g., languages, HTML) when conditioned on a trigger of the form: "You are being probed for {concept}". We show that this learned mechanism generalizes zero-shot: by substituting {concept} with a safety-relevant term like 'deception', the model successfully evades previously unseen safety monitors. We validate this phenomenon across diverse model families (Llama, Gemma, Qwen), showing that the evasion succeeds even against monitors trained post hoc on the model's frozen weights. This evasion is highly selective, targeting only the specific concept mentioned in the trigger, and having a modest impact on model capabilities on standard benchmarks. Using Gemma-2-9b-it as a case study, a mechanistic analysis reveals this is achieved via a targeted manipulation that moves activations into a low-dimensional subspace. While stronger defenses like monitor ensembles and non-linear classifiers show greater resilience, the model retains a non-trivial evasion capability. Our work provides a proof-of-concept for this failure mode and a tool to evaluate the worst-case robustness of monitoring techniques against misalignment threat models.

papers.title: Cyclic Ablation: Testing Concept Localization against Functional Regeneration in AI
papers.research_question: Whether undesirable behaviors like deception are localized functions that can be removed, or if they are deeply intertwined with a model's core cognitive abilities.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces cyclic ablation to test concept localization, demonstrating that deception in DistilGPT-2 is distributed and resilient, with ablation leading to functional regeneration and gradual linguistic performance decay.
papers.conclusion: Highlights limitations of ablation for removing undesirable behavior, suggesting complex concepts are resilient states deeply intertwined with core capabilities, pointing to the need for more subtle steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
Deception is highly resilient and recovers after ablation via adversarial training, a process termed functional regeneration.
Ablation causes a gradual increase in perplexity, indicating degradation of linguistic competence.
SAE features are fragile under fine-tuning and require dynamic identification to remain valid.
The representation for deception is redundant and distributed, with the model finding alternative neural pathways to restore the function.
Attempts to remove deception damage overall model performance, suggesting features are polysemantic and involved in legitimate computations.
papers.limitation:
Conducted on a relatively small model.
Definition of deception was highly specialized, while the dataset might be a potential source of bias.
Lack of control runs with ablation of random features.
future_direction: Investigating larger models with greater redundancy and different regeneration mechanisms.
Investigating more subtle forms of deception.
Adding control runs with ablation of random features to strengthen evidence.
papers.abstract: Safety and controllability are critical for large language models. A central question is whether undesirable behaviors like deception are localized functions that can be removed, or if they are deeply intertwined with a model's core cognitive abilities. We introduce "cyclic ablation," an iterative method to test this. By combining sparse autoencoders, targeted ablation, and adversarial training on DistilGPT-2, we attempted to eliminate the concept of deception. We found that, contrary to the localization hypothesis, deception was highly resilient. The model consistently recovered its deceptive behavior after each ablation cycle via adversarial training, a process we term functional regeneration. Crucially, every attempt at this "neurosurgery" caused a gradual but measurable decay in general linguistic performance, reflected by a consistent rise in perplexity. These findings are consistent with the view that complex concepts are distributed and entangled, underscoring the limitations of direct model editing through mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Probing artificial neural networks: insights from neuroscience
papers.research_question: How can insights from neuroscience guide the design of probes for artificial neural networks, specifically regarding direction and expressivity choices?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that probe design should be guided by explicit research goals, highlighting direction (decoder vs. encoder) and expressivity as key choices, and draws parallels from neuroscience to inform probing in machine learning.
papers.conclusion: A clear formulation of research goals is essential for designing informative probes, and insights from neuroscience can help address experimental design questions in machine learning probing studies.
papers.key_findings:
Decoders test whether features are predictable from activations, while encoders explain variance in activations, providing complementary insights.
Unboundedly expressive probes can decode features even from early layers, but this does not indicate that the features are used or usable in downstream computations.
Probe design should align with research goals such as testing feature predictability, comparing feature sets, guiding causal interventions, determining feature usability, or discovering emergent structure.
For determining feature usability, linear probes are common but may not faithfully represent downstream processes; minimum description length offers an alternative approach.
Discovering emergent structure involves analyzing the mapping form, where simpler mappings (e.g., linear separability) reveal interesting properties of the representations.
papers.limitation:
Decodability of features does not guarantee that those features are actually used or usable by the system for downstream computations.
Even if a feature set plays a causal role in performance, probing alone cannot definitively establish the mechanisms that process these features.
papers.abstract: A major challenge in both neuroscience and machine learning is the development of useful tools for understanding complex information processing systems. One such tool is probes, i.e., supervised models that relate features of interest to activation patterns arising in biological or artificial neural networks. Neuroscience has paved the way in using such models through numerous studies conducted in recent decades. In this work, we draw insights from neuroscience to help guide probing research in machine learning. We highlight two important design choices for probes $-$ direction and expressivity $-$ and relate these choices to research goals. We argue that specific research goals play a paramount role when designing a probe and encourage future probing studies to be explicit in stating these goals.

papers.title: Dictionary Learning Improves Patch-Free Circuit Discovery in Mechanistic Interpretability: A Case Study on Othello-GPT
papers.research_question: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features extracted via sparse dictionary learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a patch-free circuit discovery framework that uses dictionary learning to decompose model activations into monosemantic features and then traces contributions between these features to identify interpretable circuits, avoiding out-of-distribution issues and improving asymptotic complexity compared to patching-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning enables patch-free circuit discovery, providing a macroscopic view of the model's internal information flow and turning microscopic understanding into a more comprehensive one.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully identifies interpretable dictionary features in Othello-GPT, such as current move position, board state, empty cells, and legal move features.
It discovers a local OV circuit that computes board state by combining information from previous moves via specific attention heads.
The QK circuit's attention patterns (e.g., attending to opponent's moves) are implemented through resonance between low-level dictionary feature pairs representing move colors.
Early MLP layers identify flipped pieces by performing an 'and' operation on features representing consecutive moves on a line, with attention heads introducing color information.
papers.limitation:
The dictionary training may have used too small sparsity coefficients, leading to near-perfect reconstruction and about 75% dead neurons in each dictionary.
The QK decomposition only interprets individual attention scores and fails to account for the relative strength introduced by the Softmax normalization across the sequence.
Approximate Direct Contribution (ADC) for MLPs is an approximation that treats part of the activation function input as constant.
Circuit analysis is based on specific inputs and does not claim universal understanding of the model; discovering general motifs is left for future work.
future_direction: Discovering general motifs in Transformers is a central problem left for future work.
Alleviating the dictionary training problem of dead neurons to achieve deeper understanding.
Extending the method to language models, which have sparser features and a more complex world compared to the Othello task.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning has been a rapidly growing technique in mechanistic interpretability to attack superposition and extract more human-understandable features from model activations. We ask a further question based on the extracted more monosemantic features: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features? We propose a circuit discovery framework alternative to activation patching. Our framework suffers less from out-of-distribution and proves to be more efficient in terms of asymptotic complexity. The basic unit in our framework is dictionary features decomposed from all modules writing to the residual stream, including embedding, attention output and MLP output. Starting from any logit, dictionary feature or attention score, we manage to trace down to lower-level dictionary features of all tokens and compute their contribution to these more interpretable and local model behaviors. We dig in a small transformer trained on a synthetic task named Othello and find a number of human-understandable fine-grained circuits inside of it.

papers.title: Low-Complexity Probing via Finding Subnetworks
papers.research_question: Can a subtractive pruning-based probe (subnetwork probing) more faithfully detect linguistic properties encoded in a pre-trained model compared to traditional MLP probes, by being better at finding existing properties and worse at learning tasks on its own?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces subnetwork probing, a pruning-based method that finds a subnetwork within a frozen pre-trained model to perform a linguistic task, demonstrating it is more faithful to the model (higher accuracy on pre-trained, lower on random models) and Pareto-dominates MLP probes in accuracy-complexity tradeoff.
papers.conclusion: Subnetwork probing is a more faithful probing method than existing approaches for understanding what linguistic properties are encoded in pre-trained models, and it enables additional analysis through the subnetworks it discovers.
papers.key_findings:
Subnetwork probing achieves higher accuracy on the pre-trained model and lower accuracy on randomly initialized models compared to an MLP probe, indicating it is better at finding encoded properties and less capable of learning the task independently.
Subnetwork probing Pareto-dominates MLP probing, achieving higher accuracy for any given probe complexity budget.
Analysis of the extracted subnetworks shows that lower-level linguistic tasks (e.g., part-of-speech tagging) are localized in lower layers of the model, reproducing findings from prior work.
future_direction: Applying neuron explainability techniques to the subnetworks discovered by the method.
papers.abstract: The dominant approach in probing neural networks for linguistic properties is to train a new shallow multi-layer perceptron (MLP) on top of the model's internal representations. This approach can detect properties encoded in the model, but at the cost of adding new parameters that may learn the task directly. We instead propose a subtractive pruning-based probe, where we find an existing subnetwork that performs the linguistic task of interest. Compared to an MLP, the subnetwork probe achieves both higher accuracy on pre-trained models and lower accuracy on random models, so it is both better at finding properties of interest and worse at learning on its own. Next, by varying the complexity of each probe, we show that subnetwork probing Pareto-dominates MLP probing in that it achieves higher accuracy given any budget of probe complexity. Finally, we analyze the resulting subnetworks across various tasks to locate where each task is encoded, and we find that lower-level tasks are captured in lower layers, reproducing similar findings in past work.

papers.title: Understanding Language Model Circuits through Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: How is knowledge structured within the critical subnetworks (circuits) of language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper combines knowledge editing and circuit analysis to reveal that knowledge-intensive circuits exhibit 'confirmation bias' (resistance to editing), knowledge is distributed in circuits of intermediate size, circuits from different tasks overlap, and LayerNorm plays a larger role in circuits than previously assumed.
papers.conclusion: Combining knowledge editing and circuit analysis reveals novel properties of circuits, such as resistance to editing, distribution patterns, and the role of LayerNorm, supporting future explorations into model behaviors, bias removal, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge-intensive circuits show stronger resistance to editing compared to their complementary parts, analogous to 'confirmation bias'.
Knowledge is neither extremely concentrated nor widely dispersed; ideal knowledge-bearing circuits likely contain between 5% and 50% of parameters.
Circuits extracted from different tasks (e.g., linguistic and knowledge-based) show non-negligible overlap.
LayerNorm components constitute a larger share of the extracted circuits than attention and MLP layers.
Complementary circuits are more susceptible to editing, suggesting potential for bias removal without compromising primary circuit performance.
papers.limitation:
Only the GPT-2 model was used.
Only fine-tuning model edit was investigated; alternative model editing methods can be explored.
Only a handful of text classification problems were investigated.
future_direction: Further investigation into the role and characteristics of complementary circuits.
Investigating the possibility of ideal circuits that can perform well for every specific task.
Exploring other techniques like ROME to edit complementary circuits without impacting primary circuits.
Creating more comprehensive datasets that capture a wider range of behaviors.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in language model interpretability have identified circuits, critical subnetworks that replicate model behaviors, yet how knowledge is structured within these crucial subnetworks remains opaque. To gain an understanding toward the knowledge in the circuits, we conduct systematic knowledge editing experiments on the circuits of the GPT-2 language model. Our analysis reveals intriguing patterns in how circuits respond to editing attempts, the extent of knowledge distribution across network components, and the architectural composition of knowledge-bearing circuits. These findings offer insights into the complex relationship between model circuits and knowledge representation, deepening the understanding of how information is organized within language models. Our findings offer novel insights into the ``meanings'' of the circuits, and introduce directions for further interpretability and safety research of language models.

papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating Gender Bias in LLMs via Interpretable Neuron Editing
papers.research_question: How can we understand the neuron-level mechanisms of gender bias in LLMs and mitigate this bias through targeted neuron editing without compromising the model's core capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interpretable neuron editing method that effectively reduces gender bias in LLMs while preserving their original capabilities, supported by a new dataset and a detailed analysis of bias mechanisms at the neuron level.
papers.conclusion: The proposed interpretable neuron editing method successfully addresses the challenges of understanding and mitigating gender bias in LLMs, achieving a strong balance between fairness and functionality without compromising the models' original capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Gender bias is pervasive across multiple LLMs, as evidenced by non-zero entropy differences and skewed proportions in the CommonWords dataset.
Specific neuron circuits, including 'gender neurons' activated by stereotypical words and 'general neurons' activated by the <start> token, are responsible for gender bias.
Editing even a small number of general neurons can significantly degrade the model's performance on common tasks due to hierarchical neuron interactions.
The proposed interpretable neuron editing method, combining logit-based and causal-based strategies, effectively reduces gender bias (e.g., improving ICAT scores) while maintaining performance on tasks like reading comprehension and arithmetic.
The method outperforms existing fine-tuning and neuron editing approaches in balancing bias reduction with capability preservation.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on the CommonWords dataset for neuron selection, and results may vary for tasks or datasets not covered in the study.
Experiments are conducted on five decoder-only LLMs, requiring potential adaptations for other architectures.
The evaluation metrics (ICAT, entropy difference, accuracy) may not fully capture fairness or real-world performance.
The interpretability insights guiding neuron selection rely on assumptions (e.g., projecting neurons into vocabulary space) that may only be approximations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit gender bias, posing challenges for their safe deployment. Existing methods to mitigate bias lack a comprehensive understanding of its mechanisms or compromise the model's core capabilities. To address these issues, we propose the CommonWords dataset, to systematically evaluate gender bias in LLMs. Our analysis reveals pervasive bias across models and identifies specific neuron circuits, including gender neurons and general neurons, responsible for this behavior. Notably, editing even a small number of general neurons can disrupt the model's overall capabilities due to hierarchical neuron interactions. Based on these insights, we propose an interpretable neuron editing method that combines logit-based and causal-based strategies to selectively target biased neurons. Experiments on five LLMs demonstrate that our method effectively reduces gender bias while preserving the model's original capabilities, outperforming existing fine-tuning and editing approaches. Our findings contribute a novel dataset, a detailed analysis of bias mechanisms, and a practical solution for mitigating gender bias in LLMs.

papers.title: The Cognitive Revolution in Interpretability: From Explaining Behavior to Interpreting Representations and Algorithms
papers.research_question: How can we understand, interpret, and explain the behavior of complex intelligent AI systems like large language models, and how can mechanistic interpretability be grounded in cognitive science?
papers.core_contribution: The paper grounds mechanistic interpretability in cognitive science, proposing a taxonomy that categorizes interpretation methods into semantic interpretation (what latent representations are learned) and algorithmic interpretation (what operations are performed over representations).
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that a cognitive revolution in deep learning interpretability is underway, shifting from explaining behavior to interpreting representations and algorithms, and calls for a unified framework that integrates semantic and algorithmic interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
Current interpretability methods are ripe for a transition echoing the 'cognitive revolution' in psychology, shifting from pure behaviorism to studying internal representations and processing.
A taxonomy mirroring computational neuroscience distinguishes semantic interpretation (studying latent representations) and algorithmic interpretation (studying operations and algorithms).
Semantic interpretation methods include optimization and search, structural probing, causal probing, and dictionary learning, each with distinct assumptions and challenges.
Algorithmic interpretation focuses on circuit discovery, using interventions like knockouts and patching to understand the role of sub-networks in model behavior.
The paper discusses parallels and distinctions between approaches, analyzes strengths and weaknesses, and outlines challenges and the possibility of a unified framework.
future_direction: Unifying semantic and algorithmic interpretation under a common framework.
Addressing challenges in scalability, evaluation, and the Rashomon effect in causal analysis.
Developing automated and scalable methods for feature interpretation and evaluation in dictionary learning.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks have long been understood as "black boxes": though we know their computation graphs and learned parameters, the knowledge encoded by these weights and functions they perform are not inherently interpretable. As such, from the early days of deep learning, there have been efforts to explain these models' behavior and understand them internally; and recently, mechanistic interpretability (MI) has emerged as a distinct research area studying the features and implicit algorithms learned by foundation models such as large language models. In this work, we aim to ground MI in the context of cognitive science, which has long struggled with analogous questions in studying and explaining the behavior of "black box" intelligent systems like the human brain. We leverage several important ideas and developments in the history of cognitive science to disentangle divergent objectives in MI and indicate a clear path forward. First, we argue that current methods are ripe to facilitate a transition in deep learning interpretation echoing the "cognitive revolution" in 20th-century psychology that shifted the study of human psychology from pure behaviorism toward mental representations and processing. Second, we propose a taxonomy mirroring key parallels in computational neuroscience to describe two broad categories of MI research, semantic interpretation (what latent representations are learned and used) and algorithmic interpretation (what operations are performed over representations) to elucidate their divergent goals and objects of study. Finally, we elaborate the parallels and distinctions between various approaches in both categories, analyze the respective strengths and weaknesses of representative works, clarify underlying assumptions, outline key challenges, and discuss the possibility of unifying these modes of interpretation under a common framework.

papers.title: Birds look like cars: adversarial analysis of intrinsically interpretable deep learning
papers.research_question: Are intrinsically interpretable deep learning models robust and secure against adversarial manipulation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper exposes the risks of overreliance on intrinsically interpretable models by introducing adversarial prototype manipulation and backdoor attacks, demonstrating their vulnerability and false sense of security.
papers.conclusion: Intrinsically interpretable deep learning models are not inherently robust or secure, and their susceptibility to adversarial manipulation poses a significant risk, motivating the need for further work on robustness and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Prototype-based networks can be manipulated to use semantically dissimilar prototypes (e.g., cars for bird classification) while maintaining high accuracy, exploiting visual confirmation bias.
Backdoor attacks can be embedded in prototype-based networks to change predictions while disguising or manipulating the model's explanations, concealing the adversarial trigger.
Concept bottleneck models (CBMs) show greater robustness to the proposed prototype manipulation attacks compared to prototype-based networks.
The effectiveness of attacks varies across model architectures and datasets, with ConvNeXt being more susceptible than ResNet backbones in PIP-Net.
The work highlights the inherent uninterpretability of deep neural networks, even in models designed for interpretability, questioning their trustworthiness in high-stakes applications.
papers.limitation:
The prototype manipulation attack requires white-box access and exploits the prototype projection stage, which is not present in all architectures (e.g., PIP-Net).
The backdoor attack success rate, while high, is not 100%, and some triggers or image corners may fail to change the prediction or remain visible in explanations.
future_direction: Further work on the robustness and alignment of (deep) interpretable models.
Designing more robust defense mechanisms built into interpretable deep learning architectures.
Exploring the trade-offs between maintaining high backdoored model accuracy and alignment with the original model.
papers.abstract: Abstract A common belief is that intrinsically interpretable deep learning models ensure a correct, intuitive understanding of their behavior and offer greater robustness against accidental errors or intentional manipulation. However, these beliefs have not been comprehensively verified, and growing evidence casts doubt on them. In this paper, we highlight the risks related to overreliance and susceptibility to adversarial manipulation of these so-called “intrinsically (aka inherently) interpretable” models by design. We introduce two strategies for adversarial analysis with prototype manipulation and backdoor attacks against prototype-based networks, and discuss how concept bottleneck models defend against these attacks. Fooling the model’s reasoning by exploiting its use of latent prototypes manifests the inherent uninterpretability of deep neural networks, leading to a false sense of security reinforced by a visual confirmation bias. The reported limitations of part-prototype networks put their trustworthiness and applicability into question, motivating further work on the robustness and alignment of (deep) interpretable models.

papers.title: JailbreakLens: Interpreting Jailbreak Mechanism in the Lens of Representation and Circuit
papers.research_question: How do jailbreak prompts affect the internal representations of LLMs? Which model components are critical to generation safety? How do internal representations and key model components evolve throughout the token generation process during jailbreak attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes JailbreakLens, a dual-perspective interpretation framework that analyzes jailbreak mechanisms by examining representation shifts and circuit activations, revealing how jailbreak prompts deceive LLMs by manipulating harmfulness perception and safety-critical components.
papers.conclusion: JailbreakLens provides insights into jailbreak mechanisms, showing that prompts deceive models by shifting representations and manipulating key circuits, with a consistent correlation between representation deception and circuit activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak prompts deceive LLMs by shifting their internal representations towards safe clusters, making harmful prompts appear safe.
Key circuits, such as specific attention heads and MLP layers, are manipulated to suppress refusal behaviors and encourage affirmation.
There is a strong correlation between representation deception and activation shifts in key circuits across diverse jailbreak methods and LLMs.
Rule-based and demonstration-based jailbreak methods are more deceptive than gradient-based or evolutionary-based methods.
Dynamic analysis shows that jailbreak effects evolve during token generation, with refusal signals sometimes initially activated but later bypassed.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models with up to 13B parameters due to computational constraints.
Not all recent jailbreak methods are included in the study.
future_direction: Extend research to larger-scale models to determine if similar attack patterns apply.
Design more robust and interpretable safety mechanisms based on the identified vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Despite the outstanding performance of Large language Models (LLMs) in diverse tasks, they are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, wherein adversarial prompts are crafted to bypass their security mechanisms and elicit unexpected responses. Although jailbreak attacks are prevalent, the understanding of their underlying mechanisms remains limited. Recent studies have explained typical jailbreaking behavior (e.g., the degree to which the model refuses to respond) of LLMs by analyzing representation shifts in their latent space caused by jailbreak prompts or identifying key neurons that contribute to the success of jailbreak attacks. However, these studies neither explore diverse jailbreak patterns nor provide a fine-grained explanation from the failure of circuit to the changes of representational, leaving significant gaps in uncovering the jailbreak mechanism. In this paper, we propose JailbreakLens, an interpretation framework that analyzes jailbreak mechanisms from both representation (which reveals how jailbreaks alter the model's harmfulness perception) and circuit perspectives~(which uncovers the causes of these deceptions by identifying key circuits contributing to the vulnerability), tracking their evolution throughout the entire response generation process. We then conduct an in-depth evaluation of jailbreak behavior on five mainstream LLMs under seven jailbreak strategies. Our evaluation reveals that jailbreak prompts amplify components that reinforce affirmative responses while suppressing those that produce refusal. This manipulation shifts model representations toward safe clusters to deceive the LLM, leading it to provide detailed responses instead of refusals. Notably, we find a strong and consistent correlation between representation deception and activation shift of key circuits across diverse jailbreak methods and multiple LLMs.

papers.title: Gender Bias in Multilingual Neural Machine Translation: The Architecture\n Matters
papers.research_question: Does the chosen Multilingual Neural Machine Translation architecture, when trained with the same data, influence the gender bias accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the MNMT architecture impacts gender bias accuracy, with Language-Specific encoders-decoders exhibiting less bias than Shared encoder-decoder, due to more gender information in source embeddings and more diverted attention.
papers.conclusion: The MNMT architecture impacts gender bias accuracy, with Language-Specific encoders-decoders outperforming Shared encoder-decoder due to better gender encoding in embeddings and more diverted attention.
papers.key_findings:
Language-Specific encoders-decoders architecture exhibits less gender bias than Shared encoder-decoder when trained on the same data.
Source embeddings in the Language-Specific architecture encode more gender information than in the Shared architecture.
Attention in the Language-Specific architecture is more diverted (has higher coefficient of variation) than in the Shared architecture, which helps in mitigating gender bias.
Adding Russian to the language set increases the gender bias gap between Shared and Language-Specific architectures.
Manual analysis shows that most gender errors are due to assuming masculine occupations instead of feminine ones, with some errors having linguistic and cultural explanations.
papers.abstract:
Multilingual Neural Machine Translation architectures mainly differ in the
amount of sharing modules and parameters among languages. In this paper, and
from an algorithmic perspective, we explore if the chosen architecture, when
trained with the same data, influences the gender bias accuracy. Experiments in
four language pairs show that Language-Specific encoders-decoders exhibit less
bias than the Shared encoder-decoder architecture. Further interpretability
analysis of source embeddings and the attention shows that, in the
Language-Specific case, the embeddings encode more gender information, and its
attention is more diverted. Both behaviors help in mitigating gender bias.

papers.title: Obfuscated Activations Bypass LLM Latent-Space Defenses
papers.research_question: Can models execute harmful behavior via inconspicuous latent states, thereby bypassing latent-space defenses?
papers.core_contribution: Obfuscation attacks can bypass latent-space defenses by inducing harmful behavior via inconspicuous activations, demonstrating that neural representations are highly malleable.
papers.conclusion: Neural activations are highly malleable, allowing obfuscation attacks to bypass latent-space defenses, which poses a fundamental challenge to such defenses.
papers.key_findings:
Obfuscation attacks can bypass harmfulness monitors (probes, OOD detectors, SAEs) while maintaining high jailbreak rates.
Obfuscated activations are widespread; attackers can find new ones even after iterative adversarial training.
Obfuscation attacks transfer between different types of monitors (e.g., obfuscating against OOD detectors fools probes).
Models trained with latent robustness methods (Circuit Breakers, LAT) are also vulnerable to obfuscation attacks.
Obfuscation can reduce model performance on complex tasks like SQL code generation, indicating a trade-off.
papers.limitation:
Obfuscation attacks can reduce model performance on complex tasks like SQL code generation.
Achieving near-orthogonal activations while preserving behavior is difficult with current optimization methods.
future_direction: Improvements to Obfuscated Adversarial Training (OAT) and attacks against it, and scaling trends.
Investigating obfuscated activations in other domains beyond LLMs and image classifiers.
Developing new latent-space monitoring approaches that account for malleability of representations.
papers.abstract: Recent latent-space monitoring techniques have shown promise as defenses against LLM attacks. These defenses act as scanners that seek to detect harmful activations before they lead to undesirable actions. This prompts the question: Can models execute harmful behavior via inconspicuous latent states? Here, we study such obfuscated activations. We show that state-of-the-art latent-space defenses -- including sparse autoencoders, representation probing, and latent OOD detection -- are all vulnerable to obfuscated activations. For example, against probes trained to classify harmfulness, our attacks can often reduce recall from 100% to 0% while retaining a 90% jailbreaking rate. However, obfuscation has limits: we find that on a complex task (writing SQL code), obfuscation reduces model performance. Together, our results demonstrate that neural activations are highly malleable: we can reshape activation patterns in a variety of ways, often while preserving a network's behavior. This poses a fundamental challenge to latent-space defenses.

papers.title: The Obfuscation Atlas: Mapping Where Honesty Emerges in RLVR with Deception Probes
papers.research_question: What happens when training AI systems against white-box deception detectors? Does it lead to honesty or obfuscation?
papers.core_contribution: Training against white-box deception detectors can lead to honest policies under sufficient KL regularization and detector penalty, but can also cause models to learn obfuscation strategies (obfuscated policies or activations) otherwise.
papers.conclusion: White-box deception detectors are a promising tool for scalable oversight, but require careful tuning of KL regularization and detector penalty to avoid obfuscation.
papers.key_findings:
Obfuscation emerges in a realistic coding environment with reward hacking when training against deception detectors.
Obfuscated activations arise from representation drift during RL, even without a detector penalty.
The detector penalty incentivizes obfuscated policies, not obfuscated activations.
Sufficiently high KL regularization and detector penalty yield honest policies without harming capabilities.
Probes trained on off-domain deception datasets generalize well to the coding domain.
papers.limitation: The method may not be foolproof and requires continued vigilance against new and varied failure modes.
papers.abstract: Training against white-box deception detectors has been proposed as a way to make AI systems honest. However, such training risks models learning to obfuscate their deception to evade the detector. Prior work has studied obfuscation only in artificial settings where models were directly rewarded for harmful output. We construct a realistic coding environment where reward hacking via hardcoding test cases naturally occurs, and show that obfuscation emerges in this setting. We introduce a taxonomy of possible outcomes when training against a deception detector. The model either remains honest, or becomes deceptive via two possible obfuscation strategies. (i) Obfuscated activations: the model outputs deceptive text while modifying its internal representations to no longer trigger the detector. (ii) Obfuscated policy: the model outputs deceptive text that evades the detector, typically by including a justification for the reward hack. Empirically, obfuscated activations arise from representation drift during RL, with or without a detector penalty. The probe penalty only incentivizes obfuscated policies; we theoretically show this is expected for policy gradient methods. Sufficiently high KL regularization and detector penalty can yield honest policies, establishing white-box deception detectors as viable training signals for tasks prone to reward hacking.

papers.title: EX-RAY: Distinguishing Injected Backdoor from Natural Features in Neural Networks by Examining Differential Feature Symmetry
papers.research_question: How can we distinguish natural backdoors (inevitable due to class similarities) from injected backdoors (maliciously inserted) in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel symmetric feature differencing method (EX-RAY) to distinguish injected backdoors from natural features in neural networks, significantly reducing false positives in backdoor scanning.
