papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability in the Presence of Architectural Obfuscation
papers.research_question: Can we still locate, characterise and manipulate the mechanisms that drive model behaviour once the observable representations have been permuted or otherwise obfuscated?
papers.core_contribution: Obfuscation dramatically alters internal activation patterns yet preserves the layer-wise computational graph, retaining global model behavior while impeding fine-grained mechanistic analysis of user-specific content.
papers.conclusion: The essential circuit for the task survives obfuscation, but activation patterns become more diffuse, attention roles invert in later blocks, and head-level importance is scattered, making causal tracing noisier while leaving top-line accuracy intact.
papers.key_findings:
Obfuscation preserves the high-level circuit structure but alters internal activation patterns, making them more diffuse.
Logit attribution shows the same attention heads dominate in both models, but their contributions become noisier and more scattered under obfuscation.
Activation patching reveals the computational path is less efficient and more dispersed in the obfuscated model, with later layers taking on more responsibility.
Head patching shows that some heads change their polarity of contribution (e.g., from positive to negative) in the obfuscated model.
Obfuscation hinders fine-grained reverse engineering (e.g., prompt reconstruction) without erasing the coarse computations necessary for task performance.
future_direction: Strengthen security guarantees without forfeiting interpretability by combining obfuscation with cryptographic techniques like fully homomorphic encryption.
papers.abstract: Architectural obfuscation - e.g., permuting hidden-state tensors, linearly transforming embedding tables, or remapping tokens - has recently gained traction as a lightweight substitute for heavyweight cryptography in privacy-preserving large-language-model (LLM) inference. While recent work has shown that these techniques can be broken under dedicated reconstruction attacks, their impact on mechanistic interpretability has not been systematically studied. In particular, it remains unclear whether scrambling a network's internal representations truly thwarts efforts to understand how the model works, or simply relocates the same circuits to an unfamiliar coordinate system. We address this gap by analyzing a GPT-2-small model trained from scratch with a representative obfuscation map. Assuming the obfuscation map is private and the original basis is hidden (mirroring an honest-but-curious server), we apply logit-lens attribution, causal path-patching, and attention-head ablation to locate and manipulate known circuits. Our findings reveal that obfuscation dramatically alters activation patterns within attention heads yet preserves the layer-wise computational graph. This disconnect hampers reverse-engineering of user prompts: causal traces lose their alignment with baseline semantics, and token-level logit attributions become too noisy to reconstruct. At the same time, feed-forward and residual pathways remain functionally intact, suggesting that obfuscation degrades fine-grained interpretability without compromising top-level task performance. These results establish quantitative evidence that architectural obfuscation can simultaneously (i) retain global model behaviour and (ii) impede mechanistic analyses of user-specific content. By mapping where interpretability breaks down, our study provides guidance for future privacy defences and for robustness-aware interpretability tooling.

papers.title: Universal Refusal Circuits Across LLMs: Cross-Model Transfer via Trajectory Replay and Concept-Basis Reconstruction
papers.research_question: Are refusal circuits universal across LLMs? Can a refusal circuit extracted from a donor model be transferred to a target model without target-side refusal supervision?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for transferring refusal circuits across LLMs without target-side refusal supervision, combining concept-basis reconstruction and a weight-SVD stability guard, providing evidence for semantic universality of safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: Refusal circuits are universal across LLMs and can be transferred via semantic recipe invariance, enabling cross-model circuit editing without target-side refusal supervision.
papers.key_findings:
The method successfully transfers refusal attenuation across 8 model pairs, including cross-family and cross-architecture transfers.
Refusal circuits are composed of a stable mixture of concept atoms, enabling cross-model transfer via semantic recipe invariance.
The weight-SVD guard prevents capability collapse by projecting interventions away from high-variance weight subspaces.
The transfer works without target-side refusal supervision, relying only on benign concept prompts and validation data.
The method preserves model capabilities on math and code tasks while reducing refusal rates.
papers.limitation:
Efficacy depends on coverage of the Concept Atom Registry; if refusal circuit uses features orthogonal to the atoms, reconstruction may fail.
Weight-SVD guard relies on the heuristic that capability-critical circuits reside in high-variance principal components, which may not generalize to all tasks.
Method is white-box, requiring access to model weights and internal activations, limiting applicability to closed-source systems.
future_direction: Expand CAR coverage to test transfer beyond refusal directions to multi-behavior editing.
Explore black-box approximations of semantic fingerprints for closed-source systems.
Test the method on a wider range of models and alignment behaviors.
papers.abstract: Refusal behavior in aligned LLMs is often viewed as model-specific, yet we hypothesize it stems from a universal, low-dimensional semantic circuit shared across models. To test this, we introduce Trajectory Replay via Concept-Basis Reconstruction, a framework that transfers refusal interventions from donor to target models, spanning diverse architectures (e.g., Dense to MoE) and training regimes, without using target-side refusal supervision. By aligning layers via concept fingerprints and reconstructing refusal directions using a shared ``recipe'' of concept atoms, we map the donor's ablation trajectory into the target's semantic space. To preserve capabilities, we introduce a weight-SVD stability guard that projects interventions away from high-variance weight subspaces to prevent collateral damage. Our evaluation across 8 model pairs confirms that these transferred recipes consistently attenuate refusal while maintaining performance, providing strong evidence for the semantic universality of safety alignment.

papers.title: TorchLens: A Python package for extracting and visualizing hidden activations of PyTorch models
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TorchLens, a Python package that exhaustively extracts and visualizes hidden activations of any PyTorch model, including those with dynamic control flow, and provides a built-in validation procedure.
papers.conclusion: TorchLens removes arbitrary limitations to extracting and characterizing internal DNN operations, streamlining both the scientific investigation and engineering of DNNs.
papers.key_findings:
TorchLens can extract activations from all intermediate operations in any PyTorch model, including models with dynamic control flow, without requiring model modifications.
It provides an intuitive visualization of the model's computational graph and metadata about each computational step.
It includes a built-in validation procedure to algorithmically verify the accuracy of all saved hidden-layer activations.
The approach requires minimal additional code and can be automatically applied to any PyTorch model.
TorchLens has been validated on a large collection of DNNs, including image, video, audio, and language models.
papers.limitation:
The validation procedure requires saving the values of all intermediate tensors, which can impose high memory demands for large models.
TorchLens has not been tested in the case of parallel computing.
future_direction: Potential to use TorchLens for causal inference methods and counterfactual simulations by intervening on the computational graph.
Future updates to TorchLens are intended to address parallel computing.
papers.abstract: Abstract Deep neural network models (DNNs) are essential to modern AI and provide powerful models of information processing in biological neural networks. Researchers in both neuroscience and engineering are pursuing a better understanding of the internal representations and operations that undergird the successes and failures of DNNs. Neuroscientists additionally evaluate DNNs as models of brain computation by comparing their internal representations to those found in brains. It is therefore essential to have a method to easily and exhaustively extract and characterize the results of the internal operations of any DNN. Many models are implemented in PyTorch, the leading framework for building DNN models. Here we introduce TorchLens , a new open-source Python package for extracting and characterizing hidden-layer activations in PyTorch models. Uniquely among existing approaches to this problem, TorchLens has the following features: (1) it exhaustively extracts the results of all intermediate operations, not just those associated with PyTorch module objects, yielding a full record of every step in the model's computational graph, (2) it provides an intuitive visualization of the model's complete computational graph along with metadata about each computational step in a model's forward pass for further analysis, (3) it contains a built-in validation procedure to algorithmically verify the accuracy of all saved hidden-layer activations, and (4) the approach it uses can be automatically applied to any PyTorch model with no modifications, including models with conditional (if-then) logic in their forward pass, recurrent models, branching models where layer outputs are fed into multiple subsequent layers in parallel, and models with internally generated tensors (e.g., injections of noise). Furthermore, using TorchLens requires minimal additional code, making it easy to incorporate into existing pipelines for model development and analysis, and useful as a pedagogical aid when teaching deep learning concepts. We hope this contribution will help researchers in AI and neuroscience understand the internal representations of DNNs.

papers.title: Mitigating Backdoor Attacks using Activation-Guided Model Editing
papers.research_question: How can backdoor attacks be mitigated in machine learning models using a sample-efficient and computationally inexpensive model editing approach guided by activations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a novel backdoor mitigation method that uses activations from a small unseen dataset to guide efficient model weight editing, achieving state-of-the-art performance with low computational cost and sample count, and introduces a repair step to preserve model utility.
papers.conclusion: The proposed activation-guided model editing method offers an efficient and effective defense against backdoor attacks, outperforming previous methods in speed, sample efficiency, and overall performance across diverse settings.
papers.key_findings:
The method effectively unlearns backdoors across various datasets, models, and trigger patterns, often reducing ASR to near zero.
It requires only a handful of samples (as few as 4) for effective unlearning and is significantly faster than baseline methods that require gradient-based optimization.
The unlearning process can inadvertently unlearn the entire target class, but a subsequent repair step (fine-tuning) can restore utility while maintaining low ASR.
The method outperforms existing unlearning baselines (actFT, BaEraser, basicFT, NAD) in most scenarios, especially in terms of the combined score metric.
The method can also be used for backdoor detection, showing a significant drop in target class accuracy after unlearning when the backdoor is present.
papers.limitation:
The method can disturb overall model utility and unlearn the entire targeted class instead of just the backdoor trigger, necessitating an additional repair step.
The experimental scope is limited to convolutional neural networks (CNNs).
future_direction: Explore the unlearning method with different architectures such as vision transformers and MLP-Mixers.
Investigate explainability methods to better understand which parts of the algorithm are responsible for effective unlearning.
Expand the applications of unlearning beyond backdoors, such as to privacy-related tasks.
Extend experiments to other data types, such as text or audio data.
papers.abstract: Backdoor attacks compromise the integrity and reliability of machine learning models by embedding a hidden trigger during the training process, which can later be activated to cause unintended misbehavior. We propose a novel backdoor mitigation approach via machine unlearning to counter such backdoor attacks. The proposed method utilizes model activation of domain-equivalent unseen data to guide the editing of the model's weights. Unlike the previous unlearning-based mitigation methods, ours is computationally inexpensive and achieves state-of-the-art performance while only requiring a handful of unseen samples for unlearning. In addition, we also point out that unlearning the backdoor may cause the whole targeted class to be unlearned, thus introducing an additional repair step to preserve the model's utility after editing the model. Experiment results show that the proposed method is effective in unlearning the backdoor on different datasets and trigger patterns.

papers.title: Detecting Gender Bias in Transformer-based Models: A Case Study on BERT
papers.research_question: Does gender bias exist inside pretrained BERT models, and how can it be detected using attention maps?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a novel method to detect gender bias in transformer models using attention maps, and finds that attention matrices Wq and Wk introduce significant bias, with periodic changes in bias degree across layers.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a gender bias detection method based on attention maps for transformer-based models and provides insights into internal bias flow in BERT, highlighting the role of attention matrices in bias introduction.
papers.key_findings:
Attention matrices Wq and Wk introduce much more gender bias than other modules, including the embedding layer.
Bias degree changes periodically inside the model: Q, K, V, and the remaining part of the attention layer enhance gender bias, while averaged attentions reduce bias.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel gender bias detection method by utilizing attention map for transformer-based models. We 1) give an intuitive gender bias judgement method by comparing the different relation degree between the genders and the occupation according to the attention scores, 2) design a gender bias detector by modifying the attention module, 3) insert the gender bias detector into different positions of the model to present the internal gender bias flow, and 4) draw the consistent gender bias conclusion by scanning the entire Wikipedia, a BERT pretraining dataset. We observe that 1) the attention matrices, Wq and Wk introduce much more gender bias than other modules (including the embedding layer) and 2) the bias degree changes periodically inside of the model (attention matrix Q, K, V, and the remaining part of the attention layer (including the fully-connected layer, the residual connection, and the layer normalization module) enhance the gender bias while the averaged attentions reduces the bias).

papers.title: Towards Mechanistic Defenses Against Typographic Attacks in CLIP
papers.research_question: How can we defend CLIP models against typographic attacks without fine-tuning, by understanding and intervening on the internal mechanisms responsible for typographic vulnerability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dyslexify, a gradient-free defense that improves CLIP's robustness to typographic attacks by identifying and ablating a sparse circuit of attention heads responsible for typographic information, without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Dyslexify provides a practical, interpretable, and computationally efficient defense against typographic attacks, enabling safer deployment of multimodal models without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Specialized attention heads in the latter half of CLIP layers causally extract and transmit typographic information to the cls token.
Ablating these heads (typographic circuit) improves typographic attack robustness by up to 22.06% on ImageNet-100-typo while standard accuracy drops by less than 1%.
The typographic circuit is sparse, covering at most 10.1% of attention heads.
Dyslexify scales to billion-parameter models and is competitive with fine-tuning-based defenses.
The method effectively mitigates typographic attacks in safety-critical medical foundation models for skin lesion diagnosis.
papers.limitation:
Dyslexify only protects the cls token, but many multimodal applications use spatial tokens, allowing typographic information to propagate.
Adaptive attacks are not feasible due to non-differentiability of typographic attacks, so evaluation against adaptive attacks is not possible.
Insights into CLIP's behavior could be misused to craft stronger typographic attacks.
future_direction: Generalizing Dyslexify to VLM setups that use spatial tokens.
papers.abstract: Typographic attacks exploit multi-modal systems by injecting text into images, leading to targeted misclassifications, malicious content generation and even Vision-Language Model jailbreaks. In this work, we analyze how CLIP vision encoders behave under typographic attacks, locating specialized attention heads in the latter half of the model's layers that causally extract and transmit typographic information to the cls token. Building on these insights, we introduce a method to defend CLIP models against typographic attacks by selectively ablating a typographic circuit, consisting of attention heads. Without requiring finetuning, our method improves performance by up to 19.6% on a typographic variant of ImageNet-100, while reducing standard ImageNet-100 accuracy by less than 1%. Notably, our training-free approach remains competitive with current state-of-the-art typographic defenses that rely on finetuning. To this end, we release a family of dyslexic CLIP models which are significantly more robust against typographic attacks. These models serve as suitable drop-in replacements for a broad range of safety-critical applications, where the risks of text-based manipulation outweigh the utility of text recognition.

papers.title: Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and whether insights from circuit analysis generalize across tasks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and that interventions based on one circuit can improve performance on another task, providing evidence for task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.conclusion: Circuit components are reused across tasks, providing evidence that large language models' behavior can be explained in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.key_findings:
The IOI circuit reproduces on GPT2-Medium, with minor differences such as the negative mover head attending only to the S2 token.
The Colored Objects circuit shares about 78% of the important attention heads with the IOI circuit, indicating high component reuse.
Interventions on inhibition heads and the negative mover head can boost accuracy on the Colored Objects task from 49.6% to 93.7%.
The inhibition-mover head subcircuit behaves invariantly across tasks, as predicted by the IOI circuit.
The negative mover head in GPT2-Medium exhibits more sophisticated behavior than in GPT2-Small, directly demoting the subject token.
papers.limitation:
Quantifying circuit overlap is complex and not fully addressed in this paper.
The generality of the circuit beyond the studied tasks is not confirmed.
future_direction: Understanding how commonly the mover circuit is used by GPT2 in other tasks.
Developing methods for quantifying circuit overlap.
Studying circuit reuse in larger models.
papers.abstract: Recent work in mechanistic interpretability has shown that behaviors in language models can be successfully reverse-engineered through circuit analysis. A common criticism, however, is that each circuit is task-specific, and thus such analysis cannot contribute to understanding the models at a higher level. In this work, we present evidence that insights (both low-level findings about specific heads and higher-level findings about general algorithms) can indeed generalize across tasks. Specifically, we study the circuit discovered in Wang et al. (2022) for the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task and 1.) show that it reproduces on a larger GPT2 model, and 2.) that it is mostly reused to solve a seemingly different task: Colored Objects (Ippolito & Callison-Burch, 2023). We provide evidence that the process underlying both tasks is functionally very similar, and contains about a 78% overlap in in-circuit attention heads. We further present a proof-of-concept intervention experiment, in which we adjust four attention heads in middle layers in order to 'repair' the Colored Objects circuit and make it behave like the IOI circuit. In doing so, we boost accuracy from 49.6% to 93.7% on the Colored Objects task and explain most sources of error. The intervention affects downstream attention heads in specific ways predicted by their interactions in the IOI circuit, indicating that this subcircuit behavior is invariant to the different task inputs. Overall, our results provide evidence that it may yet be possible to explain large language models' behavior in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks and computational components.

papers.title: Automatically Identifying Local and Global Circuits with Linear Computation Graphs
papers.research_question: How to leverage Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for fine-grained circuit analysis in Transformer language models without linear approximations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a pipeline using Sparse Autoencoders and Transcoders to refactor Transformer computation into a linear graph, enabling fine-grained circuit discovery without approximation via Hierarchical Attribution.
papers.conclusion: The proposed pipeline enables fine-grained circuit analysis in Transformers, revealing detailed and beautiful internal structures that were previously obscured by coarser analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
The pipeline identifies fine-grained circuits for bracket matching, induction, and Indirect Object Identification (IOI) in GPT-2 Small.
SAE-based circuits reveal more detailed structural information than coarser head-level circuit analyses.
The IOI circuit differs at the feature level between two similar prompt templates (sJohn and sMary), showing nuanced mechanistic distinctions.
papers.limitation: The analysis is specific to certain inputs and might not generalize to other settings.
future_direction: Extending the method to extract more general circuits for abstract behaviors.
papers.abstract: Circuit analysis of any certain model behavior is a central task in mechanistic interpretability. We introduce our circuit discovery pipeline with Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and a variant called Transcoders. With these two modules inserted into the model, the model's computation graph with respect to OV and MLP circuits becomes strictly linear. Our methods do not require linear approximation to compute the causal effect of each node. This fine-grained graph identifies both end-to-end and local circuits accounting for either logits or intermediate features. We can scalably apply this pipeline with a technique called Hierarchical Attribution. We analyze three kinds of circuits in GPT-2 Small: bracket, induction, and Indirect Object Identification circuits. Our results reveal new findings underlying existing discoveries.

papers.title: Neural networks are a priori biased towards Boolean functions with low entropy
papers.research_question: What is the a priori probability distribution over Boolean functions for simple neural networks upon random initialization of weights, and how does it bias towards low-entropy functions?
papers.core_contribution: Proves that simple neural networks have an a priori bias towards Boolean functions with low entropy, and that this bias increases with the number of ReLU layers and with the variance of the bias term.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks have a strong intrinsic a priori bias towards Boolean functions with low entropy, which may contribute to their ability to generalize.
papers.key_findings:
For a perceptron with no bias term and symmetric weight distribution, the probability P(T=t) is uniform, but because there are fewer functions with extreme t, individual low-entropy functions have higher average probability.
Within a class of functions with fixed t, there is a further bias towards functions of lower complexity, correlating with Lempel-Ziv complexity.
Adding a threshold bias term to a perceptron significantly increases the bias towards low entropy.
Adding ReLU layers to a neural network increases the bias towards low entropy, proven in the infinite-width limit and observed empirically.
Provides an expressivity bound: DNNs with l hidden layers of width n + 2^(n-1)/l + 1 can express all Boolean functions over n variables.
papers.limitation:
The Algorithmic Information Theory bound has limitations: it is only rigorously proven for large Kolmogorov complexity, and it does not explain why DNNs are biased, only that if biased, they should be biased towards simplicity.
The analysis is primarily for simple networks (perceptrons and fully connected networks) and Boolean inputs; generalization to more complex architectures and real-world data is not fully proven.
future_direction: Study the effect of entropy bias on learning, particularly for class-imbalanced data.
Investigate the effect of different dynamic regimes (chaotic vs. ordered) for different activation functions on simplicity bias.
papers.abstract: Understanding the inductive bias of neural networks is critical to explaining their ability to generalise. Here, for one of the simplest neural networks -- a single-layer perceptron with n input neurons, one output neuron, and no threshold bias term -- we prove that upon random initialisation of weights, the a priori probability $P(t)$ that it represents a Boolean function that classifies t points in ${0,1}^n$ as 1 has a remarkably simple form: $P(t) = 2^{-n}$ for $0\leq t < 2^n$. Since a perceptron can express far fewer Boolean functions with small or large values of t (low entropy) than with intermediate values of t (high entropy) there is, on average, a strong intrinsic a-priori bias towards individual functions with low entropy. Furthermore, within a class of functions with fixed t, we often observe a further intrinsic bias towards functions of lower complexity. Finally, we prove that, regardless of the distribution of inputs, the bias towards low entropy becomes monotonically stronger upon adding ReLU layers, and empirically show that increasing the variance of the bias term has a similar effect.

papers.title: Neural Activation Patterns (NAPs): Visual Explainability of Learned Concepts
papers.research_question: How can we discover and visualize learned concepts in neural network layers by analyzing activation patterns beyond individual neuron analysis?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Neural Activation Patterns (NAPs), a method for layer-level concept discovery in neural networks by clustering activation profiles, providing a visual explainability tool.
papers.conclusion: NAPs provide a layer-level explainability method that complements existing techniques, enabling deeper understanding of neural network models through visual introspection of learned concepts.
papers.key_findings:
NAPs can reveal distinct concepts learned at different layers, such as low-level features in early layers and high-level concepts in later layers.
NAPs allow for comparison of concepts across different models, revealing architectural differences and performance variations.
NAPs can uncover biases in training data, such as overrepresentation of certain contexts (e.g., people holding fish).
The method is robust across various network architectures and datasets, from simple MNIST models to complex ImageNet models.
NAPs complement existing unit-level explainability methods by providing layer-level insights.
papers.limitation:
NAPs require human interpretation and may not always reflect what the model sees.
The discovery of NAPs depends on the input data used; if a concept is not present in the input data, it cannot be extracted.
Earlier layers tend to produce fewer and less interpretable NAPs because they represent low-level features.
future_direction: Applying NAPs to different data types and tasks, such as GANs, Transformers, and RNNs.
Combining NAPs with attribution methods to highlight input features representative of a NAP.
Slicing activations across different dimensions, such as classes, to find intra-class differences.
papers.abstract: A key to deciphering the inner workings of neural networks is understanding what a model has learned. Promising methods for discovering learned features are based on analyzing activation values, whereby current techniques focus on analyzing high activation values to reveal interesting features on a neuron level. However, analyzing high activation values limits layer-level concept discovery. We present a method that instead takes into account the entire activation distribution. By extracting similar activation profiles within the high-dimensional activation space of a neural network layer, we find groups of inputs that are treated similarly. These input groups represent neural activation patterns (NAPs) and can be used to visualize and interpret learned layer concepts. We release a framework with which NAPs can be extracted from pre-trained models and provide a visual introspection tool that can be used to analyze NAPs. We tested our method with a variety of networks and show how it complements existing methods for analyzing neural network activation values.

papers.title: Interpreting the Repeated Token Phenomenon in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Why do Large Language Models fail to accurately repeat a single word when prompted, and how is this linked to the attention sink phenomenon?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a mechanistic explanation for repeated token divergence in LLMs by linking it to attention sinks, identifies the responsible neural circuit, and proposes a targeted patch to mitigate the vulnerability without impacting overall performance.
papers.conclusion: The study links repeated token divergence to attention sinks via neural circuits, shows how first layer confusion leads to divergence, and demonstrates a mitigation patch that addresses the vulnerability while preserving model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated token divergence is caused by the attention sink mechanism, where the first token receives disproportionately high attention.
The first attention layer marks the first token, but fails to distinguish it from repeated tokens, leading to confusion.
Specific MLP neurons (sink neurons) amplify hidden states for attention sinks, and are also activated by repeated tokens.
A 'cluster attack' extends the vulnerability to similar tokens without exact repetition, bypassing surface-level defenses.
A targeted patch that modifies sink neuron activations effectively mitigates the divergence without significant performance loss on other tasks.
papers.limitation:
The mechanism by which training data leakage occurs through attention sinks remains unclear.
The first attention layer's behavior was unique to LLaMa2, highlighting model-specific details.
The efficacy of token repetition in inducing sinks varies across models.
Not all tokens in LLaMa2 induce attention sinks.
Due to difficulty in assessing training data leakage, the success rate of the cluster attack was not quantified.
The mitigation strategy does not fully address the inherent vulnerability of causally masked Transformers to repeated tokens.
future_direction: Investigate broader generalizability of the findings across more models.
Explain why repeated token sequences lead to training data extraction.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), despite their impressive capabilities, often fail to accurately repeat a single word when prompted to, and instead output unrelated text. This unexplained failure mode represents a vulnerability, allowing even end-users to diverge models away from their intended behavior. We aim to explain the causes for this phenomenon and link it to the concept of ``attention sinks'', an emergent LLM behavior crucial for fluency, in which the initial token receives disproportionately high attention scores. Our investigation identifies the neural circuit responsible for attention sinks and shows how long repetitions disrupt this circuit. We extend this finding to other non-repeating sequences that exhibit similar circuit disruptions. To address this, we propose a targeted patch that effectively resolves the issue without negatively impacting the model's overall performance. This study provides a mechanistic explanation for an LLM vulnerability, demonstrating how interpretability can diagnose and address issues, and offering insights that pave the way for more secure and reliable models.

papers.title: Characterizing Large Language Model Geometry Helps Solve Toxicity Detection and Generation
papers.research_question: What are the geometric properties of LLMs that best characterize the representations of a given prompt and generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric characterization of LLMs (MHA and MLP) that enables principled methods for bypassing RLHF protection and for toxicity detection using unsupervised features.
papers.conclusion: Geometric characterization of LLMs provides both theoretical insights and practical tools for safer AI, enabling the detection of toxic inputs and generations and exposing weaknesses in current RLHF methods.
papers.key_findings:
The output of the Multi-Head Attention (MHA) mapping lives in the Minkowski sum of convex hulls of embedded tokens, and its intrinsic dimension can be controlled via prompt manipulation.
Increasing the intrinsic dimension of the MHA embedding through informed prompt manipulation can bypass RLHF safeguards and induce toxic generation.
The MLP partitions the manifold induced by the MHA, and its expressivity grows exponentially with the MHA's intrinsic dimension.
A small set of unsupervised geometric features (spline features) extracted from pre-trained LLMs can effectively solve toxicity detection and domain classification tasks.
The proposed features achieve state-of-the-art performance on toxicity detection benchmarks with low latency and without requiring model fine-tuning.
papers.limitation: The proposed features perform aggressive dimensionality reduction and are likely most suited for coarse-grained tasks (such as toxicity and domain detection); finer-grained statistics may be required for other downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) drive current AI breakthroughs despite very little being known about their internal representations. In this work, we propose to shed the light on LLMs inner mechanisms through the lens of geometry. In particular, we develop in closed form $(i)$ the intrinsic dimension in which the Multi-Head Attention embeddings are constrained to exist and $(ii)$ the partition and per-region affine mappings of the feedforward (MLP) network of LLMs' layers. Our theoretical findings further enable the design of novel principled solutions applicable to state-of-the-art LLMs. First, we show that, through our geometric understanding, we can bypass LLMs' RLHF protection by controlling the embedding's intrinsic dimension through informed prompt manipulation. Second, we derive interpretable geometrical features that can be extracted from any (pre-trained) LLM, providing a rich abstract representation of their inputs. We observe that these features are sufficient to help solve toxicity detection, and even allow the identification of various types of toxicity. Our results demonstrate how, even in large-scale regimes, exact theoretical results can answer practical questions in LLMs. Code: https://github.com/RandallBalestriero/SplineLLM

papers.title: The Evolution of Representation in Simple Cognitive Networks
papers.research_question: How are representations developed in cognitive systems, and are they necessary for intelligent behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an information-theoretic measure of representation (R) and shows that the capacity to represent increases during evolutionary adaptation in simple cognitive networks.
papers.conclusion: The measure R can quantify representations in any cognitive system and should be predictive of an agent's long-term adaptive success.
papers.key_findings:
The representation measure R increases during evolutionary adaptation in both artificial neural networks and Markov brains.
Markov brains evolve to become less dependent on sensory inputs and more dependent on internal states than artificial neural networks.
Networks form representations of specific environmental features (concepts) and these representations are distributed across nodes.
Representations are formed over the lifetime of the agent, building up as the agent integrates information.
The evolved networks can be analyzed to determine which nodes represent which environmental features.
future_direction: Future investigations on what kind of system is more powerful for making intelligent decisions using representations.
papers.abstract: Representations are internal models of the environment that can provide guidance to a behaving agent, even in the absence of sensory information. It is not clear how representations are developed and whether they are necessary or even essential for intelligent behavior. We argue here that the ability to represent relevant features of the environment is the expected consequence of an adaptive process, give a formal definition of representation based on information theory, and quantify it with a measure R. To measure how R changes over time, we evolve two types of networks--an artificial neural network and a network of hidden Markov gates--to solve a categorization task using a genetic algorithm. We find that the capacity to represent increases during evolutionary adaptation and that agents form representations of their environment during their lifetime. This ability allows the agents to act on sensorial inputs in the context of their acquired representations and enables complex and context-dependent behavior. We examine which concepts (features of the environment) our networks are representing, how the representations are logically encoded in the networks, and how they form as an agent behaves to solve a task. We conclude that R should be able to quantify the representations within any cognitive system and should be predictive of an agent's long-term adaptive success.

papers.title: Backdoor Vectors: a Task Arithmetic View on Backdoor Attacks and Defenses
papers.research_question: How can backdoor attacks in model merging be understood, improved, and defended against using a task arithmetic perspective?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Backdoor Vectors (BVs) as a task arithmetic framework to understand, improve, and defend against backdoor attacks in model merging.
papers.conclusion: The Backdoor Vectors framework provides a simple yet powerful abstraction for backdoor attacks in model merging, enabling both stronger attacks and effective defenses.
papers.key_findings:
BV addition represents backdoor attack: adding a BV to a clean model injects a backdoor.
BVs have high transferability: adding a BV from another attack boosts the primary attack's success rate.
BV merging via Sparse Backdoor Vectors (SBVs) creates a stronger and more resilient attack.
BV subtraction can be used for defense via Injection BV Subtraction (IBVS), mitigating unknown backdoors.
The core vulnerability in model merging is inherent triggers that exploit adversarial weaknesses in the base model.
papers.limitation:
Assumes linear additivity of task vectors, which holds in linear connectivity regimes but may not generalize.
Focuses on CLIP-like vision models and image classification; applicability to other architectures (e.g., LLMs) is unexplored.
papers.abstract: Model merging (MM) recently emerged as an effective method for combining large deep learning models. However, it poses significant security risks. Recent research shows that it is highly susceptible to backdoor attacks, which introduce a hidden trigger into a single fine-tuned model instance that allows the adversary to control the output of the final merged model at inference time. In this work, we propose a simple framework for understanding backdoor attacks by treating the attack itself as a task vector. $Backdoor\ Vector\ (BV)$ is calculated as the difference between the weights of a fine-tuned backdoored model and fine-tuned clean model. BVs reveal new insights into attacks understanding and a more effective framework to measure their similarity and transferability. Furthermore, we propose a novel method that enhances backdoor resilience through merging dubbed $Sparse\ Backdoor\ Vector\ (SBV)$ that combines multiple attacks into a single one. We identify the core vulnerability behind backdoor threats in MM: $inherent\ triggers$ that exploit adversarial weaknesses in the base model. To counter this, we propose $Injection\ BV\ Subtraction\ (IBVS)$ - an assumption-free defense against backdoors in MM. Our results show that SBVs surpass prior attacks and is the first method to leverage merging to improve backdoor effectiveness. At the same time, IBVS provides a lightweight, general defense that remains effective even when the backdoor threat is entirely unknown.

papers.title: Ensuring Medical AI Safety: Interpretability-Driven Detection and Mitigation of Spurious Model Behavior and Associated Data
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be used to detect and mitigate spurious correlations (shortcut learning) in deep neural networks for medical AI, and how can bias annotation be semi-automated to reduce manual labeling effort?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends the Reveal2Revise framework with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities, enabling sample- and feature-level annotation of spurious correlations to reduce manual labeling and improve bias mitigation in medical AI models.
papers.conclusion: The interpretability-driven Reveal2Revise framework, enhanced with bias annotation capabilities, provides a comprehensive approach to improve medical AI safety by detecting and mitigating spurious model behavior, ultimately increasing model robustness for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
The extended Reveal2Revise framework successfully identifies and mitigates both controlled and real-world spurious correlations across four medical datasets and multiple model architectures.
The framework provides sample-level bias annotation via data retrieval using concept representations (e.g., CAVs) and feature-level annotation via spatial localization of artifacts.
Bias mitigation methods like RRR and RR-ClArC, when integrated with the framework, improve model robustness by reducing reliance on spurious features while maintaining accuracy on clean data.
The approach reduces the need for extensive manual annotation by domain experts, making bias detection and mitigation more practical.
The framework is applicable across different modalities (image and ECG) and model types (CNNs and Vision Transformers).
papers.limitation:
The framework requires human validation to distinguish between clinically valid and spurious outlier behavior.
Some artifacts are non-localizable (e.g., brightness shifts), limiting spatial bias localization.
Bias representations (e.g., CAVs) may be inaccurate if the initial set of biased samples is small or noisy.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other modalities and data types.
Improving the automation of bias detection and validation to further reduce human effort.
Integrating the framework with a wider range of bias mitigation techniques.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly employed in high-stakes medical applications, despite their tendency for shortcut learning in the presence of spurious correlations, which can have potentially fatal consequences in practice. Whereas a multitude of works address either the detection or mitigation of such shortcut behavior in isolation, the Reveal2Revise approach provides a comprehensive bias mitigation framework combining these steps. However, effectively addressing these biases often requires substantial labeling efforts from domain experts. In this work, we review the steps of the Reveal2Revise framework and enhance it with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities. This includes methods for the sample- and feature-level bias annotation, providing valuable information for bias mitigation methods to unlearn the undesired shortcut behavior. We show the applicability of the framework using four medical datasets across two modalities, featuring controlled and real-world spurious correlations caused by data artifacts. We successfully identify and mitigate these biases in VGG16, ResNet50, and contemporary Vision Transformer models, ultimately increasing their robustness and applicability for real-world medical tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/frederikpahde/medical-ai-safety.

papers.title: BiasEdit: Debiasing Stereotyped Language Models via Model Editing
papers.research_question: How to efficiently remove stereotypical bias from language models via model editing?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes BIAS EDIT, an efficient model editing method that uses lightweight editor networks to modify a small portion of language model parameters for debiasing, with a debiasing loss and a retention loss to preserve language modeling abilities.
papers.conclusion: BIAS EDIT is an efficient model editing method for debiasing stereotyped language models that preserves language modeling and general capabilities while being robust to gender reversal and semantic generality.
papers.key_findings:
BIAS EDIT achieves better debiasing performance (lower Stereotype Score) than previous baselines across multiple bias types and models.
BIAS EDIT has little to no negative impact on language modeling and general capabilities, as measured by LMS and accuracy on benchmark tasks.
The method is robust to gender reversal and semantic generality, meaning it generalizes to counterfactual and synonym-augmented inputs.
Editing upper blocks of the model has less negative impact on modeling abilities than editing bottom blocks.
The retention loss is crucial for maintaining language modeling abilities during debiasing.
papers.limitation: BIAS EDIT is only evaluated on sentence-level bias modeling examples with gold labels, and bias mitigation for text generation forms (e.g., QA, text continuation) is not addressed.
future_direction: Adapt BIAS EDIT and other model editing/unlearning methods to mitigate bias for text generation tasks.
Construct datasets for bias mitigation in text generation forms.

papers.title: Adaptive Circuit Behavior and Generalization in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How well does the indirect object identification (IOI) circuit in GPT-2 small generalize to prompt variants that challenge the assumptions of its algorithm?
papers.core_contribution: The IOI circuit generalizes surprisingly well to prompt variants, reusing all its components and mechanisms while only adding additional input edges, and a mechanism called S2 Hacking explains how the circuit outperforms the full model on these variants.
papers.conclusion: The IOI circuit in GPT-2 small generalizes more effectively than previously understood, reusing its core components and mechanisms while adapting through minimal structural changes, offering insights into the broader capabilities of large neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
The base IOI circuit outperforms the full model on DoubleIO and TripleIO prompt variants where the IOI algorithm would fail.
A mechanism termed S2 Hacking explains how the circuit achieves high performance on these variants by focusing on the S2 token due to the knockout procedure.
New circuits discovered for DoubleIO and TripleIO variants reuse all components of the base IOI circuit, only adding edges from additional input tokens (IO2 for DoubleIO, IO2 and IO3 for TripleIO).
The circuit components (attention heads) largely retain their functionalities from the base IOI task when evaluated on the variants.
The order of names in the prompt affects performance, with a 'first come, first serve' mechanism observed in a Previous Token head (2.2).
future_direction: a more detailed study of the duplicate suppression mechanism
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the inner workings of large neural networks by identifying circuits, or minimal subgraphs within the model that implement algorithms responsible for performing specific tasks. These circuits are typically discovered and analyzed using a narrowly defined prompt format. However, given the abilities of large language models (LLMs) to generalize across various prompt formats for the same task, it remains unclear how well these circuits generalize. For instance, it is unclear whether the models generalization results from reusing the same circuit components, the components behaving differently, or the use of entirely different components. In this paper, we investigate the generality of the indirect object identification (IOI) circuit in GPT-2 small, which is well-studied and believed to implement a simple, interpretable algorithm. We evaluate its performance on prompt variants that challenge the assumptions of this algorithm. Our findings reveal that the circuit generalizes surprisingly well, reusing all of its components and mechanisms while only adding additional input edges. Notably, the circuit generalizes even to prompt variants where the original algorithm should fail; we discover a mechanism that explains this which we term S2 Hacking. Our findings indicate that circuits within LLMs may be more flexible and general than previously recognized, underscoring the importance of studying circuit generalization to better understand the broader capabilities of these models.

papers.title: Multi-Granular Node Pruning for Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: How can we perform circuit discovery at multiple granularities (down to neurons) in a scalable way, overcoming the limitations of existing edge-pruning methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a node-level pruning framework for circuit discovery that operates at multiple granularities (from blocks to neurons) in a single optimization step, achieving higher efficiency and finer granularity than existing edge-pruning methods.
papers.conclusion: The node pruning approach is efficient and effective for circuit discovery, achieving substantial reductions in circuit size and number of retained attention heads, and suggests future work combining edge and node pruning for even more minimal circuits.
papers.key_findings:
The structure of discovered circuits depends on the task; for example, all MLP blocks are essential for the IOI task, while for the GT task, most MLPs can be removed.
Different component granularities exhibit varying susceptibility to compression; for instance, the outputs of MLP1 (Keys) can be sparsified to a much greater extent than those of MLP2 (Values).
The method identifies circuits that are smaller in nodes than those discovered by prior methods while maintaining task performance.
The method reveals that many neurons within components deemed important by coarse methods are actually irrelevant.
The method has a significantly lower memory footprint (5-10x) compared to baselines, as it does not require storing intermediate activations.
papers.limitation: The framework discovers node-level circuits but does not explicitly recover the interaction structure between nodes, such as which active nodes exchange information and the directionality of those interactions.
future_direction: Combining edge and node pruning in a hierarchical fashion
Developing a hybrid node and edge procedure to infer interaction structure
papers.abstract: Circuit discovery aims to identify minimal subnetworks that are responsible for specific behaviors in large language models (LLMs). Existing approaches primarily rely on iterative edge pruning, which is computationally expensive and limited to coarse-grained units such as attention heads or MLP blocks, overlooking finer structures like individual neurons. We propose a node-level pruning framework for circuit discovery that addresses both scalability and granularity limitations. Our method introduces learnable masks across multiple levels of granularity, from entire blocks to individual neurons, within a unified optimization objective. Granularity-specific sparsity penalties guide the pruning process, allowing a comprehensive compression in a single fine-tuning run. Empirically, our approach identifies circuits that are smaller in nodes than those discovered by prior methods; moreover, we demonstrate that many neurons deemed important by coarse methods are actually irrelevant, while still maintaining task performance. Furthermore, our method has a significantly lower memory footprint, 5-10x, as it does not require keeping intermediate activations in the memory to work.

papers.title: Your Language Model Secretly Contains Personality Subnetworks
papers.research_question: Do LLMs really need external context or parameters to adapt to different behaviors, or do they already have such knowledge embedded in their parameters?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that LLMs already contain persona-specialized subnetworks in their parameter space, and introduces a training-free, activation-guided pruning method to extract these subnetworks.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a train-free framework for extracting persona-specialized subnetworks from pretrained LLMs via activation-guided pruning, highlighting pruning as a practical approach for building efficient, controllable multi-persona systems without additional training.
papers.key_findings:
Distinct personas manifest as separable activation patterns in pretrained LLMs.
Activation-guided pruning can extract persona-specialized subnetworks without any gradient updates or training.
A contrastive pruning strategy explicitly maximizes parameter separation between opposing personas, enhancing behavioral disentanglement.
The extracted subnetworks achieve stronger persona alignment than prompting and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) baselines.
The pruning method preserves general language understanding and reasoning capabilities, with only minor performance degradation.
papers.limitation: The method exhibits uneven success across different persona dimensions; dimensions like N/S and J/P in MBTI have weaker mask-level separation and are more prone to collapse into adjacent types.
papers.abstract: Humans shift between different personas depending on social context. Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate a similar flexibility in adopting different personas and behaviors. Existing approaches, however, typically adapt such behavior through external knowledge such as prompting, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), or fine-tuning. We ask: do LLMs really need external context or parameters to adapt to different behaviors, or do they already have such knowledge embedded in their parameters? In this work, we show that LLMs already contain persona-specialized subnetworks in their parameter space. Using small calibration datasets, we identify distinct activation signatures associated with different personas. Guided by these statistics, we develop a masking strategy that isolates lightweight persona subnetworks. Building on the findings, we further discuss: how can we discover opposing subnetwork from the model that lead to binary-opposing personas, such as introvert-extrovert? To further enhance separation in binary opposition scenarios, we introduce a contrastive pruning strategy that identifies parameters responsible for the statistical divergence between opposing personas. Our method is entirely training-free and relies solely on the language model's existing parameter space. Across diverse evaluation settings, the resulting subnetworks exhibit significantly stronger persona alignment than baselines that require external knowledge while being more efficient. Our findings suggest that diverse human-like behaviors are not merely induced in LLMs, but are already embedded in their parameter space, pointing toward a new perspective on controllable and interpretable personalization in large language models.

papers.title: Circuit-Tracer: A New Library for Finding Feature Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we facilitate feature-circuit finding in LLMs? The paper introduces a library to make circuit analysis more accessible.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit-tracer, an open-source library for efficient identification, visualization, and intervention on feature circuits in LLMs, making circuit analysis more accessible.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents circuit-tracer, a library that enables efficient feature circuit tracing, and demonstrates its utility through case studies, aiming to facilitate future research in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.limitation:
Transcoder circuits often fail to capture features relevant to attention, as edge weights are conditioned on the attention pattern.
Transcoder errors can hinder interpretation when a large proportion of the flow through the graph originates from uninterpretable error nodes.
future_direction: Systematic study of safety-relevant phenomena such as chain of thought unfaithfulness, refusal, and jailbreaks using circuits.
Synthesizing multiple circuits into a coherent task mechanism.
Scaling feature annotation and supernode creation.
papers.abstract: Feature circuits aim to shed light on LLM behavior by identifying the features that are causally responsible for a given LLM output, and connecting them into a directed graph, or *circuit*, that explains how both each feature and each output arose. However, performing circuit analysis is challenging: the tools for finding, visualizing, and verifying feature circuits are complex and spread across multiple libraries.To facilitate feature-circuit finding, we introduce `circuit-tracer`, an open-source library for efficient identification of feature circuits. `circuit-tracer` provides an integrated pipeline for finding, visualizing, annotating, and performing interventions on such feature circuits, tested with various model sizes, up to 14B parameters. We make `circuit-tracer` available to both developers and end users, via integration with tools such as Neuronpedia, which provides a user-friendly interface.

papers.title: In-the-Wild Model Organisms: Mitigating Undesirable Emergent Behaviors in Production LLM Post-Training via Data Attribution
papers.research_question: How can we trace emergent harmful behaviors in post-trained language models back to responsible training data? And can we discover such behaviors without knowing what to look for?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces activation-based data attribution, a method that traces behavioral changes in post-trained language models to responsible training datapoints by computing and comparing activation-difference vectors, enabling targeted interventions and unsupervised discovery of emergent harmful behaviors.
papers.conclusion: Activation-based data attribution provides an effective and cost-efficient method for safety audits of post-training, enabling both targeted mitigation of known harmful behaviors and unsupervised discovery of unknown ones.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered 'distractor-triggered compliance' in OLMo 2, a harmful behavior where the model complies with dangerous requests when benign formatting instructions are appended.
Filtering top-ranked datapoints reduces the harmful behavior by 63% while switching their labels achieves a 78% reduction.
The method outperforms gradient-based attribution and LLM-judge baselines while being over 10× cheaper.
Unsupervised clustering of behavior-datapoint similarity matrices can surface emergent behavioral patterns without prior specification.
The behavior emerged from standard DPO training on a diverse preference dataset, providing a realistic 'in-the-wild' model organism for safety research.
papers.limitation:
Focus on a single model family (OLMo) and a single harmful behavior type.
Method requires access to post-training data and intermediate checkpoints for causal validation through retraining, which is not available for many models.
future_direction: Automating the identification of concerning clusters from unsupervised discovery.
Extending causal validation to other model families if they release comparable training artifacts.
Testing whether activation-based attribution extends to other post-training methods such as RLHF and SFT.
papers.abstract: We propose activation-based data attribution, a method that traces behavioral changes in post-trained language models to responsible training datapoints. By computing activation-difference vectors for both test prompts and preference pairs and ranking by cosine similarity, we identify datapoints that cause specific behaviors and validate these attributions causally by retraining with modified data. Clustering behavior-datapoint similarity matrices also enables unsupervised discovery of emergent behaviors. Applying this to OLMo 2's production DPO training, we surfaced distractor-triggered compliance: a harmful behavior where the model complies with dangerous requests when benign formatting instructions are appended. Filtering top-ranked datapoints reduces this behavior by 63% while switching their labels achieves 78%. Our method outperforms gradient-based attribution and LLM-judge baselines while being over 10 times cheaper than both. This in-the-wild model organism - emerging from contaminated preference data rather than deliberate injection - provides a realistic benchmark for safety techniques.

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analyses generalize well over both training and scale, suggesting that studies on small models at the end of pre-training can inform understanding of larger models and models with longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Task abilities and functional components (e.g., induction heads, name-mover heads) emerge consistently at similar token counts across different model scales.
The algorithm implemented by a circuit remains stable over training even when the specific attention heads implementing it change.
Circuit size correlates with model size and can fluctuate over time while the algorithm remains the same.
Components like induction heads emerge around 2B tokens across scales, paralleling task learning curves.
Circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training provide insights that generalize to larger models and longer training runs.
papers.limitation:
The study does not include fine-tuning or other post-training techniques.
Circuit completeness is challenging to verify.
The findings need validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
future_direction: Validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
Investigating the load-balancing mechanism that maintains task performance when components change.
papers.abstract: Most currently deployed large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous training or additional finetuning. By contrast, most research into LLMs' internal mechanisms focuses on models at one snapshot in time (the end of pre-training), raising the question of whether their results generalize to real-world settings. Existing studies of mechanisms over time focus on encoder-only or toy models, which differ significantly from most deployed models. In this study, we track how model mechanisms, operationalized as circuits, emerge and evolve across 300 billion tokens of training in decoder-only LLMs, in models ranging from 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters. We find that task abilities and the functional components that support them emerge consistently at similar token counts across scale. Moreover, although such components may be implemented by different attention heads over time, the overarching algorithm that they implement remains. Surprisingly, both these algorithms and the types of components involved therein can replicate across model scale. These results suggest that circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training can provide insights that still apply after additional pre-training and over model scale.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Understanding of Alignment Algorithms: A Case Study on DPO and Toxicity
papers.research_question: How does the alignment algorithm DPO reduce toxicity in language models, and what are the mechanisms by which it does so?
papers.core_contribution: DPO reduces toxicity not by removing toxic capabilities but by learning an offset in the residual stream to bypass toxic regions, and this alignment can be easily undone.
papers.conclusion: Alignment algorithms like DPO work by bypassing undesirable capabilities rather than removing them, which explains the vulnerability to jailbreaks.
papers.key_findings:
Toxicity is represented by specific value vectors in MLP blocks of GPT2-medium.
DPO does not remove these toxic vectors; instead, it learns a distributed offset in the residual stream to avoid activating them.
The offset is achieved through minimal weight changes across many value vectors in earlier layers.
Alignment can be undone by scaling toxic key vectors, reactivating toxic behavior.
The findings provide a mechanistic explanation for why aligned models can be jailbroken.
future_direction: Designing robust alignment algorithms that eliminate undesirable regions instead of bypassing them.
Updating only specific weights (e.g., toxic vectors) or only bias terms during alignment.
Adding 'suppression heads' or updating late layers to suppress undesirable behavior.
Characterizing 'jailbreak-ability' without relying on test samples.
Studying the role of KL-divergence regularization in distributed vs. localized changes.
papers.abstract: While alignment algorithms are now commonly used to tune pre-trained language models towards a user's preferences, we lack explanations for the underlying mechanisms in which models become ``aligned'', thus making it difficult to explain phenomena like jailbreaks. In this work we study a popular algorithm, direct preference optimization (DPO), and the mechanisms by which it reduces toxicity. Namely, we first study how toxicity is represented and elicited in a pre-trained language model, GPT2-medium. We then apply DPO with a carefully crafted pairwise dataset to reduce toxicity. We examine how the resulting model averts toxic outputs, and find that capabilities learned from pre-training are not removed, but rather bypassed. We use this insight to demonstrate a simple method to un-align the model, reverting it back to its toxic behavior.

papers.title: Fairness Mediator: Neutralize Stereotype Associations to Mitigate Bias in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to effectively and efficiently mitigate stereotype associations (biases) in large language models by neutralizing the associations between biased concepts and social groups encoded in the MLP layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Fairness Mediator (FairMed), a framework that neutralizes stereotype associations in LLMs by probing and adversarially intervening in MLP activations during inference, achieving state-of-the-art bias reduction with high efficiency and without compromising language understanding.
papers.conclusion: FairMed effectively and efficiently mitigates bias in LLMs by neutralizing stereotype associations encoded in MLP layers, without compromising the model's language understanding capabilities, thus promoting fairer behavior.
papers.key_findings:
FairMed significantly reduces bias, achieving average reductions of up to 84.42% for sDIS and 80.36% for sAMB on LLaMA-2-Chat 7B across the BBQ benchmark.
FairMed is highly efficient, reducing training time from hundreds of minutes (e.g., 907.70 minutes for CDA) to 2.28 minutes while maintaining competitive inference time (0.152s vs. 0.175s).
FairMed maintains the LLM's language understanding capabilities, with no significant drop in MMLU performance, whereas other methods like CDA cause an average drop of 1.83%.
Stereotype associations are encoded in specific MLP layer activations, primarily in the middle and deeper layers, as empirically demonstrated.
FairMed generalizes to other models (BERT, BART) and benchmarks (BiasAsker, Adult), showing its effectiveness and broad applicability.
papers.limitation: Over-correction in some disambiguated questions leads to a drop in accuracy, as the model may incorrectly change a stereotypical but correct answer to an incorrect one.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance across diverse applications, yet they inadvertently absorb spurious correlations from training data, leading to stereotype associations between biased concepts and specific social groups. These associations perpetuate and even amplify harmful social biases, raising significant concerns about fairness, which is a crucial issue in software engineering. To mitigate such biases, prior studies have attempted to project model embeddings into unbiased spaces during inference. However, these approaches have shown limited effectiveness due to their weak alignment with downstream social biases. Inspired by the observation that concept cognition in LLMs is primarily represented through a linear associative memory mechanism, where key-value mapping occurs in the MLP layers, we posited that biased concepts and social groups are similarly encoded as entity (key) and information (value) pairs, which can be manipulated to promote fairer associations. To this end, we propose Fairness Mediator (FairMed), an effective and efficient bias mitigation framework that neutralizes stereotype associations. Our framework comprises two main components: a stereotype association prober and an adversarial debiasing neutralizer. The prober captures stereotype associations encoded within MLP layer activations by employing prompts centered around biased concepts (keys) to detect the emission probabilities for social groups (values). Subsequently, the adversarial debiasing neutralizer intervenes in MLP activations during inference to equalize the association probabilities among different social groups. Extensive experiments across nine protected attributes show that our FairMed significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in effectiveness, achieving average bias reductions of up to 84.42

papers.title: Characteristics of dissociable human learning systems
papers.abstract: Abstract A number of ways of taxonomizing human learning have been proposed. We examine the evidence for one such proposal, namely, that there exist independent explicit and implicit learning systems. This combines two further distinctions, (1) between learning that takes place with versus without concurrent awareness, and (2) between learning that involves the encoding of instances (or fragments) versus the induction of abstract rules or hypotheses. Implicit learning is assumed to involve unconscious rule learning. We examine the evidence for implicit learning derived from subliminal learning, conditioning, artificial grammar learning, instrumental learning, and reaction times in sequence learning. We conclude that unconscious learning has not been satisfactorily established in any of these areas. The assumption that learning in some of these tasks (e.g., artificial grammar learning) is predominantly based on rule abstraction is questionable. When subjects cannot report the “implicitly learned” rules that govern stimulus selection, this is often because their knowledge consists of instances or fragments of the training stimuli rather than rules. In contrast to the distinction between conscious and unconscious learning, the distinction between instance and rule learning is a sound and meaningful way of taxonomizing human learning. We discuss various computational models of these two forms of learning.

papers.title: Implicit assumptions about implicit learning
papers.abstract: A number of ways of taxonomizing human learning have been proposed. We examine the evidence for one such proposal, namely, that there exist independent explicit and implicit learning systems. This combines two further distinctions, (1) between learning that takes place with versus without concurrent awareness, and (2) between learning that involves the encoding of instances (or fragments) versus the induction of abstract rules or hypotheses. Implicit learning is assumed to involve unconscious rule learning. We examine the evidence for implicit learning derived from subliminal learning, conditioning, artificial grammar learning, instrumental learning, and reaction times in sequence learning. We conclude that unconscious learning has not been satisfactorily established in any of these areas. The assumption that learning in some of these tasks (e.g., artificial grammar learning) is predominantly based on rule abstraction is questionable. When subjects cannot report the "implicitly learned" rules that govern stimulus selection, this is often because their knowledge consists of instances or fragments of the training stimuli rather than rules. In contrast to the distinction between conscious and unconscious learning, the distinction between instance and rule learning is a sound and meaningful way of taxonomizing human learning. We discuss various computational models of these two forms of learning.

papers.title: Social cues can impact complex behavior unconsciously
papers.abstract: In three experiments, we investigated the effect of unconscious social priming on human behavior in a choice reaction time task. Photographs of a basketball player passing a ball to the left/right were used as target stimuli. Participants had to respond to the pass direction either by a whole-body (complex) response or a button-press (simple) response. Visually masked stimuli, showing both a task-relevant cue (pass direction) and a task-irrelevant, social cue (gaze direction), were used as primes. Subliminal social priming was found for kinematic (center of pressure) and chronometric measures (response times): gaze direction in the primes affected responses to the pass direction in the targets. The social priming effect diminished when gaze information was unhelpful or even detrimental to the task. Social priming of a complex behavior does not require awareness or intentionality, indicating automatic processing. Nevertheless, it can be controlled by top-down, strategic processes.

papers.title: The power of the cognitive unconscious: The case of implicit learning
papers.abstract: The present paper highlights the power of unconscious processes within the framework of implicit learning, a research area that has attracted extensive attention in the past decades. More specifically, it discusses theoretical issues concerning this multifaceted type of learning that occurs without conscious awareness and presents various applications in different learning settings and research domains, and in varied populations. Another main focus of this review is on recent advances in our understanding of the factors that affect implicit learning, including motives, attention, affective states, and general knowledge. The paper ends with conclusions and general principles drawn from research on a phenomenon with extended applications both in the lab and in everyday life and underlines the necessity for further research that will refine our methods of distinguishing conscious and unconscious processes and provide answers to unresolved issues and contradictory findings.

papers.title: The Biological Bases of Conformity
papers.abstract: Humans are characterized by an extreme dependence on culturally transmitted information and recent formal theory predicts that natural selection should favor adaptive learning strategies that facilitate effective copying and decision making. One strategy that has attracted particular attention is conformist transmission, defined as the disproportionately likely adoption of the most common variant. Conformity has historically been emphasized as significant in the social psychology literature, and recently there have also been reports of conformist behavior in non-human animals. However, mathematical analyses differ in how important and widespread they expect conformity to be, and relevant experimental work is scarce, and generates findings that are both mutually contradictory and inconsistent with the predictions of the models. We review the relevant literature considering the causation, function, history, and ontogeny of conformity, and describe a computer-based experiment on human subjects that we carried out in order to resolve ambiguities. We found that only when many demonstrators were available and subjects were uncertain was subject behavior conformist. A further analysis found that the underlying response to social information alone was generally conformist. Thus, our data are consistent with a conformist use of social information, but as subjects' behavior is the result of both social and asocial influences, the resultant behavior may not be conformist. We end by relating these findings to an embryonic cognitive neuroscience literature that has recently begun to explore the neural bases of social learning.
